props.content:
The Divya Desams are defined explicitly as shrines where the divine saints known as Azhwars have sung hymns of praise, also known as Mangalaasasanam. These Azhwars are considered to be Amsams (manifestations) of Sriman Narayanan himself.
There are a total of 108 Divya Desams. Of these, 106 are located on Earth (105 in
India, 1 in Nepal), while the remaining two are celestial abodes: Thiruppārkadal (the
Ocean of Milk) and Paramapadam (Vaikuntham).

Understanding the Azhwars and Their Devotion:
A unique insight into the Azhwars reveals that "Not all Āzhwārs lived at the same time.".
While some, like Periyāzhwār and Āṇḍāḷ, or Nammāzhwār and Madhurakavi, knew each other, others lived centuries apart. Their immersion in divine bhakti transcended timelines, as they expressed their spiritual experiences through poetry.
A profound principle regarding the Azhwars is that "Quantity Doesn’t Equal Status." It is emphasized that "It’s about depth of devotion, not number of verses". For instance, while Nammāzhwār and Tirumaṅgai Āzhwār composed over 1000 Pasurams, Madhurakavi Āzhwār composed only 11. Significantly, Madhurakavi Āzhwār's verses
were not even on Perumāḷ (Lord Vishnu) but on his Āchārya, Nammāzhwār. Despite
this, "each is revered equally", underscoring the qualitative nature of their devotion.
It is also crucial to distinguish Āzhwārs from other deeply revered figures like Kūrattāzhwān, Chakrattāzhwān, or Prahlāda Āzhwān. While these figures are indeed revered, they are "not part of the 12 canonical Āzhwārs". The title "Āzhwār" refers explicitly to "one who is fully immersed—āzhndu pōnavaṛku—in Perumāḷ-bhakti".

The twelve canonical Azhwars are:
1. Poigai Azhwar (7th Century AD, Kanchipuram, Amsam: Panchajanya/Conch)
2. Bhoothath Azhwar (7th Century AD, Mahabalipuram, Amsam:
Kaumodakee/Mace)
3. Pey Azhwar (7th Century AD, Mylapore, Amsam: Nandhagam/Sword)
(Poigai Azhwar, Bhootath Azhwar, and Pey Azhwar are collectively known as Mudhal
Azhwars).
4. Tirumazhisai Azhwar (7th Century AD, Thirumazhisai, Amsam:
Sudarsanam/Discus)
5. Tirumangai Azhwar (8th Century AD, Thiru Kurayalur, Amsam: Sharngam/Bow)
6. Tondaradipodi Azhwar (8th Century AD, Thirumandangudi, Amsam:
Vanamaalai/Garland)
7. Tiruppan Azhwar (8th Century AD, Uraiyur, Amsam: Srivatsam)
8. Kulasekhara Azhwar (8th Century AD, Thirvanjikkolam, Amsam:
Kaustubham/Gem Necklace)
9. Periya Azhwar (9th Century AD, Sri Villiputhur, Amsam: Garuda/Chariot/Vehicle)
10.Sri Andaal (9th Century AD, Sri Villiputhur, Amsam: Bhoodevi)
11. Nammaazhwar (9th Century AD, Azhwar Thirunagari/Kurugoor, Amsam:
Viswaksenar/Commander of Army)
12.Madhurakavi Azhwar (9th Century AD, Thirukollur, Amsam: Vainatheya/Garuda)

Compilation of Pasurams (Hymns):
The Azhwars composed their divine hymns, collectively known as Naalayira Divya Prabandham, in adoration of the deities of the 108 Divya Desams. These verses, in simple Tamil, encapsulate the essence of the Vedas, Upanishads, and Vyasa's Brahmasutras. It was the scholar-saint Nathamuni, in the 10th century, who diligently retrieved and compiled this treasure of bhakti literature. The Sri Vaishnava guru parampara (lineage of preceptors) begins with Lord Sri Narayana himself and centers around Sri Nathamuni and his grandson Sri Yamunacharya. Nathamuni specifically compiled the works of Azhwars upon listening to the Tamil hymn “Aravamude,”
composed by Nammazhwar, at the Tirukudandai temple.
Understanding how Āzhwārs' verses were linked to specific temples is a result of
scholarly effort. As Āzhwārs "never kept a diary" and "sang and moved on," scholars
like Periyavāchān Piḷḷai meticulously identified terms like “Kozhi” as Uraiyūr, linking
verses to temples. This mapping process sometimes resulted in "Some temples appear
multiple times" within the compiled Pasurams.
Postures of Presiding Deities:
The presiding deities in these Divya Desams are found in various Thirukkolams
(postures):
● Reclining posture (Kidantha Thirukkolam) in 27 Divyadesams
● Sitting posture (Veetrirundha Thirukkolam) in 21 Divyadesams
● Standing posture (Nindra Thirukkolam) in 60 Divyadesams

An interesting note on posture classification is that "Such temples challenge neat classification by posture or Āzhwār," as exemplified by Thirunēermalai, which uniquely "features four forms of the Lord: Standing (nindra-kolam), Sitting (irunda-kolam),
Reclining (kidantha-kolam), and Walking (nādandha-kolam)".

Geographical Classification of Divya Desams:
The regional classification of Divya Desams into logical groups is attributed to "Swāmi
Pillai Perumāl Iyengar’s Insight." This revered Āchārya "proposed a geographic
framework based on rivers and ancient kingdoms". The 108 Divya Desams are thus
categorized as follows:
● Chola Nādu: 40 Divya Desams
● Tondai Nādu: 22 Divya Desams
● Pandya Nādu: 18 Divya Desams
● Malai Nādu (Kerala): 13 Divya Desams
● Vada Nādu: 11 Divya Desams
● Nadu Nādu: 2 Divya Desams
● Vinnulaga Tirupatigal (Celestial): 2 Divya Desams (Thiruppārkadal and Paramapadam)

Vaishnava Agamas and Branches:
The Agamas are texts derived from the Vedas, detailing various forms and methods of worship. The Sri Vaishnava Sampradaya recognizes two authoritative Agamas:
Pancharatra Agama and Vaikhanasa Agama. 
Pancharatra is considered the primary source of authority for Sri Vaishnavas and is believed to have been revealed by Lord Vishnu Himself. It took five days for the Lord to teach this method of worship, hence the name Pancharatra, meaning "work of the five nights". Vaikhanasa Agama is primarily utilized for temple worship and is restricted to a specific group of Vedic priests. While
Pancharatra is more universal and widely used to propagate Vishnu worship among the masses, the Kerala Tantram is followed in Divyadesams in Malainadu, and Badrinath follows a protocol established by Adi Sankaracharya.
Within the Srivaishnava school, two main branches emerged after Sri Ramanuja:
Vadakalai (Northern) and Tenkalai (Southern). Although named geographically, there is no real geographical polarization. This distinction likely arose from the former emphasizing the Sanskrit Vedas (prevalent in North India) and the latter stressing the importance of the Tamil Divya Prabandhams (commonplace in South India). Despite these philosophical differences, "both in temple worship and in the hearths and homes, the two streams have been so integrated and observed by both the branches". Swami Sri Vedanta Desika is often associated with the Vadakalai sect. Still, his monumental
works in both Sanskrit and Tamil suggest he and his followers could be more accurately termed 'Ubhaya Kalai' (both Kalais).

Significance of "Perumal":
The Tamil word "Perumal" is used in the Vaishnava tradition to denote both the
Supreme Divinity and the idol (archa) of the Divine. The word combines "perum"
(meaning 'the great,' 'the gigantic,' 'the supreme') and "al" (meaning 'personality'),
corresponding to the Sanskrit term 'purushottama'.

Current State of Temples:
While kings and local rulers historically patronized these temples with funds and jewelry for their upkeep, maintenance, and the conduct of Utsavams, it is regrettable that presently some of these temples are neglected, and funds are often squandered. Many temples now rely heavily on philanthropists, visiting pilgrims, and devotees, or bhaktas, for financial support to conduct even their daily rituals. Fortunately, members of several Vaishnava and religious groups are taking supportive steps by choosing a temple of their choice to organize the conduct of Nitya pooja for a day, and participating in the rituals. Your kainkaryam (voluntary service) in this direction, in any form, is welcome.

Sthala Puranam : 
The idol as we see it today is said to have originated from the milky oceans of Sri Vaikuntham. Lord Brahma then took the idol to worship, and for many eons, was worshipped by Lord Brahma in Satyalokam. A time came when the great king Ikshvaku approached Lord Brahma and asked him to install the idol of the Lord in Bhoolokam. Considering the king’s request, Lord Brahma obliged and installed the idol of the Lord along with the Pranavaakara Vimanam at Ayodhya, along the banks of the river Saryu. The Lord then remained in Ayodhya even till Lord Rama was the king of Ayodhya. After the battle with Ravana, the Lord returned to Ayodhya to be coronated formally. Here, he gifted all his army generals with something unique and meaningful. When Vibishana’s turn came during the distribution of divine gifts after Lord Rama’s victory over Ravana, he humbly requested Lord Rama to give him the idol of Sri Ranganathar so that he could take it back to Lanka for worship. Lord Rama, recognizing Vibishana's unwavering devotion and righteousness, agreed without hesitation. Thus, the divine idol, along with the Pranavakara Vimanam—a sanctified structure shaped in the form of the sacred syllable Pranavam (a-u-m)—was entrusted to Vibishana, who then began his journey southward aboard the Pushpaka Vimanam. As Vibishana reached the sacred banks of the river Cauvery, it was the auspicious month of Panguni. According to the ancient traditions upheld by Lord Rama and his Ikshvaku lineage, this period marked the celebration of the grand Brahmotsavam festival. In reverence to this dharmic custom, Vibishana paused his journey and conducted a nine-day festival in honor of the Lord on the riverbank. During the course of these festivities, the idol and the Pranavakara Vimanam were placed at a site later known as Sesha Peetam, near the sacred tank Chandrapushkarani. But when Vibishana attempted to resume his journey, he found the Vimanam immovable—it had firmly anchored itself to the earth. Overcome with grief and confusion, Vibishana was then graced with a divine vision of Lord Vishnu, who appeared before him. The Lord consoled His devotee, declaring that He had chosen this very spot to be His eternal abode. He assured Vibishana that although He would remain in Bharata Varsha, He would face southward toward Lanka as a mark of blessing and everlasting connection. Touched by this revelation, Vibishana accepted the divine will with devotion and humility. It is believed that to this day, Vibishana comes at midnight to offer his prayers to Lord Ranganathar in an invisible, celestial form. Thus, the reclining Lord of Srirangam, ensconced in the Pranavakara Vimanam that embodies the essence of the Pranavam (a-u-m), took His place on the banks of the Cauvery by His own will. This sacred event established Srirangam as the foremost among the 108 Divya Desams—a sanctum where divine grace, eternal dharma, and boundless devotion converge. This temple is enormous in size and is the largest temple complex, spanning 156 acres, surrounded by seven concentric walls (the outermost wall has a perimeter of over 3 km) and 21 gopurams. It has seven Prakarams or Tiru Veedhis surrounding the sanctum, with a total length of approximately 9 km. The 236-foot-high, thirteen-tiered Rajagopuram, built at the southern rampart, is a notable recent addition. It is significant that Ramanuja completely overhauled the administrative system in this temple. The physical remains of Ramanuja, who lived for nearly 120 years, are still preserved in a sitting posture in the sannidhi dedicated to him on the southwest corner of the fifth prakaram. Furthermore, Arayar Sevai, an ancient art form that involves rendering and expressing the Naalaayira Divya Prabandham through dance, originated at this kshethram under the auspices of Nathamuni. *Swayamvyaktha kshethram, according to the Sri Vaishnavas There are certain idols of the Lord that nobody has carved, or there is no godly origin, sagely origin, or humane origin to the idols, as the Lord Himself has incarnated into these places. The list of these kshethrams is as follows: 
1) Vanamamalai 
2) Sri Rangam 
3) Sri Mushnam 
4) Tirumala 
5) Naimisharanyam (as a forest)
 6) Pushkar (as water) 
7) Badri 
8) Muktinath

Sthala Puranam:
There was once a Chozha king by the name Dharmavarman who lived in Kumbakonam. Once, when the king had gone on a hunting trip, he found that a few rishis were distressed by the attack of demons and sought the king's help to kill them. The king bravely defended the rishis and stayed in the forest for some time to look after the welfare of the rishis. At this time, the king was saddened by his inability to father any children. The rishis then performed a yajna to help the king in his time of difficulty. As the rishis were performing the yajna, a voice boomed from the sky, stating that if the king wanted children, he must pray to Goddess Lakshmi. Thus, the king prayed to Goddess Lakshmi. One day, as he was going through the forest, he noticed a very peculiar lotus blooming in a pond. Upon further inspection, he saw that the lotus had a thousand petals, and in the center, a beautiful baby girl was nestled. Goddess Lakshmi had answered the king’s prayers by reincarnating herself as the baby girl. As she was found in a lotus, Dharmavarman named the child Kamalavalli.
Here, the meaning of Kamala can be interpreted as Ka meaning Paramathma, Ma meaning the Jeevathma, and La meaning the one who helps reach. Therefore, Kamala means she who leads the Jeevathma to the Paramathma to attain moksham. Soon, a time came when Dharmavarman began to seek a suitor for Kamalavalli. Among the men in the swayamwaram, Lord Ranganathar of Sri Rangam was present. Seeing the Lord, Kamalavalli immediately garlanded the Lord. The Lord then left a form of Himself in the form of Sri Azhagiya Manavalan there in his stead. Thus, all the people gathered at the event witnessed the grand spectacle of the wedding of the Lord with Goddess Lakshmi.
During the Panguni Brahmotsavam in Sri Rangam, on the sixth day, the Lord travels to Urayur to marry Sri Lakshmi. Thus, between the two kshethrams, there is only one utsava moorthy. This kshethram does not conduct Brahmotsavam on its own.

Sthala Puranam:
The name of the kshethram is Tirukarambanur. This is because the Lord showed Himself to Maharishi Kadambha. Additionally, the Lord had taken the form of a Kadambha tree, to which Lord Brahma used to perform aaradhanam by pouring holy water from his kamandalam. Another story associated with this kshethram is similar to that of Tirukandiyoor. It is said that Lord Brahma once had five heads. In a rage, Lord Shiva once slapped Lord Brahma’s fifth head, as he also had five heads, and it stuck to his hand as a curse. The only way the Bramhakapalam falls from one’s hand is to beg for alms, and for that to fill up the kapalam. In his search for alms, Lord Shiva reached Karambanur. Here, when he begged Poornavalli thayaar for alms, the kapalam burst, and Lord Shiva was free of the curse. Thus, it is said that people without a means of obtaining food can come here to pray to Poornavalli Thayar to gain her blessings.
* This is said to be the only temple where one can see the Trinity with their wives all under the same temple. There are temples where one can see Lord Vishnu, Lord Brahma, and Lord Shiva together. However, this is the only temple where you will see Lord Vishnu with Poornavalli Thayaar (Lakshmi), Lord Brahma with Saraswati, and Lord Shiva with Parvati.

Prathyaksham To: Shibi Chakravarthy, Markandeya Maharishi, Brahma, and Rudran

Sthala Puranam:
It is said that Shibi Chakravarthy, the grandson of Yayati, a ruler of Ayodhya belonging to the Chandravamsham dynasty, once undertook a trip to South India. One night, he decided to stay at the place known as Shwetagiri, which in Sanskrit translates to a hill with white rocks. Shwetagiri in Tamizh may be split as Vella+Arai, which means white hill. One night during his stay, Shibi Chakravarthy’s army chieftain complained that a wild white boar was running around and causing trouble to the army. Hearing this, the king ordered its capture. A few days passed, and the army chieftain came back with a complaint, saying the boar would magically disappear as they got close to catching it. Hearing this, Shibi Chakravarthy himself decided to go after the boar. He took his bow and set out in search of the animal. As he was searching, he saw the boar and began pursuing it. As he chased after the boar in the forest, he saw Sage Markandeya in penance. Seeing the sage, Shibi Chakravarthy offered his respects and went to inquire of the great sage if he had seen a wild boar pass by. The sage immediately directed the king to an anthill near the tree where he was meditating. He tells the king that he was in penance, waiting for the day the king would arrive seeking out a boar. He hands the king a pitcher of milk and asks him to pour the milk down the anthill. The king follows the sage’s instructions and does as he says. As the king poured the milk down the anthill, it began to melt, revealing a beautiful idol of Lord Pundarikakshan. The king wasted no time in installing the idol of the Lord into a temple. Sage Markandeya then tells the king that he should bring three thousand seven hundred Vaishnavas from his kingdom and help them to settle down here. The king immediately returned to Ayodhya and, according to the sage’s instructions, found three thousand seven hundred Vaishnavas and brought them to the temple. As Shibi counted the number of Vaishnavas that he had brought, he discovered that one of them had mysteriously vanished. The Lord then appeared in the king’s dream, saying He was one among the three thousand seven hundred, and told the king that he wanted to experience firsthand what bhakti felt like. In the Garbhagriha, we can see the Lord holding a prayoga chakram, along with His consorts, Sridevi and Bhoodevi, as well as Sooryan, Chandhran, Garudan, and Aadiseshan.

Sthala Puranam:
Legend has it that the Lord Brahma and Valmiki worshipped the Lord at this kshethram. Another story tells the episode of Mandooka Maharishi. Mandooka Maharishi earned his name as he would perform penance in cold water, holding his breath for extended periods. Once, when he was in deep penance, Maharishi Durvasa visited the water body. When Mandooka Maharishi did not notice his presence, Maharishi Durvasa cursed Mandooka Maharishi that he would take the form of a toad. Upon worshipping the Lord at this kshethram, the curse was said to be broken, and he regained his human form. Hence, the pushkarani at this kshethram is named Mandooka-Pushkarani.

Prathyaksham: Upamanyu, Markandeya Maharishi

Sthala Puranam:
Once King Upamanyu (Pandya King) had gone hunting in the forest to hunt a rogue elephant, he accidentally killed a brahmin who was performing tapas by the banks of a river. In repentance for his act, the king renounced his throne and began roaming the vast expanse of his former kingdom. When the king reached Tiruperrnagar, Lord Shiva appeared in front of the king and told him to serve food to a  thousand brahmins daily with appam. The king started to follow the instructions that he had received. One day, Lord Vishnu decided to participate in the king’s daily meal service. The Lord came in the disguise of a brahmin and approached the king, saying He was very hungry and asked that He be fed. The king asked the brahmin to wait until he had fed the remaining brahmins who had assembled before Him. The Lord was very strong with His claim and demanded that He be fed first. The king obliged and served the brahmin food.
To the king’s astonishment, the brahmin ate all the food that was prepared for the gathered thousand brahmins. The king then asked the brahmin if he was satisfied with the meal. The Brahmin said he was still hungry and asked the king to give him an appam, as it had not been served to him. No sooner had the king obtained a pitcher (kudam) with the appam than the Brahmin snatched the kudam from the king’s hands. Immediately, the Lord turned into an idol reclining on Adiseshan, putting his hand inside the kudam. Hence, the Lord gained the name Appa Kuduthan. At the same time, Markandeya Maharishi was directed by Lord Shiva to pray to Lord Vishnu for the gift of longevity. When Markandeya Maharishi reached the kshethram, the Lord removed his hand from the kudam and blessed him with the longevity of life and also relieved the king of his Brahmahatidosham.
Another story tells the tale of Kamalavalli Thayaar asking the Lord to get her Parijaatham flowers. Parijaatham flowers are divine flowers that grow in the gardens of Indra. When the Lord approached Indra to obtain some flowers for Thayaar, Indra refused to acknowledge that the Paarijatham was a divine flower and did not belong in Bhoolokam. He further tried to hurl the Vajraayudham on the Lord when the Lord was persistent with His request. The Lord, in his shayanam, raised his left hand and plucked the Vajraayudham from Indra’s hand. Indra then provided the flowers, consisting of defeat at the Lord’s hands. Thus, the vimanam and pushkarani here are named in Indra’s honor as he provided the Parijaatham.

Sthala Puranam:
 It is said that Ambareesha was such an ardent devotee that the Sudharshana Chakra had made himself self-obligated to rush for Ambareesha’s protection. One day, the great sage Durvasa decided to pay a visit to Ambareesha. Ambareesha had undertaken the Dwadashi-Vratam, in which one must break the fast after Ekadashi and feed their people at the start of Dwadashi. Durvasa Maharishi told Ambareesha that he would take a bath and then join him in the Dwadashi-Vratam. Ambareesha agreed to wait for Durvasa Maharishi. Hours went by, but Durvasa Maharishi was nowhere to be seen. On the advice of Sage Vasishta, Ambareesha broke his fast by taking holy water. At this moment, Durvasa Maharishi arrived and, in his temper, threw a lock of his hair to the ground. This hair grew into a monstrous demon that chased Ambareesha to devour him. At this moment, the Sudharshana Chakra of the Lord came to Ambareesha’s rescue and cut the demon into tiny pieces. Further, the Chakra started to chase after Durvasa Maharishi. Durvasa Maharishi began to run and sought refuge with Lord Brahma, Lord Shiva, and ultimately at the heavenly abode of Lord Vishnu himself. Still, the Chakra continued to pursue Durvasa Maharishi. Lord Vishnu instructed Durvasa Maharishi to go and fall at Ambareesha’s feet and ask for his forgiveness. Durvasa Maharishi then falls at Ambareesha’s feet for his forgiveness. Ambareesha forgives Durvasa Maharishi, and the Sudharshana Chakra stops going after Durvasa Maharishi. It is said that 
Ambareesha used to pray to this Lord, and with this Lord’s grace, he was protected.

Azhwar Pasuram: 
Tirumangai Azhwar- 1 pasuram

Pratyaksham: Hanuman and Gajendran

Sthala Puranam:
It is said that Lord Hanuman had performed tapas at this kshethram. When the Lord appeared in front of him, Lord Hanuman asked the Lord to re-enact the scene of Gajendra Moksham. 

The story of Gajendra Moksham is as follows. King Indradyumna was a renowned ruler of the Pandya Dynasty. It is said that he was the one who constructed the Puri Jagannath Temple. One day, the King was engaged in deep meditation when Sage Agastya visited the Kingdom and sought hospitality from the king. The King was so deep in his meditation that he overlooked the Sage. The sage got irritated and cursed the king, saying he would be reborn as an elephant. Similarly, a Gandharva named Huhu was cursed by Sage Devala to turn into a crocodile as he attempted to break the Sage’s penance. Many years passed, and King Indradyumna reincarnated as an elephant who had once been the ruler of an elephant herd on the Mountain of Trikuta. Gajendra used to visit a lake on the mountain daily and offer the Lord a lotus as dakshina every day. On one such visit to the lake, a crocodile caught Gajendra’s leg. This crocodile was none other than the cursed Huhu. Gajendra started to wail in pain and called out to the Lord by holding up a lotus that he had just plucked to give to the Lord. Gajendra referred to the Lord as “Aadhimoola” and called out a plea for help. All the gods saw Gajendra's plight, but when they heard the call, Aadhimoola refused to help him as they were not qualified to do justice to that title. It is said that as soon as Lord Sriman Narayana heard the call of the devotee, he didn’t even wait for Garuda. He ran at the top of his speed, and soon Garuda caught up and took the Lord to the Trikuta mountain, where the Lord’s Sudarshana Chakra had already taken off, even before he could release it. The chakra killed the crocodile and released Huhu from the curse. It is also said that the lotus held by the Lord is the same Lotus that Gajendra presented to the Lord that day. Following this, Gajendra was granted moksham.

Details of Kshethram:
Moolavar: Valvil Ramar
Thayaar: Hemambujavalli Thayaar
Vimanam: Sobhana Vimanam
Pushkarani: Jatayu Theertham
Prathyaksham: Tirumangai Azhwar
Travel: 5 km from Kumbakonam

Azhwar Pasuram: 
Tirumangai Azhwar- 10

Sthala Puranam: 
During the Ramayana period, when Ravana abducted Devi Sita and started to fly away in the Pushpaka Vimanam, a vulture by the name of Jatayu stood in his way and put up a valiant battle against Ravana until Ravana cut off Jatayu’s wings, causing him to fall in the Panchavati forest. Jatayu held on to his life till he could see Lord Rama and tell him what had transpired so far. After relaying the information of Devi Sita’s kidnapping to Lord Rama, Jatayu lost his life. Lord Rama is then supposed to have cremated Jatayu, offering him salvation(moksham). The Lord here is assuming a sleeping posture after performing the final rites for Jatayu. The Lord shows this entire scene to Tirumangai Azhwar.

Details of Kshethram:
 
Moolavar: Sri Aandalukum Aiyyan Perumal
Thayaar: Bharghavi/Ranganayaki Thayaar
Vimanam: Pranava Vimanam
Pushkarani: Surya Theertham
Travel: This temple is about 3 km from Kumbakonam.

Azhwar Pasuram: 
Tirumangai Azhwar - 1

Sthala Puranam: 
Once there was a dancer who wanted to impress the goddess, Maha Lakshmi. The dancer performed a very intricate set of dances, and soon the goddess appeared before her, presenting the dancer with a garland. Soon after this, it is said that Sage Durvasa was passing by and saw the lovely garland on the neck of the dancer. The dancer offered the sage the garland and left the scene. It is said that the garland possessed a very fragrant smell that attracted bees. Soon, the sage started to get irritated by the buzzing of the bees and was looking to dispose of the garland when Indra arrived atop his mount, Airavata. Durvasa presented the garland to Indra. Airavata took the garland, but instead of throwing it on Indra, it crushed it beneath its legs. Durvasa was immensely angered by this insult and cursed Indra, saying he and the world would lose all their wealth. As the phrasing of the curse was vague, all wealth-bearing substances and creatures, such as the Kalpa Vriksha, Kamadhenu, and even the Goddess Lakshmi, disappeared. To retrieve all his lost wealth, Indra prayed to Ranganayaki Thayaar, who instructed him to perform the Samurda Manthanam and attend her marriage to Lord Sriman Narayana. By doing so, he would regain his lost wealth. Another story tells that Kamadhenu had performed tapas here, as well as Agni had performed worship to the Lord here. From the following story, we can see that this temple predates even Sri Rangam.

Details of Kshethram:
Moolavar: Aravamudham Perumal
Uthsavar: Sarangapani Perumal
Thayaar: Sri Komalavalli Thayaar
Vimanam: Vaidheega Vimanam
Pushkarani: Hema Pushkarani
Travel: This temple is located in Kumbakonam

Azhwar Pasuram: 
Sri Andal – 1 pasuram.
PeriyAzhwar – 3 Pasurams.
Thirumizhisai Azhwar -7 Pasurams.
Boothat Azhwar – 2 Pasurams.
Pey Azhwar – 2 Pasurams.
Nam Azhwar – 11 Pasurams.
Tirumangai Azhwar- 25 Pasurams
Total – 51 Pasurams

Sthala Puranam:
The rishis, headed by Kashyapa, began to perform a sacrifice on the banks of the Ganga. Sage Narada visited them and asked them why they were performing the sacrifice and who would be pleased by it. Unable to answer the question, the rishis approached Sage Bhrigu to find a solution through direct ascertainment of reality.
Bhrigu first went to Satyalokam, the abode of Lord Brahma. At Satylokam, he found Lord Brahma reciting the four Vedas in praise of Lord Narayana, with each of his four heads, and attended upon by Saraswati. Lord Brahma did not take notice of Bhrigu offering obeisance. Concluding that Lord Brahma was unfit for worship, Bhrigu left Satyalokam for Kailasham, the abode of Lord Shiva.
At Kailasham, Bhrigu found Lord Shiva spending his time pleasantly with Parvati, unaware of his presence. Parvati drew Shiva's attention to the presence of the sage. Lord Shiva was furious at Bhrigu’s intrusion and tried to destroy him. The sage cursed Lord Shiva and left for Vaikuntam. At Vaikuntam, Lord Vishnu was reposing on Adisesha with Sri Mahalakshmi in service at His feet. Finding that Sriman Narayana also did not notice him, the sage became infuriated and kicked the Lord on his chest, the place where Mahalakshmi resides.
At once, Lord Vishnu hastened to apologize to the angry sage and pressed his feet to allay the pain caused to Bhrigu’s leg. In doing so, the Lord removed the eye in the foot of the sage, which gave Bhrigu power to defy the Devas. Thereupon, the sage decided that Lord Vishnu was the most supreme of the Trimurtis and informed the rishis accordingly. Thereupon, they decided that Lord Vishnu was the fruit of the yaga. Sri Mahalakshmi was angered by the action of her Lord in apologizing to Bhrigu, who committed an offense. She, therefore, left Vaikuntam without heeding the entreaties of the Lord. She furiously ran to Kolhapur and began to perform tapas to get the Lord’s attention once more. At the same time, the Lord had taken the form of Sri Srinivasa and was marrying Devi Padmavathi. When Mahalakshmi found out what was happening, she rushed to take her anger out on the Lord. The Lord is said to have run to Kumbakonam and hidden in the temple as Pathala Srinivasar. Mahalakshmi was determined to be reunited with the Lord; thus, she stayed in Kumbakonam and performed tapas to fulfill her desires. 
At around the same time, Brighu Maharishi had reincarnated as Hema Maharishi and was residing in Kumbakonam. One day, in the temple, a pushkarani found a baby girl among thousands of lotus flowers blooming in the tank. Hema Maharishi realized that this child was none other than the incarnation of Mahalakshmi and decided to adopt her. As she came of age, She desired to get married to the Lord. During Makara Sankranthi, the Lord descended from Sri Vaikuntham in a grand chariot, and after marrying Komalavalli, Thayaar stayed in Kumbakonam along with his chariot. Even today, when we visit this temple, we can see that the garbha griha features a grand chariot in which the Lord is reclining in the Udyoga Shayanam posture.
 Udyoga Shayanam is a peculiar posture, as the Lord is neither completely asleep nor completely upright. It is said that Tirumahisai Azhwar was once having a conversation with the Lord. The Lord then was about to get up to greet Tirumahisai Azhwar when he told the Lord that he looked notably different and lovely in that position. Hence, the Lord is said to have permanently taken that posture.
***This kshethram is credited for the resurfacing of the Naalayira Divyaprabandhangal (compilation of all the Azhwar Pasurams).  At one point, all of the Naalayira Divyaprabandhangal were lost except for ten Pasurams that were being sung at this temple. Here, Naathamunigal heard this, and the verses told ten out of a thousand Pasurams. This had Naathamunigal intrigued as to where the other nine hundred and ninety Pasurams had disappeared. These ten Pasurams also spoke of Kurugur (present-day Azhwar Tirunagari) and Sadagopan (Nam Azhwar). Thus Naathamunigal went in search of Nam Azhwar. Upon reaching Kurugur and inquiring about these ten Pasurams, the locals denied knowing of the ten Pasurams he had asked for, but they were familiar with eleven other Pasurams. Naathamunigal recited these eleven Pasurams twelve thousand times in front of the divine tamarind tree where Nam Azhwar had once resided. Upon completion of the recitation, Nam Azhwar is said to have appeared in front of Naathamunigal and blessed him with the thousand Pasurams sung by him as well as the three thousand other Pasurams which were sung by the nine other Azhwars.

Details of the Kshethram:
Moolavar: Uppiliappan
Thayaar: Bhoomidevi Thayaar
Vimanam: Vishnu Vimanam
Pushkarani: Ahoratra Pushkarani
Travel: 4 km from Kumbakonam
Azhwar Pasuram: 
Pey Azhwar – 2 Pasurams
Nam Azhwar – 11 Pasurams
Thirumangai Azhwar – 34 Pasurams
Total – 47 Pasurams
Prathyaksham: Markandeya Maharishi, Lord Garuda, Devi Kaveri, Yaman

Sthala Puranam: 
The legend has it that Bhudevi was reborn as the daughter of Markandeya Maharshi, and one day, Lord Vishnu, disguised as an old man, sought her hand in marriage. To ward off the marriage, the Maharshi informed the old man that his daughter was not well-versed in household duties, and she would even forget to season the salt in the food she prepared. The old man revealed Himself and took Bhudevi as his wife. As per the wishes of the Lord, the prasadam is prepared without salt and offered to the presiding deity to date. Thus, the deity is also called Uppiliappan. (Uppillatha appan). It is believed that those who take salt or salted food inside the temple will go to hell. During the festival, Perumal is always accompanied by Thayaar when He is taken in procession outside the temple.

***Oplliappan Perumal is treated as the older brother of Srinivasa Perumal of Tirumala Tirupati. Therefore, all offerings due to Tirupati Perumal can be made here, and they are considered equivalent to those offered at Tirupati.

Details of Kshethram:
Moolavar: Tirunaraiyur Nambi
Thayaar: Vanchulavalli Thayaar
Vimanam: Srinivasa Vimanam
Pushkarani: Manimuktha Pushkarani
Specialty: Kal Garudan ( Stone Garudan)
Travel: This kshethram is located in Tirunaraiyur, which is en route to Tiruvarur via Kumbakonam

Azhwar Pasuram:
Tirumangai Azhwar – 110 Pasurams

Sthala Puranam:
Legend has it that Devi Lakshmi was born as Vanchulavalli at the foot of a Vanchula tree to Medhavi Muni. Lord Vishnu is believed to have manifested himself in the Pancha Vyuha forms and married Vanchulavalli Thayaar. In the sanctum, one finds the idols of the deities – Sankarshanan in the east, Pradyumnan in the south, Anirudhan in the west, Purushottaman in the north, and Vasudevan in the center.
It is said that the Lord had performed Pancha-Samskaram for Tirumangai Azhwar at this kshethram. The story is as follows:
Tirumangai Azhwar wanted to marry a woman named Kumudhavalli. She placed two conditions, namely, 1) to get Pancha-Samskaram done, and 2) to perform tadhiyararadhanam (annadhanam) for a thousand people for one year. Tirumangai Azhwar satisfied the second condition, but when it came to fulfilling the first condition, no acharya was ready to perform Pancha-Samskaram, as Tirumangai Azhwar was a very fierce personality. Thus Tirumangai Azhwar approached the Lord here, and the Lord himself performed the Pancha-Samskaram. Hence, we can see the Lord holding his arms out with the Panchajanyam in His right hand and the Sudharshanam in His left hand.

***This temple is regarded as a Mani Mada Mantapam, which means the temple is divided into partitions known as mantapams, wherein one must climb up a flight of stairs to move from one mantapam to the next to reach the garbha griha, which is placed internally. As one moves closer to the main garbha griha, we can see a shrine outside the garbha griha dedicated to Kal Garudan. There is a peculiarity with Garudan here. At any other kshethram, one can find a Garuda Vahanam made of wood or panchaloha, but at this kshethram, we see a Garuda made of saligrama shila. Another peculiarity is when Garudar comes out for uthsavam. As Kal Garudan comes out of the shrine, we see that four people hold up Garudar. As the first mantapam is crossed, eight people are required to carry Garudar. Similarly, by the time Garudar reaches the temple gates, sixty-four people carry Garudar. As Garudar makes his journey back to the shrine again, only four are needed to place Garudar back in the shrine. 

Anyone afflicted by sarpa-dosham is said to be relieved of those impediments by the Garudan here at this kshetram.

Details of Kshethram: 
Moolavar: Saranathan Perumal
Thayaar: Saranayaki Thayaar
Vimanam: Sara Vimanam
Pushkarani: Sara Pushkarani
Travel: 15 km from Kumbakonam

Azhwar Pasuram:
Thirumangai Azhwar – 13 Pasurams

Sthala Puranam:
According to legend, it is believed that Markandeya Maharishi and Kaveri Thayaar meditated upon Lord Vishnu. It is also believed that Brahma made a clay pot to rescue and preserve the Vedas during pralaya, but none of the pots made by Brahma would last. Thereupon, he was directed by Lord Vishnu to proceed to Tirucherai (Saarakshethram) and make a pot out of the clay on the banks of Kaveri, and thus the Vedas were protected in a pot made out of tough mud at this place. Another legend recounts a feud between the Ganga and Kaveri rivers. It is said that seven rivers were meditating at the foothills of the Vindhya hills. At this moment, a Gandharva is said to have appeared and paid his respects to the devis. The question then arose: seven women were present, but to whom did the Gandharva pay his respects? Ganga and Kaveri started to argue. Ganga claimed that she was a greater entity than Kaveri. To solve this feud, both of the devis went to Lord Brahma. Lord Brahma, in a bias, declared that Ganga was a greater entity than Kaveri. Kaveri wanted to be the greatest river and hence performed penance to the Lord here at Tirucherai. The Lord appeared and showed her Vishwaroopa Darshanam, but this did not satisfy her. The Lord then showed her His form as He appears in Sri Vaikuntham and told her that soon He would lie in Bujanga Shayanam at Sri Rangam, and she would flow by His Tiruvadi (His holy lotus feet) until the end of Kali Yuga, thereby making her a greater entity than Ganga.

*** Here, the Lord can be seen with five of his spouses, namely, Sri Devi, Bhoodevi, Neela Devi, Mahalakshmi, and Saranayaki Thayaar.

Details of Kshethram: 

Moolavar: Bhakthavathsala Perumal
Thayaar: Abhishekavalli Thayaar
Vimanam: Uthpala Vimanam
Pushkarani: Darshana Pushkarani
Travel: 6 km west of Tiruvarur

Azhwar Pasuram: 
Thirumangai Azhwar – 14 Pasurams

Sthala Puranam:
During Samudra Manthanam, Mahalakshmi appeared from the Ksheerasagaram. Upon appearing, she was searching for Lord Vishnu so that she could be reunited with him once again. She sees the Lord but is embarrassed to put the Varamala around his neck as there were thirty-three crore gods(men) who were present there at the time. She thus decided to seek the Lord in private and went to Tirukanamangai, where she performed penance within the Darshana Pushkarani to bring the Lord there in solitude. The Lord appeared, and as Mahalakshmi was about to put the Varamala around the Lord’s neck, all the Devas appeared once more to witness the spectacle of the Lord’s marriage. The Lord thought that if the devas continued to stay in the form of men, Mahalakshmi would once again run away in embarrassment. Hence, he changed all the Devas into bees. As soon as this was done, Mahalakshmi married the Lord.

***Even today, outside the shrine of Abhishekavalli Thayaar, one can find a hive of bees buzzing around, symbolizing the presence of the Devas at the temple to date.

Nammazhwar – 11 Pasurams

Sthala Puranam:
Legend has it that Uparisravas, a Fisherman King, performed the Ashwamedha sacrifice and begot a daughter named Padmini, whom he offered in marriage to Lord Vishnu at this shrine. It is believed that Neelamegha Perumal vanquished a demon called Veekatakshan with His chakram, and hence the presiding deity is found with the prayoga chakram. It is also thought that the Lord in the sanctum miraculously showed the growth of hair to protect the words of a devout priest, Rangabhattar. It is said that the local king was visiting the temple on a given day, and Rangabhattar had already given the garland the Lord adorned to his lover. When the king arrived at the temple, there was no garland to perform the required honors. He requested the king to perform pradakshinam of the temple, by which time he would arrange for a garland. He sent a boy to fetch the garland from his lover. When the garland was presented to the king, he found a strand of hair in it. The king then questioned Rangabhattar as to where that hair had come from, to which Rangabhattar said the hair was that of the Lord’s. When the king came to examine the same in the morning, he found hair behind the crown that was placed atop the Lord’s head.  Hence, the Lord attained the name Sowrirajan.

***Tirumangai Azhwar is believed to have been initiated with the ashtaakshara mantram at this temple.

Details of Kshethram:

Moolavar: Lokanatha Perumal / Damodara Narayana Perumal
Thayaar: Shyamalameni Thayaar
Vimanam: Uthpala Vimanam
Pushkarani: Shravana Pushkarani
Travel: This kshethram is about 8 kilometers from Nagapattinam

Azhwar Pasuram: 
Thirumangaiazhwar – 10 Pasurams

Sthala Puranam:
Brighu Maharshi, Gautama Rishi, and Brahma worshipped Lord Vishnu at this kshethram. It is also believed that Vasishtar created an image of Lord Krishna out of butter and meditated upon it. Lord Krishna is said to have appeared one day when Vasishtar was performing aaradhanam for the butter idol. When the Lord saw the butter idol, he was tempted and gobbled it up. When Vasishtar started to look for the butter idol, he saw a boy running away, saying he had eaten up the butter. Vasishtar began to chase the child. As the Lord was being chased by Vasishtar, a group of sages who were meditating under a Magizha tree caught sight of the boy, recognizing Him to be the Lord. The Lord is then said to have taken the form of Damodaran( the one who was tied up). Thus, this kshethram became the home of Lord Krishna. Hence the name Tirukkannankudi. 

Thirukannangudi Divyadesam and Thirumangai Azhwar

Once, when Thirumangai Azhwar was building the massive outer walls of the Srirangam temple, he ran out of money. To find a way, he went to the Buddhist Vihara at Nagapattinam. There, he sang a verse saying that for Buddha, it was enough to have a statue made of iron, wood, brass, or any simple metal—there was no need for it to be made of gold.

As he sang, something strange happened. The gold from the Buddha statue started to melt and flowed towards him, turning into gold bars. With that gold, he set off to Srirangam.

On the way, he became tired and rested under a tamarind tree. Before lying down, he buried the gold near the tree and told the tree to wake him up if anyone came by. The tree, taking his words seriously, stayed alert all night and didn’t “sleep.” That’s why it’s known as Urangaa Puli—the Tamarind Tree That Didn’t Sleep.

The next morning, a landlord from that area came by. The tree dropped a few leaves on Azhwar, waking him up just in time. Seeing the gold, the landlord claimed that since it was found on his land, it belonged to him. But Thirumangai Azhwar told him the land actually belonged to him and that he had the documents to prove it in Srirangam. He said he would go there, bring back the papers, and settle the matter. But he never came back. The issue was never resolved and is still said to be “pending.” That’s why it’s called Theraa Vilakku—the Case That’s Still Not Settled.

On the journey, Azhwar became very thirsty. He saw a few women near a well and asked them for some water. But since he had an argument with the landlord from their village, they refused to give him any. Angry at this, Azhwar cursed that the wells in that village would go dry forever. That’s why the place came to be called Oorak Kinaru—the Village of Dry Wells.

Tired, thirsty, and hungry, Thirumangai Azhwar lay down under a Maghizham Tree. The tree gently fanned him with its cool breeze and gave him some comfort. At that moment, Lord Parthasarathy (Paranthaman) appeared in the form of a Brahmin. He gave Azhwar some food and water. After eating, when Azhwar looked around, the Brahmin had disappeared. He then realized it was the Lord Himself. Feeling blessed and happy, he gave a boon to the tree that it would never dry up. From then, that tree has been called Kaaya Magizhai—the Maghizham Tree That Never Dries.

Details of Kshethram:
Moolavar: Soundaraja Perumal / Neelamegha Perumal
Thayaar: Soundaryavalli Thayaar
Vimanam: Soundarya Vimanam
Pushkarani: Sarapushkarani
Travel: This temple is located in the town of Nagapattinam

Azhwar Pasuram:
Thirumangaialwar – 10 Pasurams

Sthala Puranam:
Modern-day Nagapattinam was believed to be a dense forest back in the Krita Yugam known as Sundara-Aranyam. The town is said to have derived its name from Nagapattinam, as Nagaraja Adiseshan had performed tapas here in the Lord's honor.
 The Lord here is said to have shown Himself to Dhruva. The story is as follows.
Dhruva was the son of King Uttanapada. Uttanapada had two wives, named Suruchi and Suneethi. Suruchi was a very pompous and cruel person. She had a son named Uttama. Suruchi was hell-bent on outshining Suneethi in anything she did. On one occasion, when Uttanapada was sitting on the throne in the throne room, Dhruva approached Uttanapada and asked him if he could sit on his lap. No sooner had Dhruva asked than Suruchi dragged him away from his father and put Uttama on his father’s lap. She told Dhruva that he was in no way blessed to sit on his father’s lap and further went on to insult Suneethi by telling Dhruva that he wasn’t destined for greatness as he was born in Suneethi’s womb. She told him never to try approaching his father ever again. Dhruva innocently went to his mother and told her what had happened. She told Dhruva that if he couldn’t sit on his father’s lap, it was no big deal, as another father would accept anyone. She told Dhruva that Lord Sriman Narayana would never reject his requests. Hearing his mother’s words, Dhruva went into the forests, committed to performing penance to see the Lord. When Dhruva went into the forest, he was greeted by Narada, who described the Lord’s appearance to Dhruva. Sage Narada instructed Dhruva to visualize a dark-complexioned person with a conch-like neck, broad shoulders, slender hips, coral-like lips, lotus-like feet, and four hands holding the Shanka, Chakra, Gadha, and Padma in each hand.
Given the Lord’s appearance, Dhruva, without any second thought in his head, started his penance to see the Lord. The Lord was soon impressed by seeing a five-year-old boy and appeared before Dhruva. The boy, upon seeing the Lord, was dumbstruck and didn’t know what to say. The Lord then touched the boy’s cheek with the Panchajanyam and brought out the boy’s voice. The innocence and devotion shown by the boy touched the Lord, who granted him and his mother a special position beyond the Brahmandam and told him that it would become known as the Dhruva Mandalam. When the boy could not get any attention from his father, he turned to see the Lord, who granted him far more than he ever asked for.

2) Manikkunram

3) Thanjaiyazhinagar

Pushkarani: Surya Pushkarani
Travel: The three temples are 200 meters apart and are all located on the outskirts of Tanjavur.

Azhwar Pasuram: 
Thirumangai Azhwar – 3 Pasurams
NammAzhwar – 1 pasuram
BhoodathAzhwar – 1 pasuram.
Total – 5 Pasurams.

Sthala Puranam:
The legend is said to have taken place in Krita Yugam. Parashara Maharishi was said to have been performing tapas when three demons, known as Thanjakan, Dhandakan, and Gajamukhan, began to interrupt him. It is then that Parashara Maharishi asked Lord Vishnu to intervene and help him. The Lord mounted Garudan and first released his Sudarshana Chakram to deal with Thanjakan. On his deathbed, Thanjakan asked the Lord to name the land where he died after him. Thus, the land where he died became Tanjavur. Next, the Lord went after Dhandakan. The Lord took the form of Varaha and bore his teeth into Dhandakan, digging through the land and emerging out of Srimushnam just as He had after killing Hiranyaksha. Dhandakan asked for the land where he was buried to be named after him. Thus emerged the Dhandaka Vanam. The last demon, Gajamukhan, was killed by the Lord in his Narasimha form. Therefore, the three temples were combined to form one kshethram, known collectively as Tanjai Mamanikoyil.

Details of Kshethram:
Moolavar: Jagannathan Perumal
Thayaar: Shenbagavalli Thayaar
Vimanam: Mandaara Vimanam
Pushkarani: Nanditheertha Pushkarani
Travel: This temple is located near Korrukai, outside Kumbakonam

Azhwar Pasuram: 
Thirumangai Azhwar-10 Pasurams

Sthala Puranam:
According to legend, Nandi had once visited Vaikuntham to see the Lord, but the Dwarapalakas Jaya and Vijaya refused entry to Vaikuntham. In a rage, Nandi insulted Jaya and Vijaya. Thus, Jaya and Vijaya cursed Nandi that he would experience excruciating heat and would perspire intensely. Jaya and Vijaya then felt sorry for cursing Nandi and suggested that Nandi go to Kumbakonam and meditate upon the Lord. Taking their suggestion, Nandi proceeded to Kumbakonam and began meditating on the Lord. Impressed with Nandi’s tapas, the Lord appeared in front of Nandi and released Nandi from his curse.

Sthala Puranam:
This kshethram is associated with the story of Vamana Avataram. Let us now see the story. It is said that the Lord took this form to defeat the demon king Bali. Bali was a mighty demon king. He was the grandson of Prahalada. Bali was such a powerful demon that he was individually capable of keeping all the Devas at bay. The Devas then approached Lord Vishnu to aid in defeating Bali. Bali was a Chiranjeevi, hence he could not be killed. He could merely be pushed down to Patala-Lokam. The Lord assured the Devas that he would look into the situation. At the same time, Aditi, the mother of the Devas, wanted to make sure that the Lord would be born to her. To ensure this, Aditi used the means of payovratam (a complete milk-based diet over twelve days). The Lord was born in Aditi’s womb to Aditi and Sage Kashyapa. The Lord was born as a dwarf. As soon as he was born, the Lord revealed to Aditi the various stages of his life, and he grew into a young boy. The upanayanam ceremony was performed, and each of the gods presented Vamana with a gift. Brahma gave him a kamandalam, and Brihaspati gave him the umbrella. Thus, the Lord set out to fulfill the promise given to the Devas. He reached Bali’s palace, where he was giving alms to the brahmins assembled. As the Lord reached the assembly, Shukracharya warned Bali that the person responsible for killing his grandfather had come to defeat him. He advised Bali not to give alms to him. Bali was honored that the Lord had come to his assembly. He proceeded with the program and soon reached Vamana. Bali asked him what he desired as alms. The boy replies, saying all he desires is three paces of land. Bali granted the boy’s wish. To prevent Bali from giving alms, Shukracharya assumed a tiny form and sat at the mouth of Bali’s kamandalam. When water did not come out of the kamandalam, Lord Vamana took a dharba grass and poked the opening of the kamandalam. In the process of poking the opening, Lord Vamana poked one of Shukracharya’s eyes. In pain, Shukracharya left the opening of the kamandalam. The boy started to grow. With the first step, he measured the entire earth. With the second step, he took the heavens. By the time he had to take the third step, there was no space left. Bali got onto his knees and, with a posture of namaskaram, bent his head and asked the Lord to place the third step on his head and push him into Patala-Lokam. The Lord, now in his Trivikrama form, fulfills Bali’s wish and places the third step on his head, sending him to Patala-Lokam. 
It is said that Shukracharya performed tapas here, and the Lord appeared as Kolavilli Ramar, reclined in the bhujanga shayanam, and granted Shukracharya his eye once again.  

***This is one of the special kshethrams in which one can find Lord Rama in a reclining posture.

Sthala Puranam:
Legend has it that Lord Brahma caused the herds of cattle being grazed by Lord Krishna to disappear, upon which Lord Krishna created another herd. Finding this, Brahma apologized to Krishna and requested Him to take abode at Tiruvazhandur. In the sanctum, Prahlada is to the right of the moolavar and Garudan to His left. After witnessing Narasimha Avataram of the Lord, Prahlada asks to see the lord in a Shantha-Swaroopam (calm form), to which the Lord gave him darshanam at this kshethram. It is said that the vimanam of this kshethram was given by Garudan, hence the name Garuda Vimanam.

*** This kshethram is also the birthplace of the great Tamizh poet Kambar, who has given us the magnum opus of Kamba Ramayanam, which rivals and trumps Valmiki Ramayanam in terms of poetic beauty. One can find a shrine dedicated to Kambar and his wife here at this kshethram.

Tirumangai Azhwar – 10 Pasurams

Sthala Puranam:
It is said that Garuda and Adiseshan were once mortal enemies, engaging in a fierce battle due to the injustice committed by Adiseshan’s mother against Garuda’s mother. The story is as follows. Kadru ( Adiseshan’s mother) and Vinata ( Garudan’s mother) were both wives of Kashyapa Maharishi. One day, Kashyapa Maharishi asked his wives to ask him for a boon each. Kadru asked that she be blessed with a thousand sons. Vinata asked for two sons who would be brighter and stronger than all of Kadru’s sons combined. Thus, both Kadru and Vinata were blessed. Slowly, all of Kadru’s children were born. Five hundred years passed, but neither of Vinata’s eggs hatched into a  thousand nagas (snakes). In desperation, Vinata opened one of the eggs manually.
The offspring in the egg was still half-formed and, in anger at Vinata’s impatience, cursed her, saying she would become Kadru’s slave. But he also told her that in another five hundred years’ time, his brother would hatch, and he would be extremely powerful, and he would relieve Vinata of this curse. This offspring is known to us by the name of Arunan, the charioteer of Suryan. Even though he was half-formed, he had extreme tolerance and power. Hence, he was taken by Suryan as a charioteer. As time passed, the curse came into effect. One day, Kadru and Vinata were arguing about the color of Ucchaishravas' tail. Vinata claimed that the divine horse was a pure white color throughout, but Kadru said the horse’s body was white, but the tail was black. Thus, the two had a bet to see who was right. The one who would lose the bet would become the other’s slave. Kadru knew very well that the tail of Ucchaishravas was pure white, and knowing she would lose the bet, she told her sons to wrap themselves around the tail of Ucchaishravas so that she could win the bet. One day, in the presence of Kadru and Vinata, Ucchaishravas passed by with a black tail. Thus, Kadru won the bet, enslaving Vinata. For five hundred years, Vinata was a slave to Kadru. After five hundred years, Vinata’s second egg hatched, and from that egg was born Garudan. As soon as he was born, he went straight to his aunt and demanded that his mother be freed from slavery.
To this, Kadru put a condition, saying that if Garudan could bring the Amruthakalasham (the divine pitcher that contained the sacred nectar of immortality) for her and her children, she would release Vinata from slavery. Thus, Garudan immediately left for Swargalokam and defeated all the Devas in battle, successfully retrieving the Amruthakalasham. After retrieving the Amruthakalasham, Garudan returned to Bhulokam. On Bhulokam, Lord Vishnu was very impressed with Garudan for his strength and dedication. The Lord then offered Garudan a boon. Garudan asked that he should always be soaring far above the Lord; thus, Garudan is present in the Dwajasthambham outside the temple. The Lord also then told Garudan that he wanted Garudan to be constantly under his command, and thus asked Garudan to become his vaahanam. The Lord also relieved Vinata from slavery and returned the Amruthakalasham to the Devas.
In one of the battles between Garudan and Adiseshan, Adiseshan is said to have hidden in the pushkarani and performed tapas to the Lord to save him. Thus, the Lord appeared on the bank of the pushkarani and made Adiseshan his recliner. Hence, the Lord made sure that as long as He is present, both of His bhaktas do not fight amongst themselves.
It is said that if one prays to the Lord here, they will be relieved of all and any sarpa-dhosham.
***There is an interesting story that Vyagrapadar, who obtained a boon from Lord Shiva to possess the legs, hands, and eyes of a tiger, worshipped Lord Vishnu at this kshethram, and hence it gained the name Sirupuliyur.

Sthala Puranam: 
It is said that Chandran was the husband of the twenty-seven nakshatras, who were the daughters of Daksha Prajapati. It is noted that Chandran showed more affection towards Rohini and was ignoring his other twenty-six wives. Thus, Daksha Prajapati was angered by Chandran’s behavior and cursed him, saying he would suffer from Kshaya-Rogam(tuberculosis). It is said that to relieve himself of the curse, Chandran came here to this kshethram and prayed to the Lord after taking a dip in the temple’s pushkarani. The Lord is then said to have appeared here and relieved Chandran of his curse.

Sthala Puranam:
According to legend, it is said that during the Krita Yugam, two demons by the name Madhu and Kaitabha stole the Vedas from Lord Brahma and disappeared into the Pralaya Samudram (Ocean of Deluge). It is said that Lord Maha Vishnu took the Matsya Avataram and retrieved the Vedas. It is also said that the Vedas had lost their fragrance as they were robbed. The Lord is then said to have taken the form of Parimala Ranganathan, restoring their fragrance and returning them to Lord Brahma. It is said that Ganga Devi is present near the head of the Lord. As seen at Tirucherai, Kaveri Devi was deemed greater than Ganga Devi. Hence, it is said that Ganga comes to this kshethram and bathes here in the Kaveri river to rid herself of her sins.

*** A peculiarity seen here with Lord is that he is seen in the Veera Shayanam. Anywhere one goes and sees the Lord in Shayana Kolam, one can see that the Lord will not be holding His shankam and chakram. However, here at this kshethram, as He carries His weapons and is in a reclined posture, He is said to be in the Veera Shayanam.

Details of Kshethram:
Tirunangur consists of 11 temples + 1 temple at Sirkazhi.
These 11 temples are said to house deities who quenched the rage of the 11 Rudras, who were born from Lord Shiva’s matted locks when he performed Rudra-tandavam after the loss of Parvati Devi during the Daksha Yagnam. It is said that each of the eleven preceding deities gave darshan to each of the rudras and quenched their rage.

Travel: 10 km from Sirkazhi

Sthala Puranam: 
Narakasura was the son of Bhoomi Devi. Having allied himself with Banasura, Naraka became a force to be reckoned with. To show his power, Naraka had kidnapped 16001 maidens and was planning to offer them to Kamakya Devi.  Naraka then attacked Amaravati, the heavenly capital of Indra. Naraka stormed into Amaravati and stole all of Indra’s elephants, Varuna’s Umbrella, and mother Aditi’s earrings. As Naraka was to attack Indra, Indra mounted Airavata and fled to Dwarka to seek the help and protection of Lord Shree Krishna. Indra narrated what had happened at Amaravati and asked Krishna to bring back Mother Aditi’s earrings. Lord Krishna, along with Satyabhama, mounts the Lord’s vehicle, Garuda, and leaves for Pragjyothisham (modern-day Assam), the kingdom of Naraka.
To stop intruders from entering his kingdom, Naraka had set up elaborate traps to take care of any who was daring enough to try and challenge him. Lord Krishna destroyed all the traps that were laid one by one. The first trap was a divine boulder that would crush anyone who tried to enter the border. The Lord destroyed the boulder with his mace. The second trap was a swirling pit of fire that would rise and engulf anyone who passed the first trial. The Lord sent his Sudharshana Chakra into the pit. The Chakra engulfed the flames and absorbed them. The last trap that was laid was a demon named Mura. Mura was the commander-in-chief of Naraka’s army. Mura tried his best to keep the Lord at bay but was easily defeated. Following the death of Mura, his seven sons tried to avenge his death, but all of them were easily defeated. Finally, Naraka showed himself and had a long battle with the Lord. At the end of the battle, Lord Shree Krishna emerged victoriously. Naraka, in his dying breath, asked Krishna for a boon. He asked that one day in a year, to let Ganga reach everyone so that they can atone for the sins that might have been committed by them knowingly or unknowingly. Lord Krishna granted the boon and said that day would henceforth be referred to as Naraka Chaturdashi. After Naraka’s death, the Lord freed all the maidens and is said to have married all of them to protect them. He also placed Naraka’s son Bhagadatta on the throne of Pragjyothisham and recovered Indra’s elephants, Varuna’s umbrella, and mother Aditi’s earrings.
When Lord Shree Krishna and Satyabhama reached Tirukavalampadi, Satyabhama is said to have asked the Lord to bring her the divine Parijatham flower. Thus, the Lord went back to Indra and asked that he spare a flower for the sake of Satyabhama. Indra promptly refused, saying the divine flower does not belong on Bhulokam. Lord Shree Krishna is then said to have defeated Indra and established a Parijatham garden here at this Kshethram.
***The specialty of these eleven temples together is the Padhnor Garudothasavam(eleven Garudothsavam) that takes place together during Thai Maasam(January 15- February 15) on the day of Amavasya.

Sthala Puranam:
The legend is that Lord Vishnu blessed Romesa Maharishi with a vision of Trivikrama with his left foot raised in the gesture of dominating the three worlds. Romesa Maharishi had once performed tapas here to seek the Lord. When the Lord appeared before Romesa Maharishi, he asked the Lord to bring down the pride and arrogance possessed by Lord Brahma, as he was the creator of the three worlds. The Lord told Romesa Maharishi that as and when a hair would fall from his head, the lifetime of Lord Brahma would be reduced by one year. It is said that Lord Brahma soon lost all of his pride and served his purpose diligently. After seeing the Lord, Romesa Maharishi requested to see the Lord in His Trivikraman form. Thus, the Lord showed Romesa Maharshi the form in which He was ready to measure the world by raising His left foot.

Utanka Maharishi, upon seeing the Lord, is said to have stopped the Lord’s chariot and asked him to visit his Ashramam. When the Lord reached the Ashramam, Utanka Maharishi began to pose indirect questions to the Lord about how He ensured the Pandavas won the battle. The Lord sensed that the Maharishi had other intentions and asked him what he had in mind. Utanka Maharishi then told the Lord that he desired to see the Vishwaroopa Darshanam as He had shown Arjuna. The Lord then showed the Maharishi His Vishwaroopam.

Sthala Puranam:
It is said that Lord Rama was responsible for establishing this temple at this kshethram. After defeating Ravana, Lord Rama was faced with Brahmanhatyadosham, as he had killed Ravana, who was born a Brahmin. To engage in pariharam for the dosha, the Lord was seeking solutions. It was then that Dridanetramuni suggested to the Lord that he make an idol of a cow out of pure gold, large enough for the Lord to remain seated within it. Dridanetramuni then asked the Lord to remain seated within the gold edifice for four days, following which he requested that the Lord engage in charitable activities. The Lord did as he was instructed. After the four days had passed, Lord Rama donated the gold idol to Dridanetramuni. When Dridanetramuni returned to his ashram near Sirkazhi, he sold the gold statue to raise money for the temple's construction. Hence, the temple is called Semponsei (Sempon-gold, Sei-made of) Kovil.
*** Lord Rama is said to have performed daily rituals for the Lord here.

Sthala Puranam:
It is said that this Lord was the first among the Tirunangur deities to appear to help Lord Shiva get relief from Brahmahatyadosham. The Lord is said to have given Tirukkoshtiyur Nambigal ( Guru of Srimad Ramanujacharya) the ashta-akshara mantram. Thus, one can find an idol of Tirukkoshtiyur Nambigal here at this kshethram.
Another story recounts how Indra was cursed by Durvasa, a maharishi, which led to the Samudra Manthanam. Once there was a dancer who wanted to impress the goddess, Maha Lakshmi. The dancer performed a very intricate set of dances, and soon the goddess appeared before her, presenting the dancer with a garland. Soon after this, it is said that Sage Durvasa was passing by and saw the lovely garland on the neck of the dancer. The dancer offered the sage the garland and left the scene. It is said that the garland possessed a very fragrant smell that attracted bees. Soon, the sage started to get irritated by the buzzing of the bees and was looking to dispose of the garland when Indra arrived atop his mount, Airavata. Durvasa presented the garland to Indra. Airavata took the garland, but instead of throwing it on Indra, it crushed it beneath its legs. Durvasa was immensely angered by this insult and cursed Indra, saying he and the world would lose all their wealth. As the phrasing of the curse was vague, all wealth-bearing substances and creatures, such as the Kalpa Vriksha, Kamadhenu, and even the Goddess Lakshmi, disappeared. Indra never knew a world without getting whatever he desired.
Thus, to regain his lost wealth, Indra is said to have performed tapas here. The Lord is said to have appeared here and given him the idea to perform Samudra Mathanam.
***Tirumangai Azhwar, in his pasuram, starts to address the Lord as nanda villake ananthakariyay, which translates to an Upanishad-Vaakyam which describes the Lord as सत्यम् ज्ञानम् अनंतम् ब्रह्म. The word-for-word translation of this gives us:
सत्यम् – The One who does not change and is the One true Universal Truth.
ज्ञानम् – The most knowledgeable. One who knows everything. Past, present, and future.
अनंतम् – The One who has no end by any cause.
Tirumangai Azhwar refers to the Lord as Nanda Villake, which means a figurative burning lamp, signifying the Upanishad-Vaakyam.

Sthala Puranam:
The legend of this kshethram tells the tale of a king named Shwetaketu. Shwetaketu was said to have reached the gates of Karya-Vaikuntham(A replica of Sri Vaikuntham and is regarded to be the penultimate stage in one’s journey to reach moksham), but is said to have felt hunger. At this point, the king began to question why this was happening, as when one becomes eligible to enter Vaikuntham, they are supposed to be rid of all worldly senses, such as hunger and thirst. To have his problem resolved, the king visited Narada to find out why he was still feeling hungry. Narada told the king that during his lifetime, he had not performed the charitable duties of a king. Thus, he was still feeling worldly sensations. Narada advised the king to perform tapas at Nagavanam ( Naga in Sanskrit means elephant. In connection with Tirumanimada Kovil’s sthala puranam, Airavatha is said to have performed tapas here at Tirunangur to the Lord to redeem himself, as he had insulted Mahalakshmi without knowing that he had done so. Nagavanam, over time, has become Nangur.) to convince the Lord that he was worthy of attaining moksham. Thus, the king’s aathma is said to have descended to Bhulokam and performed tapas here at this kshethram to gain moksham. The Lord appeared as he would appear at Karya-Vaikuntham and granted moksham to the king. It is said that Utanka Maharishi guided the soul to the Lord.

Details of Kshethram:
This kshethram comprises two places, Tiruvaali and Tirunagari.  Tiruvaali is said to be the birthplace of Amritavalli Thayaar, and Tirunagari is said to be the birthplace of Lord Vayalali Manavalan.

Tirunagari

Thayaar: Amritavalli Thayaar
Vimanam: Ashtakshara Vimanam
Pushkarani: Illakshani Theertham

Tiruvaali

Thayaar: Amrita Ghatavalli

Travel: Tiruvaali is located 10 km from Sirkazhi, and Tirunagari is located 5 km from Tiruvaali.

Azhwar Pasuram: 
Tirumangai Azhwar: 30 pasuram
Kulasekara Azhwar: 12 pasuram

Sthala Puranam: 
At Tiruvaali, we can see Lakshmi Narasimhar. It is said that after killing Hiranyakashipu, the Lord was still furious. To calm down all the devas, Lord Brahma and Lord Shiva asked Mahalakshmi to isolate the Lord in a different location. Thus, the Lord was taken to Tiruvaali. Usually, we see Lakshmi seated on the Lord’s left lap, but here, she is sitting on the Lord’s right, allowing her to hug and embrace the Lord. Thus, the place got its name Tiruvaali (Tiru meaning "Lakshmi" and Aali meaning "Aalinganam" or "hug" in Sanskrit).
*** Vedupari Utsavam
Tiruvaali is said to be the birthplace of Amritavalli Thayaar, and Tirunagari is said to be the birthplace of Lord Vayalali Manavalan. It is said that on the night that the Lord got married to Thayaar, they were targeted and looted by Tirumangai Azhwar. Before becoming a saint, Tirumangai Azhwar was known as Kaliyan, a dacoit.
Tirumangai Azhwar wanted to marry a woman named Kumudhavalli. She placed two conditions, namely, 1) to get Pancha-Samskaram done, and 2) to perform tadhiyararadhanam (annadhanam) for a thousand people for one year. To satisfy the second condition, Tirumangai Azhwar would often steal gold from anyone he could find and sell it to raise money to serve people. As fate would have it, Tirumangai Azhwar ran into the Lord and Thayaar. He pulled out a knife and told them to remove all the jewelry that they were wearing. The Lord and Thayaar gave up all their jewelry. Tirumangai Azhwar tied up all of the jewelry in a cloth, and as he was about to lift it, the Lord performed an enchantment in such a way that he could no longer lift it. Sthala Puranam:
Legend has it that Lord Shiva and Devi Parvati once engaged in a competition to determine who was the better dancer. When the world was asked, they all responded, saying Lord Shiva was the better dancer. In hopes of getting a second opinion, Devi Parvati suggests that the divine couple go to Vaikuntham and ask Lord Vishnu for his opinion, as His opinion was supreme, and nobody could question Him. When the question was put before the Lord, he said he would watch the divine couple dance and would decide then who among them was a better dancer. Thus, a mandapam was constructed by Vishvakarma, known as the Chitra Mandapam. The Lord descended from Vaikuntham along with Sridevi and Bhudevi reclining on Adiseshan. Lord Shiva appeared as Nataraja at the forefront of the Chitra Mandapam. All the devas and Lord Brahma descended to Bhulokam to witness the spectacle of Lord Nataraja and Devi Parvati’s dance. Thus, Lord Nataraja and Devi Parvati began dancing, and all those present to witness the spectacle watched in awe as the duo danced at a level never before seen. After the divine dance performance was concluded, Lord Vishnu asked everyone present at the event who they thought performed better. Everyone voted in favor of Lord Nataraja, and Lord Vishnu simply obliged by lifting his head. Devi Parvati, in anger, fled the scene and took the form of Devi Kali outside Chidambaram. Thus, one can still see a temple of Devi Kali here outside Chidambaram.

*** The Lord here is said to be a direct reincarnation of Tirumalai Srinivasa Perumal. The Lord here is reclining on the seven-headed serpent Adiseshan, whereas the Lord standing at Tirumalai is standing atop seven hills. Govindaraja Perumal is depicted with Shankam and Chakram, one hand supporting his head and the other hand displaying the Varada Mudra. Similarly, Srinivasa Perumal can be seen with Shankam, Chakram, one hand tucked inside and another hand showcasing Varada Mudra.
This temple has a rich history. During the Chola rule, Kulothunga Chola II was said to have uprooted the presiding idol of the Lord from the Shrine at the Nataraja temple to show Shaiva dominance. It is said that Bhagavat Ramanujacharya took the utsava moorthy (Paartasarathy Perumal) to Govindrajapatnam at Tirupati. When the kings changed over time, Krishnappa Nayaka of the Madurai Nayaka dynasty played a crucial role in reinstalling the Lord in this temple. There was considerable resistance from the Shaivaites present at Chidambaram at the time to reinstalling an idol of Lord Vishnu in a temple dedicated to Lord Shiva. However, the king remained unmoved and reinstated the idol of the Lord, as seen in modern times.

The first three of the Azhvars — Poigai Azhwar, Bhoothath Azhwar, and Pey Azhwar — came to Thirukkovilur on a rainy night. First to arrive was Poigai Azhwar, from Kanchipuram, who sought refuge for the night at the ashram of Mrugandu Rishi. The rishi told him that there was a place for just one person to sleep and that he was welcome to stay for the night.
Bhoothath Azhwar, from Mamallapuram, followed shortly, and he too requested that he stay at the ashram for the night. PoigaiAzhwar welcomed him, saying there was a place for one to sleep and two to sit, and took him inside.
Pey Azhwar, from Mylapore, too, reached the ashram. He was told that there was a place for one to sleep, two to sit, and three to stand. It is explained as a slogan by
“Oruvar Padukka – Iruvar Irukka – Moovar Nirkalam”.
 The three of them stood there through the night, sharing their experiences with each other.
A little later, the three Azhwars sensed the presence of a fourth person, and with space only for three to stand, they felt uncomfortable. Through their exceptional vision, the three Azhwars realized that the fourth person was none other than Lord Vishnu himself. Delighted at this, they showered praises on the Lord.
This is the first temple where the first three Azhwars sang praises (Pasurams) of Lord Vishnu, the compilation of which later came to be known as the Naalayira Divya Prabhandham.
It is believed that this ashram, where the 3 Azhwars stayed that rainy night, is the one where one, today, finds the sanctum. The first of the three Azhwars also finds a place inside the Sanctum.
