Sthala Puranam:
According to temple history, the Lord first appeared in the Satya Yuga. The first account of the Lord is mentioned in the Ramayana. As we know, the great King Dasharatha performed the Putrakameyishti Yagam to obtain children. The Putrakameyishti is a supplement to the Ashwamedha Yagna. It is said that Dasharatha first performed the Ashwamedha, and the origin of the Lord is believed to be found in this act. It is noted that Dasharatha asked his son-in-law, the sage Rishyashringa, to make arrangements to perform the Ashwamedha, where he recounts the story of an Ashwamedha Yagna performed by Lord Brahma. The story states that Lord Brahma once performed an Ashwamedha Yagna in a very sacred place that would yield a multifold increase in merit. In his research, he decided to perform this Yagna at a place known as Hasthigiri. It is said that he sat atop Hastigiri and prepared the sacrificial altar. According to Vaideeka Shastram, Goddess Saraswati had to accompany Lord Brahma to perform this Yagna. At this point, he was faced with two problems. The first being that Goddess Saraswati was not present, and the second being that there was no image of Lord Vishnu present at the sacrifice.  Lord Brahma decided to address the second problem first. To address this problem, Lord Brahma summoned Vishwakarma, the architect, and had him design an image of Lord Vishnu for the Devas. Lord Brahma wanted this idol to be useful for generations to come. He hence sought to make the idol of the Lord from a material whose properties would be beneficial to anyone who sought the Lord's blessings. Lord Brahma’s four heads signify each of the four Vedas. That is when Lord Brahma recollected that in the Atharvana Veda, there was a mention of a tree known as Udhumbara, which, when worshiped with devotion, has the power to annihilate any forces of enmity to the worshiper. So, what is Udumbara? Udumbara is a tree known as Ficus racemosa, which belongs to the fig family (athi tree). Brahma selected this tree because it offers numerous benefits, as per Ayurveda. Hence, Vishwakarma crafted the wood from the fig tree into a resplendent idol of the Lord. So the second problem was solved. To address the first problem, Lord Brahma decided to call upon his second wife, Goddess Savitri, to take Goddess Saraswati’s place. It is said that Goddess Saraswati had gotten into a tussle with Lord Brahma and had decided to seek solace to contemplate what had gone wrong. When Goddess Saraswati learned what Lord Brahma was doing, she became furious. In a fury, she decided that she wanted to destroy the sacrificial altar and hence put a stop to the Yagna in totality. It is said that the Goddess Saraswati took the form of a river known as Vegavathy and began to flow at a rapid speed towards the altar. Before Goddess Saraswati could reach the altar, she witnessed the idol of Athi Vardar and decided to flow beneath his feet as a mark of respect to her father-in-law. Thus the Yagna reached a conclusion. During the culmination of the Yagna, a resplendent Vimanam, known as the Punyakoti Vimanam, rose from the sacrificial altar. In the shade of this Vimanam stood a beautiful utsava moorthy of the Lord, known as Perarulaalan or Varadarajan. 
 

Modern Day
Around the 1520s, the Vijayanagara empire was the ruler of South India. They contributed immensely to the temple. One such contribution is the “Noor-Kaal Mandapam,” or a Hundred Pillared Mandapam, which Achyutha Deva Raya, the brother of the great Krishna Deva Raya, built. Around the 16th century, a significant shift occurred in the Delhi Sultanate when the Mughals gained control of North India and began expanding south. Towards the end of the Mughal Rule, when Aurangzeb took over, he began to plunder the temples and loot their wealth. The Vaishnavas of Kanchipuram sought to protect both the Moola Vigraham and the Utsava Moorthy from the invasion. To protect the Utsava Moorthy, the idol was carried by palanquin to a remote place called Udayarpalayam, where the local chief agreed to host and protect the Lord. Now, protecting the Moola Moorthy was a herculean task, as the idol was nearly 9 feet in length. Thus, a place had to be discovered where the Lord could be kept safe. The Vaishnavas then dug a giant pit within the temple tank (Ananthasaras) and embalmed Athi Varada, placing him alongside Adisesha to protect the Lord.
Over a while, the temple did not have a Moola Moorthy or a Utsava Moorthy. After Aurangzeb’s invasion, the temple was in ruins, with the Punyakoti Vimanam destroyed. Thus, the temple was reconstructed, but the daily rituals of the temple couldn’t be performed in the absence of the Lord. Hence, after major tussles with the chief of Udayarpalayam, the Utsava Moorthy was brought back to the temple. But the Moola Moorthy was lost as the people who had dug the pit were either very old or had passed away. Thus, the temple needed to install a Moola Moorthy in the temple. Hence, an idol of the Lord, known as Devaraja, found in a hamlet called Pazhayasheevaram, was brought to Kanchipuram and installed in the temple. Later, sometime in the 18th Century, when the temple tank was being cleaned, the idol of Athi Varada was found. At this time, the scholars came to the consensus that the idol would be preserved, and the idol of the Lord would be displayed for the devotees for 48 days, after which it would be returned to the temple tank to remain there for 40 years.

Swami Vedanta Desikan:
Swami Desikan is considered to be an incarnation of the divine bell of Sri Venkateshwara Swami of Tirumalai. Swami Desikan was born here in Tooppul to Sri Anantha Suri and Devi Totaramba. By birth, Swami Desikan was named Venkatanatha. When Swami Desikan was just five years of age, he was taken by his maternal uncle, Kidambi Appular, to attend a discourse by Nadadhoor Ammal, a revered Sri Vaishnava Scholar at the time. As soon as Nadadhoor Ammal saw Venkatanatha, he saw a divine radiance in the child and stopped his lecture to hug the child affectionately. After this, when Nadadhoor Ammal said that he had forgotten where he had stopped his lecture, Venkatanatha reminded him of where he had stopped. This act astonished the crowd, as they had never seen a five-year-old boy comprehend the deep intricacies of philosophical knowledge being discussed. It was then that Nadadhoor Ammal predicted and blessed Venkatanatha, stating that he would become the torch-bearer to spread Sri Vaishnavism everywhere in the future.
At each place, he composed numerous works in languages such as Tamil, Sanskrit, Prakrit, and Manipravalam (a blend of Sanskrit and Tamil), which revealed his ingenuity, creativity, logic, linguistic expertise, devotional fervor, and erudite scholarship.

1) Hayagreeva Stotram
2) Sudarshana Ashtakam
3) Paduka Sahasram
4) Abheetistavam
5) Achyuta Shatakam
6) Daya Shatakam
7) Hamsa Sandesham
8) Sri Stuti
9) Yadavabyudayam
10) Kamasikashatakam

Shree Krishna told the Pandavas that he would, for the last time, visit the court of Hastinapur and try his hand at imploring reason to Duryodhana, trying to make him realize that nothing good could come out of a war. Shree Krishna arrived in Hastinapur and, instead of staying in the palace, chose to spend some time with Vidura. He stayed the night at Vidura’s house and in the morning went to the court of Hastinapur to try and convince Duryodhana out of the idea of war. Krishna presented his argument, asking that if the Kauravas did not want to return the entire kingdom, then at least provide the Pandavas with five villages.
Duryodhana, in a crimson fury, snapped at Krishna, saying that he was not qualified to come to the court with such an issue and told him to go back to herding cattle. He further told Krishna that he would not give even a single needle-head’s worth of land. He then instructed the guards to tie Krishna up and make him a prisoner. As the guards were tying Krishna, he started to grow to an immeasurable height and took his Vishwaroopam Form. 
Vaisampayana Maharishi was narrating the Bhagavatham to Janamejaya and was referring to Lord Krishna’s visit to Hastinapuram as the Pandavas' Dhoota (Ambassador). Desiring to have the Vishwaroopa darsana, they performed Ashwamedhayagam at Kanchipuram. On completion of the yagam, the Lord gave darshan as Pandavadhootar. Hence, after the Lord pushed Bali down to Pathalam, Bali requests the Lord to once again see Him as Ulangalanthan(The one who measured the three worlds). To fulfill his wish, the Lord revealed this form to Bali.

*** 
The Lord can also be seen here in a sarpam form(serpent form). It is said that if one prays here, one is relieved of all Sarpa-Dosham.

Sthala Puranam: 
According to legend, when all of Saraswati Devi’s efforts to stop Lord Brahma’s Ashwamedha Yagnam failed, she decided to flow like a river(a personification of the speed at which she could deliver any knowledge). Thus, she took the form of Vegavathy and decided to flow over the homa kundam. At this point, Lord Brahma requested the Lord to stop Devi Saraswati. Thus, the Lord took this form and acted as a dam, redirecting the flow of the river. Therefore, this kshethram came to be known as Vegavathy Annai, which later became Vegka.
When Thirumizhisai Azhwar was living in Kanchipuram, an old lady who worked as a servant (Daasi) used to clean his house every day. She did this small act of service with full dedication. Pleased by her sincere effort, the Azhwar blessed her and transformed her into a young and beautiful woman.
Soon, her beauty caught the attention of the king of the region. Surprised by her charm, the king married her, and she became the queen. After some time, the king came to know the story behind the transformation and was curious to meet Thirumizhisai Azhwar himself.
Now, Kani Kannan—who was the Azhwar’s close disciple and companion—was called to the palace. The king asked him to request Azhwar to visit the palace and compose a poem in his praise. But Kani Kannan respectfully told the king that Thirumizhisai Azhwar only sings for the Lord Srivaikuntanathan (Sriman Narayana) and that it was not possible for him to write or sing anything to praise a human being.
Still hoping, the king offered Kani Kannan gold, silver, diamonds, and all kinds of riches if he himself would sing in the king’s praise. But Kani Kannan firmly refused, saying he would not sing about any human, no matter the reward. This made the king angry. In his fury, he ordered Kani Kannan to leave Kanchipuram immediately.
Kani Kannan returned to Thirumizhisai Azhwar and explained everything that had happened. Hearing this, the Azhwar decided that if his devotee was being thrown out of the city, he too would leave along with him.
Before leaving, Thirumizhisai Azhwar composed a verse addressing the Lord Yathothakari Perumal (the presiding deity of the Thiruvekka temple). In it, he told the Lord that since Kani Kannan was leaving the city, and he himself was also leaving, Perumal too should get up from his serpent-bed (Adiseshan), roll it up, and leave Kanchipuram.
To everyone’s shock, the Lord actually obeyed. He rose from His resting posture, folded up His bed, and left the temple to follow His devotee.
The king and the people of Kanchipuram were shaken by this miracle. They ran after them, pleaded for forgiveness, and begged Kani Kannan and Azhwar to return. Moved by their repentance, Kani Kannan agreed to come back.
When they returned, Thirumizhisai Azhwar once again sang to the Lord, asking Him to return to the temple and rest on Adiseshan as before. The Lord came back to the Thiruvekka temple and resumed His reclining posture.
Because the Lord acted exactly according to what the Azhwar said—first leaving, then returning—He came to be known as “Sonna Vannam Seitha Perumal”, which means "The Lord who did exactly as He was told."

*** A peculiarity of this kshethram is that when one sees the Lord reclining here, they can notice that the Lord is laterally inverted, i.e., the Lord’s tiruvadi( His lotus feet) are where His head usually rests and vice versa. This is because when Tirumazhisai Azhwar asked the Lord to return, he did not specify in which direction He must rest.

Sthala Puranam:
There is no explicitly known sthala puranam for this particular kshethram. The presiding deity Karunakara Perumal is so named because of his character of showing karunai or daya. The Lord here is compared to a cloud. This is for two reasons: one being his color, and the other being that he showers affection on all his devotees. This kshethram is called Kaaragam. This is because Kaara means karunai or affection, and agam means place. Thus, at this kshethram, the Lord showers his affection on all his devotees as Karunakara Perumal.

This kshethram again does not have a particular sthala puranam of its own. This kshethram is closely related to Tiruneeragam and Tirukaaragam. Kaarvaanam means a sky filled with clouds. The world cannot survive without water, and clouds play a crucial role in bringing water to the world. Thus, the Lord standing here is an embodiment of rain clouds bringing rain to the world, helping it survive.

The Vimanam in this temple has three tiers. In the first tier, the Lord gives darshanam in the sitting posture. Sthala Puranam:
During the Ramayana period, when Ravana abducted Devi Sita and started to fly away in the Pushpaka Vimanam, a vulture by the name of Jatayu stood in his way and put up a valiant battle against Ravana until Ravana cut off Jatayu’s wings, causing him to fall in the Panchavati forest. Jatayu held on to his life till he could see Lord Rama and tell him what had transpired so far. After relaying the information of Devi Sita’s kidnapping to Lord Rama, Jatayu lost his life. Lord Rama is then supposed to have cremated Jatayu, offering him salvation(moksham). The Lord here is holding Jatayu on His lap to cremate him.

***A peculiarity of this kshethram is that Sridevi Thayaar and Bhudevi Thayaar have interchanged places, i.e., Bhudevi Thayaar is on the right, and Sridevi Thayaar is on the left. When one sees Sridevi Thayaar here, one can observe that she is standing about two feet behind the Lord, as She was unable to handle the heat of the pyre. 
On new moon day (Amavasya), pilgrims congregate here at this kshethram to perform tharpanam(rites to the departed souls). In this temple, barren women receive the prasadam, which consists of roasted lentils soaked in water. While taken home, it is believed that if the lentils sprout, they will beget children.

It is also believed that the Lord visiting this kshethram, followed by Lakshmi, made it His home, and hence the name Triu Ninravoor. It is said that Tirumangai Azhwar, after worshipping at this shrine, left without singing a pasuram. The Lord followed him to Mamallapuram, where he sang the pasuram, referring to this kshethram.

Sthala Puranam:
Legend tells the story of Salihotra Maharishi, who had his hermitage in this place. He used to grind rice for a living and offered half of the flour to the seekers, while he consumed the rest himself. He was an ardent devotee of Lord Vishnu. To test his devotion, the Lord appeared as a guest to him one day. He requested Salihotra Maharishi to offer him food, which the sage did. The guest felt hungry and requested the sage to provide more food. The sage offered the other half of the flour, which he used to consume himself. The guest asked for a place to rest(Evvul), and the sage readily offered his hermitage. On arriving at the hermitage, the guest revealed His true form and blessed the sage. 

*** This kshethram has a few specialties. It is said that if one bathes in the Hruthapanashini Pushkarani on Thai Ammavasi, all of their ailments will be cured. Another belief that has seen fruit here is when a person takes a handful of jaggery and dissolves it in the water on any Ammavasi, all their wishes come true. 
When Lord Shiva had Brahmahatya dosham for killing Daksha Prajapati, it is said that after he bathed in this Pushkarani, all his sins were absolved. 
Another story tells the story of the Lord’s marriage to Vasumathi Thayaar. It is said that Thayaar belonged to a village called Dharmasenapuram, located near Tiruvallur. Vasumathi Thayaar was the daughter of the king of Dharmasenapuram. She wanted to get married to the Lord. Her father agreed, but he had a condition: his Son-in-law should not leave his kingdom and take his daughter with him. The Lord agreed to this condition and promised the king that He would never leave Tiruvallur.

Sthala Puranam:
As per temple legend, there was once a king named Sumathi. He had once taken a trip to Tirumalai, where he asked to see the Lord in the form of Krishna bearing two hands. Tiruvengadamudayan told the king that it was not possible, as he was in the form of an archa-avataram and not in Sri Vainkuntham. He advised the king to go further south, where he could find Kairavini Pushkarani. He asked the king to perform tapas there and told him that his prayers would be heard. At around the same time, Atreya Maharishi, a disciple of Maharishi Vyasa, brought an idol of Parthasarathy Perumal here. When Sumathi Raja’s tapas was completed, the Lord appeared to him as Venkata Krishna Perumal, holding the Panchajanyam in one hand and displaying the Varada Mudra in the other. Along with the Lord appeared Rukmini Devi, Balarama(the Lord’s older brother), Pradyumna(the Lord’s son), Anirudha( the Lord’s grandson), and Satyaki(the Lord’s charioteer).
*** The utsava murthy, i.e., Parthasarathy Perumal, can be seen with scars that are said to have been inflicted on Him by Bheeshma during the Mahabharata war.

Sthala Puranam:
The legend tells the story of Tirumangai Azhwar visiting this kshethram. When he visited this kshethram, the hill was surrounded by water, hence giving the kshethram the name Tiruneermalai. This kshethram features shrines for Ranganatha Perumal, Ulagalantha Perumal, and Shantha Nrisimha Perumal atop a small hillock. At the base of the hillock, one can find the temple of Neervana Perumal and a shrine for Rama, Lakshmana, Bharatha, Shatrughna, along with Devi Sita.
It is said that Maharishi Valmiki visited this kshethram and paid his homage to the Lords atop the hill, but was not satisfied by his darshan of the Lords. Thus, he requested the Lords to show themselves as Lord Rama. Therefore, the Lords collectively took the form of Rama. Sridevi and Bhudevi became Devi Sita. Adisesha, Shankam, and Chakra appeared as Lakshmana, Bharatha, and Shatrugna, and Garuda as Hanuman.
*** As one enters the premises of the Neervana Perumal temple, they can see that the Dwaja-Sthambam is displaced and not in line with the entrance, and the same is true with the position of the garbha griha of Neervana Perumal. This is because when Lord Rama appeared, he assumed the primary deity of the kshethram, displacing the position of Neervana Perumal. The Dwaja-Sthambam is in line with Sri Ramar.

Sthala Puranam: 
The legend tells the tale of Gavala Maharishi, who had 360 daughters. When he was faced with the trouble of getting each of them married, he was directed to perform tapas to the Lord here at Tiruvidandai. Upon completion of his tapas, the Lord came to the Maharishi daily and personally married each of his 360 daughters. On the 360th day, a question arose whether there had to be 360 different households for each daughter. Thus, the Lord took each of the 360 daughters and consolidated them into a single person. This is how Akilavalli Nachiyar came to be. Here, the Lord can be seen with his right tiruvadi placed on the earth (Bhoomi Devi), and his left tiruvadi can be seen resting on the head of Adiseshan, with his spouse blessing them eternally.
*** It is said that those who have been unable to get married can visit this kshethram and pray to the Lord and Thayaar here to find a suitable partner for marriage. The couple will be given two garlands and will be advised to revisit the temple after a while for the marriage to take fruit. The philosophy that can be seen at this kshethram is the relationship between the jeevaathma and Paramaathama. The 360 daughters here represent the various jeevaathmas, and the Lord is the Paramaathama. Each of the individual jeevaathmas longs to reach the Paramaathma, who will grant us moksham (Varaha Perumal, who lifted Bhoomi Devi from the waters of the deluge during pralayam, is the One who will liberate us from the ocean known as Samsara or life).

Sthala Puranam: 
According to legend, Pundareeka Maharshi, desirous of worshipping Lord Vishnu with lotus flowers, proceeded eastward and attempted to drain the waters of the ocean to make his way. The Lord came in the guise of an old man and asked for some food. The Maharishi went to fetch him some food, and when he returned, he found Lord Vishnu adorning Himself with the flowers and giving darshan as Ananthasayanam. Hence, this place gained the name Sthalasayanam.

*** A peculiarity of this kshethram is that one can see the Lord in reclining posture without Adiseshan. The Lord is reclining on the ground; hence, he is known as Sthalashayana Perumal (Sthala meaning 'ground'). The Lord can be seen with four hands. His left hand displays the aahwaana-mudra, welcoming his devotees, and his right hand is seen in the varada-mudra along the left and right lengths of his bed.

Total: 4 Pasurams

Sthala Puranam:
The legend recounts the story of how the Lord appeared at this kshetram as the Saptarishis performed tapas, with the intention of seeing the Lord in the form of Sri Nrisimha. The rishis requested a local ruler to protect them from the prevailing demons in the area while they performed the necessary yagnams to please the Lord. The king tried his best to keep the rishis safe, but was defeated after some time. At this point, Lord Rama had just defeated Ravana and was on his way back to rule Ayodhya. Thus, He instructed Hanuman to go and protect the rishis from all and any danger that was prevalent in the area. It is said that Hanuman held the Shankam and Chakram at this kshethram to protect the rishis from every possible risk. After successful completion of the tapas and yagnams, Lord Nrisimha emerged seated in padmasana as Yoga Nrisimha.
*** Another name of this kshethram is Gadikachalam, as Gadika means 24 minutes. It is said that if one spends 24 minutes at the top of the hill, it absolves all sins that one has committed throughout one's life. There are two hills at this kshethram: one large hill with 1,300 steps, which houses Sri Yoga Nrisimha Perumal, and a smaller hill with 750 steps, which houses Sri Yoga Anjaneya Perumal. This is the only place where one can see Anjaneyar with Shanku and Chakram seated in padmasana. Sri Anjaneyar faces Lord Nrisimha. It is said that Lord Nrisimha constantly blesses Lord Anjaneyar. It is said that if one visits both of these temples, they will never be plagued by any kind of ghosts, spirits, or ghouls of any kind.

Travel: This kshethram is situated on the banks of the Bharathapuzha River, near Shoranur in Kerala, and is also a railway station on the Chennai-Calicut line.

Azhwar Pasuram:

Total: 13 Pasurams

Sthala Puranam:
Legend tells the story of nine yogis who offered worship to the Lord present at this kshethram and attained moksham. According to the rules of prathistapana (the process of establishing the Lord in stone), the Lord is established, and all associated rituals are performed, sealing the Lord in the garbha-griha for eight days. Thus, the first yogi performed prathistapana of the Lord and opened the door of the garbha-griha after eight days. When he opened the doors, he found the Lord missing. Similarly, eight of the nine yogis found the Lord missing from the garbha-griha. The ninth yogi performed the prathistapana of the Lord, but instead of waiting eight days, he opened the door on the third day. The yogi found that the Lord was slowly sinking into the earth in the garbha-griha. The yogi then concluded that the Lords previously established by the other eight yogis must have also sunk into the earth in the same manner. Thus, the yogi asked the Lord to stop sinking into the ground and asked Him to remain there at the kshethram to serve all the devotees who would visit the kshethram. Thus, when one visits this kshethram, they can only see the Lord above the waist.
This is the only temple in the Malainadu Divyadesams that houses Lakshmi Devi separately in a shrine.

*** It is said the Lord here is prathyaksham to Gajendran and Sri Lakshmi. It is said that there was a competition between Gajendran and Lakshmi Devi as to who would present the Lord with a lotus first. One day, Gajendran asked the Lord to allow his devotee to perform kainkaryam (divine service to the Lord). Thus, the Lord requested Lakshmi Devi to come and sit next to Him and enjoy the divine service, and not to engage in any competition with the devotees.

Azhwar Pasuram: 
Kulasekara Azhwar : 10 Pasurams

Sthala Puranam:
Legend tells the story of Ambareesha Maharaja, who was one of the greatest devotees of Lord Vishnu. It is said that one day, the Lord took the form of Indra, mounted Airavata, and appeared in front of Ambareesha Maharaja. The Lord then asked Ambareesha to ask for any wish. Ambareesha refused by saying he would not ask anyone but Lord Sriman Narayana for any sort of wish. The Lord was thus impressed by Ambareesha and revealed Himself in the form of Uyyavantha Perumal here at this kshethram. Ambareesha then asks the Lord to show Himself as His four Vyuhamurthys. Thus, the Lord shows Himself as Vasudeva, Sankarshana, Anirudha, and Pradyumna. As seen in the picture, there are four vyuhamurthys, which the five Pandava brothers established. The first Murthy was that of Sankarshana by Yudhishthira, followed by Vasudeva by Arjuna, Anirudha by Bheema, and Pradyumna by Nakula and Sahadeva.

*** Another story that is connected to the kshethram is as follows. There was once a brahmin who came to South India from the temple of Kashi Vishwanathar. The brahmin is said to have been carrying an umbrella, which he left near the dwajasthambam and went to bathe in the Bharathapuzha River. When he came back, he noticed that the umbrella had become so heavy that he could not lift it, no matter how hard he tried. It is said that Kashi Vishwanathar was so attached to his devotee that He had placed Himself inside the umbrella. When the brahmin left the umbrella near the dwajasthambam, the Lord thought it was the ideal place for Him to establish Himself at the kshetram alongside Lord Vishnu; thus, a Lingam appeared, which is worshipped to this day.

Sthala Puranam:
It is said that Mahabali Chakravarthy had offered Lord Vamana three paces of land from where the Kapila Theertham pushkarani now stands. As the Lord took the three steps, with the first step, the Lord measured the entire earth; with the second step, He measured the heavens and hell. By the time he could take the third step, there was no more space where He could place His foot. Thus, He placed His foot on Mahabali Chakravarthy’s head upon his request, sending him to Patala-lokam. It is said that Mahabali then asked the Lord to come back one day to the world of the living to see his subjects. To fulfill this wish, the Lord let Mahabali visit his subjects on the day of Onam in the month of Avanni. It is said that Kapila Maharishi had performed tapas at this kshethram to see the Lord in His Vamana form.
*** There is a very peculiar story of how the Nendram Vazha, a local variety of plantain, started to grow in this area. It is said that there was once an orchard that used to grow plantains. The yield of the orchard was terrible. The owner of the orchard came to this temple and prayed to Lord Vamana, offering Him a plantain made of gold. Lord Vamana is said to have opened His eyes upon seeing the golden plantain, which is said to have triggered an excellent yield of plantain henceforth. As the Lord opened His eyes, the fruit came to be known as Nethra Vazha, which over time has become Nendram Vazha.

Azhwar Pasuram:
Nam Azhwar: 10 Pasurams

Sthala Puranam:
This shrine is associated with legends from the Ramayana. Bharata, the brother of Sri Rama and Lakshmana, came to invite Sri Rama, then in exile, to take over the reins of the kingdom, an angry Lakshmana suspecting Bharata’s intentions intended to kill Him; however, Bharata’s innocence was very soon revealed, and then the two of them offered worship together at Tirumoozhikkalam. 

***As per another legend, Hareetha Maharishi was performing penance at this place. Lord Vishnu was pleased by his devotion and appeared to him. The sage requested the Lord to guide how all men can proceed with Varnashrama Dharma. Vishnu uttered the sacred words, after which the place came to be known as Thirumoozhikkalam. Sthala Puranam:
King Rukmangathan of the Suryavamsam is said to have offered flowers to the Lord daily as a form of kainkaryam. One day, the Devas saw the flowers and thought they were to be worshipped first by those beautiful flowers, and hence started to steal the flowers, making garlands for themselves and adorning themselves with them. One day, the king performed a yagam to reveal who was stealing the flowers. The king added numerous medicinal herbs to the divine flames of the yagnam, which released a cloud of smoke that revealed the devas wearing floral garlands. The king told the devas that if they had asked for the flowers, he would have given them the flowers without any second thought. The king said to the devas that they could take the flowers at any time and asked them to return to Amaravati(Devalokam). The devas informed the king that they were unable to return, as their powers had been rendered useless by the divine smoke emanating from the yagnam. The devas told the king that the only way they could return to Amaravati was if someone in the kingdom who was observing Ekadasi-vratham with a staunch following, without deviating from any of the rules, gave away the punyam that they gained by following the vratham. The king went searching throughout his kingdom and found a woman who was the only one in the entire kingdom who was religiously following the norms of the vratham.
The king explained the situation to her, and she gifted away all her punyam to the Devas, enabling them to reach Devalokam.

*** This is the second Pancha-Pandava Kshethram. Yudhishthira established this temple. Thus, this temple is referred to as Dharmaputra Prathista Kovil.

Sthala Puranam:
During the Mahabharata war, on the fifteenth day of the war, Bheema and Drishtadyumna attacked Dronacharya in full fury, but it had no avail. Drona still had many divine weapons left in his Astra-Bhandara. Then Krishna devised a plan wherein Drona would voluntarily drop his weapons, thereby presenting the opportunity for the Pandavas to kill him. Krishna told Bheema to kill an elephant named Ashvatthama, and then told everyone on the battlefield to announce that Ashvatthama was dead. As instructed, Bheema immediately killed Ashvatthama, the elephant, and all the warriors in the Pandavas' army started screaming, saying Ashvatthama was dead. When Drona heard these words, he was in disbelief. He immediately went to Yudhisthira and asked what all the warriors were saying was true. Yudhisthira was put in a spot at that moment. He went into deep thought about how to convey the information. He says अश्वत्थामा हत: which translates to Ashvatthama is dead. As soon as he had lied, the chariot, which always used to hover four inches above the ground, immediately fell to the ground. Drona was heartbroken and laid down his arms, renouncing war. He assumed a yogic stance and prayed to Lord Vishnu, then instructed Karna to take charge of the army and protect Duryodhana.
As soon as Drona had laid down his arms, Drishtadyumna came and beheaded Drona. 
It is said that Yudhisthira came to this kshethram, bathed in the Chitraaru river, and performed tapas to the Lord here. The Lord appeared in front of Yudhisthira and gave him atonement for his sin of lying to Dronacharya. 

*** An interesting point that can be seen here is that the Lord holds the Panchajanyam in the right hand and the Sudharshanam in the left hand.

***This is the last of the five Pancha-Pandava Kshethrams. Nakula established this temple.

Sthala Puranam:
At the time of creation, Lord Brahma is said to have summoned his four sons, the Sanathkumaras, for a deliberation session to discuss what had to go into creation. It is said that his four sons refused to attend this session on the advice of Devarishi Narada, who instructed them to meditate upon Lord Vishnu rather than waste their time in unwanted deliberation. Thus, Lord Brahma summoned Devarishi Narada and cursed him to wander the three worlds, aimlessly preaching about the Lord. When the Devarishi arrived at this kshethram, he is said to have meditated upon the Lord here and requested Him to write a Purana. Thus, this kshethram is the site where Naradeeya Puranam was written. Another story recounts the tale of Markandeya Maharishi, who sought to see the Lord in His true form. Thus, Markandeya Maharishi is said to have meditated upon the Lord here. The Lord is said to have appeared in front of Markandeya Maharishi and inhaled him. In the nose of the Lord, Markandeya Maharishi is said to have seen the entire process of creation and destruction of the whole universe, along with the Lord’s form as a baby(His miracles as a child in His Krishna Avataram) to His Vishwaroopam form.

Travel: This kshethram is located in the city of  Thiruvananthapuram.

Azhwar Pasuram:
Nam Azhwar: 11 Pasurams

Sthala Puranam:
History:
According to legend, there was once a Nambudhri Priest by the name of Bilwa Mangala Samiyar who used to perform Tiruvaradhanam daily to many Shalagramams. It is said that there was a young boy who accompanied the priest daily during his kanikaryams. The boy was very naughty, but had told the priest not to question anything that he would do. One day, the boy stole some of the Shalagramams from the priest and started to run. The priest pursued the boy. As the chase continued, the boy ran into a dense forest known as Ananthavanam. As the priest ran after the boy, a humungous illupa-maram (Indian Butter Tree) fell in front of him. The height of the tree can be comprehended as follows. It is said that the Lord’s tirumukham rested in Tiruvattar, His nabhi rested in Thiruvananthapuram, and his tiruvadi rested in a place known as Tirupaapur.
Similarly, another story states that Diwakara Maharishi chased a boy into the Ananthavanam, and the tree fell; as a result, the Lord appeared in the tree. It is said that Diwakara Maharishi was holding a tridandam, and he asked the Lord to reduce his length to match the tridandam. Thus, the Lord shrank Himself to a length of 18 feet. As the Lord shrank Himself from a humungous length to a more viewable length, He got the name Ananthapadhmanabhan. Anantha, which means immeasurable, and Padmanabhan, as Lord Brahma emanates from the divine lotus in His navel. Thus, a temple was constructed, and the Lord was present in a wooden form for many years. Even today, one can get a sight of Bilwa Mangala Samiyar as well as Diwakara Maharishi inside the garbha-griha.

Modern Day:
In 1686, a massive fire reportedly broke out in the temple. The then king Marthanda Varman is said to have reconstructed the temple over the course of forty years and performed the samprokshanam for the temple in 1726. It is said that the Lord appeared in the king’s dream and told him that He wished to be converted into a shila-vigraham form. It is said that elephants carried 2400 shalagramams on their heads from Nepal and delivered them to the king. The Lord further instructed the king to use 1200 shalagramams to constitute Him in the shila-vigraham form. The remaining shalagramams were to be stored safely till they would be necessary to reconstruct the Lord once more. To this day, that requirement has not arisen. In the year 1750, Marthanda Varman is said to have written down all his wealth in the name of the Lord and the temple and given his family the title of Padmanabha-Dasan, which translates to those who serve Lord Padmanabha. To this day, the Kings of the Travancore family visit the temple in the early hours of the morning and pay their respects to the Lord. Due to being unable to visit the temple on any given day, they pay a fine to the temple. There are two annual festivals during the Tamil months of Panguni and Aippasi.

The significance of the three doors for viewing the Lord:
Given the length of the Lord being eighteen feet, there are three doors through which one can view the Lord. In the first door, one can see the Lord’s tirumukham. This door is said to have been meant for the Nityasooris, such as Garudan and Vishwaksenar. In the second door, one can see the Lord’s naabhi (navel) from which emanates the divine lotus, inside which is seated Lord Brahma. This door is said to have been meant for the Devas. In the third door, one can see the Lord’s tiruvadi (His holy lotus-feet). This door is said to be meant for all His devotees who seek his refuge as instructed by Him in the Gita, where Lord Krishna says, “Sarva Dharman Parityajya maam ekam sharanam vraja.”

*** Other specialties in this temple include Anjaneya Swami, who is always adorned in butter. There is a shrine hosting Ugra-Narasimha Swami. To keep the Lord’s anger under control, Valmiki Ramayana Parayanam is done daily in front of the shrine.

Sthala Puranam:
The legend tells the tale of the Lord defeating the demon named Adikeshi. After his death, Adikeshi's wife performs penance and asks the Ganga and Tamraparani rivers to flow in a circular pattern, engulfing the area. The Lord is said to have taken His reclining form and slept atop the demon, using Adisesha as His bed, at the meeting point of the rivers. Seeing that her efforts to take revenge were in vain, Adikeshi's wife is said to have surrendered to the Lord.
Another story tells us how the Lord came to take His current form. There was a Maharishi named Hathalekar, who was very short in stature but extremely learned from a young age. One day, the Lord decided to test Hathalekar Maharishi. He approached and began teasing the sage about his height. At one point, when the sage was standing next to a banana tree, the Lord asked if his parents were dwarves too, having given birth to someone of his stature. The sage, in a fit of anger, pointed at the tree and said, “These are my parents.”
Not wanting to disappoint His devotee, the Lord caused the parents to emerge from the tree, and then gave him upadesham of the Ashtaakshara mantram, telling the sage that it had all been a test of his faith and devotion. The Lord, pleased with the sage, then instructed him to reconstruct His form as Adikesava Perumal.
Hathalekar used to perform aaradhanam daily to 16,008 shalagramams. It is said that the Lord was brought into His present form using these 16,008 shalagramams, along with a mixture of karungal (black teak wood) ash, mustard seeds, and jaggery.
As a result, there is no abhishekam performed for the murti at this kshetram. The Lord is preserved through the application of medicinal herbs and oils, as prescribed by the Ayurveda Shastram.
The Lord here is very similar to Sri Ananthapadmanabha Swamy at Thiruvananthapuram. The Adikesava Perumal murti is 22 feet long, compared to 18 feet at Thiruvananthapuram. Another difference lies in the Nabhi Kamalam (navel lotus) of Adikesava Perumal; Lord Brahma is not present, as this form of the Lord is said to have appeared before Brahma was created.
There are three doors through which devotees can have darshan—one to see the Lord's face, one for His navel, and another for His feet.
It is said that Sri Ananthapadmanabha Swamy reclines in such a direction that He faces Adikesava Perumal.

Sthala Puranam:
The Sthala Puranam of this kshethram is found in Varaha Puranam. It is known as Kaisika Maahathmiyam.
Kaisika Ekadesi is celebrated in the Tamil Month of Kaarthigai on the succeeding Ekadesi in the Sukla Paksham. This is named after the Kaisika Puranam, which is the 48th Chapter in the Sri Varaha Puranam. The message behind the day reinforces the fact that caste is not a hindrance in attaining the lotus feet of Sriman Narayana, and true Bhakti alone is enough. This story took place in the Divyadesam of Thirukurungudi, one of the Nava Tirupati in Thirunelveli. Nambaduvaan was born in a low chandala kulam but was a devotee of Sriman Narayana. On every Ekadasi, he observed Vratham, sleeping not a single night, singing the glory of the Lord, and thinking about Him. On one Karthigai Ekadasi, Nambaduvaan left for the Kurungudi Nambi temple to observe his fast and recite some Pasurams using various Paan on Sri Kurungudi Nambi.On his way, Nampaduvan was confronted by a Brahma Rakshas. This Rakshas, who has been starved of food, tells Nampaaduvaan that he would devour him. Nampaduvan humbly requests that he has the duty of nama sankeerthanam. Nampaduvan pleads with the rakshas that he would return after his vratham and darshan of Kurungudi Nambi. He promises that he would indeed return; he mentions the various sins that he would incur if he were not to return. But for none of Nampaduvan’s promises, BrahmaRakshas was not satisfied. At last, Nambaduvaan promised that “Whoever thinks/says that Supreme Lord Sriman Narayanan is equivalent/on par with or inferior to other devathas, that paaapam would catch me!” After hearing this, Brahma Rakshas was moved and impressed by such a firm promise and said, 'Now I believe in you; you can go now and return soon.' I will wait for you till your return.” Nambaduvaan happily went to Sri Kurungudi temple, observed his jakratha vratham, and completed his vratham with singular determination. He returned as stated to BrahmaRakshas. Nampaduvan went and offered himself to the Rakshas. But his hunger had vanished, and instead, he was moved by the truthfulness of the Vishnu devotee. The Brahma Rakshas then told his story – he was a Brahmin who had been cursed to become a Brahma Rakshas by his elders because he had not performed the yajnas carefully. The Rakshas then asked Nampaduvan to give the reward of one of his prayers so that he could get liberation. Hearing the pleas of the BrahmaRakshas, Nambaduvan said that he never sang for any palam. However, he will still request Thirukurungudi Nambi to absolve the BrahmaRakshas of his sins. Nambi gives the palam of the last pasuram and relieves BrahmaRakshas of its sins. This story strongly reiterates that true Bhakti is sufficient to attain Him, and a person's caste is entirely insignificant. It is believed that those who read or listen to ‘Kaisika Purana’ on that day will be showered with the Lord’s abundant mercy! The story of Nampaduvan is narrated and acted in Vishnu Temples in South India on the Kaisika Ekadasi. Sri Parasara Bhattar chanted the Kaisika Puranam before Lord Ranganatha, and this tradition continues to date with the descendants of Bhattar chanting the puranam on Kaisika Dwadashi day at Srirangam each year. Kaisika Ekadasi is considered even more significant to Vaishnavas than Vaikunta Ekadasi, as it implies the steadfast Bhakti towards Sriman Narayana and His abundant mercy on His devotees.
Thirukurungudi Sri Vaishnava Nambi Dhivya Sevai in Kaisika Mandapam

This kshethram is one of the most important of all the Divyadesams. 
The following summarizes the importance of this kshethram:
1) It is said that Swami Bhagawad Ramanujacharya wanted uniformity in the way rituals were conducted throughout South India. To achieve this, he is said to have traveled to Tiruvananthapuram to plead with the Nambudri priests to follow practices as per the Pancharatra Agama Shastras. It is said that the Nambudri priests pleaded with Ananthapadmanabha Swamy to allow their prevailing traditions, which were being followed, to continue throughout Kerala. It is said that in the middle of the night, when Bhagawad Ramanujacharya was asleep, Kurungudi Nambi Swamy is said to have brought Bhagawad Ramanujacharya here to this kshethram. When Bhagawad Ramanujacharya awoke in the morning, he is said to have had a conversation with the Lord. The Lord tells Bhagawad Ramanujacharya that he has accomplished what He could not achieve in all His births. The Lord asks to be initiated into Sri Vaishnavism by Bhagawad Ramanujacharya. Bhagawad Ramanujacharya is said to have performed the Pancha-Samskara for the Lord here, thereby bestowing upon Him the name Sri Vaishnava Nambi.
2) It is said that Nam Azhwar’s parents came to this kshetram to pray for the birth of a child. The Lord is said to have had a conversation with Nam Azhwar’s parents, asking them what kind of child they desired. The parents are said to have asked for a child who is just like the Lord Himself. As none in this universe is like the Lord, it is said that the Lord Himself incarnated as Nam Azhwar.
3) This is the kshethram where Tirumangai Azhwar attained Paramapadam. There is a shrine here for Tirumangai Azhwar.

There is a mention of this kshethram in the Ramayana. It is said that Hanuman jumped from Mahendragiri Parvatham to fly to Sri Lanka in search of Sita, the wife of Lord Rama. Mahendragiri Parvatham is located within this kshethram. This is also the site of the Malai Mel Nambi Temple.

*** This is one among the eight Sri Vaishnava Swayam Vyaktha Kshethrams

Sthala Puranam:
There are multiple legends associated with this temple. Let’s go through them one by one.
How the Lord appeared:
Lord Mahavishnu is said to have defeated the demon brothers, Madhu and Kaitabha. When He defeated them, their blood is said to have spilled over the earth, causing the world to smell with a very foul odor. Bhoomi Devi is said to have performed tapas at this kshethram to relieve Herself of the odor. The Lord is said to have answered Her tapas and appeared here for the first time. Vishwakarma is said to have designed the temple here. Over time and improper maintenance, the Lord is said to have gotten buried under the earth. Many years passed, and the Lord was forgotten. Then came a king named Karya Maharaja, who had no children. The king was growing anxious as he grew older, and he did not have any children.
One night, the Lord appeared in the king’s dream and told him that He wanted to be reestablished in the temple. The Lord directed the king to Nanguneri and told him where He lay buried below the earth. The king began digging and, at one point, saw that the tip of one of his tools had blood on it. Upon closer inspection, the king found the Lord, Sri Devi, Bhoomi Devi, Suryan, Chandran, Brighu Maharishi, Markandeya Maharishi, Urvashi, Thilothama, Vishwaksenar, and Garudan. (Among all the Swayam Vyaktha Kshethrams, this is the only kshethram where there have been 11 vigrahams that have emerged.) The king was bamboozled by the blood and did not mean to hurt the Lord in any way. The king immediately begged for the Lord’s forgiveness. The Lord told the king not to be worried and asked him to apply some gingelly oil, and the wound would heal. The king followed the Lord’s instructions. To date, this tradition is still observed, where the Lord is massaged with a mixture of gingelly oil and sandalwood oil, along with a blend of medicinal herbs, and abhishekam is performed daily.

After the abhishekam is performed, all the oil is collected and poured into a well that is 25 feet deep. This well is known as the yennai kannar. The oil from this well ages over time and undergoes multiple chemical reactions when exposed to sunlight. All devotees who visit this kshethram take some amount of this oil with them to their households without fail. This oil has multiple medicinal benefits, including the ability to alleviate arthritis symptoms, and it can also be used to treat leprosy.
Another legend goes that once upon a time, there was a righteous king in the kingdom of Sind named Gunaseelan. In his usual pastime, he went out hunting, followed by his attendants on horseback. The King missed his companions in the trackless forest, and when he was feeling the pinch of thirst and hunger, he could locate a mysterious animal in the form of a deer with eight legs. This phenomenon diverted the king's mind, and he pursued it. But alas! The deer, with its swift legs, quickly disappeared, drawing the King deep into the forest. At its disappearance, the King felt dejected and retraced his steps to find his companions. By then, he felt thirsty and hungry. He noticed at a distance a small hermitage made of mild leaves. He halted in front of it and, finding the door wide open, alighted from his horse and entered it. He could not find the owner of the hermitage. There was no temple there till then. But the sanctity of the place gained significant prominence. It was a dense mango forest where many sages, including Roma, Narada, Vaikhanasa, Dadhichi, Angeerasa, Jabali, Kalavar, Kanva, and others, were engaged in deep meditation and penance. But to his utter surprise, he found in a corner food and drink spread over a leaf as if offered to somebody. His acute thirst and hunger did not allow him to wait long. He unceremoniously helped himself to the food and drink. When he had finished the meal, he realized he was an intruder in the hermitage.
Sage Kusasanan, who had been to the river for his daily ablution, was entering the hermitage. The Rishi became angry and immediately cursed the intruder to turn into a dog for his canine actions, as only dogs sneakily creep into households and desecrate food. The intruder had not only desecrated the hermitage through his actions but had also violated the country's moral code. The curse became immediately effective, and the King turned into a roaming mongrel. Gunaseelan begged the Sage to take back his curse in place of his entire domain and wealth, but the words of the sage, who had already attained Vak Siddhi, were irrevocable. But seeing the humility, distress, and penitence of the King, Sage Kusasanan retorted to lighten the cruel rigor of the curse by saying that in due course of time, he would come across a holy place where he would regain his original form after a bath. In the form of a mongrel, the King had to roam around the earth, how long none could say. Once, during his wanderings, a juggler came before him and, finding him relatively healthy and plump, utilized his services to demonstrate sleight-of-hand tricks in the art of juggling.
Time passed, the mongrel in the company of the juggler roamed around the earth and, at last, reached Nanguneri. Before starting his show, the juggler took his bath in the temple tank and bathed the mongrel too. But to his surprise, the mongrel stood transformed as a king after the holy dip. People thronged around the juggler to see the wonderful jugglery of God. Such is the power of the holy waters of the sacred tank at Nanguneri.

*** The Vanamamalai Jeeyar Mutt headquarters are situated here at this kshethram. It is said that Manavaala Maamunigal used to preach here at this kshethram, and the Mutt was founded by Ponnadikaal Jeeyar, who was one among Manavaala Maamunigal’s eight sishyas.

Details of Kshethram:
Moolavar: Vaikunthanathar
Thayaar: Vaikuntavalli Nachiyar
Vimanam: Chandra Vimanam
Pushkarani: Brighu Theertham

Travel: This kshethram is situated on the banks of the Tamaraparani, approximately 35 km from Tirunelveli.

Azhwar Pasuram:
Nam Azhwar: 2 Pasurams

Sthala Puranam: 
The legend has it that a local thief, known as Kaladushaka, would donate half of the loot he stole to the deity in the temple. While the King caught him, Vaikunthanathar appeared before the king and expressed that He was also a culprit and thus gained the name Kallapiran. Another sthala puranam mentions a demon named Somakan who stole the texts of knowledge from Lord Brahma. Upon praying to the Lord, Vaikunthanathar killed Somakan, recovered the texts, and presented them to Lord Brahma.

Details of Kshethram:
Moolavar: Vijayaasana Perumal
Thayaar: Varagunamangai Thayaar
Vimanam: Vijayakoti Vimanam
Pushkarani: Agni Theertham

Travel: This kshethram is part of Nava Tirupati and is approximately 3 km from Srivaikuntam.

Azhwar Pasuram:
Nam Azhwar: 1 pasuram

Sthala Puranam:
The legend tells the story of a brahmin named Vedavit. Vedavit is said to have been looking for the best place to perform dhyanam and tapas, and he is said to have come to this kshethram. When he performed tapas at this kshethram, the Lord is said to have appeared as Vijayaasana Perumal and performed the ashtaakshara mantra padhesham. Another story tells the tale of Romasa Maharishi and his student Satyavan, who came to this kshethram. It is said that they arrived along the banks of the Tamaraparani river and saw a fisherman dropping his net into the water on the opposite bank. As the fisherman dropped his net into the water, a snake is said to have bitten him, and he passed away on the spot. Satyavan is said to have seen a Swarna-vahanam ( a golden chariot) appear and take the aathma to Vaikuntham. Satyavan is said to have asked his guru why the man was taken to Vaikuntham. Romasa Maharishi is then supposed to have told Satyavan that it's the power of the kshethram that, regardless of what the person was doing when he passed away on this pure land, he achieved moksham.

Details of Kshethram: 
Moolavar: Kaaisinavendan
Thayaar: Malarmagal Nachiyar
Vimanam: Vedasara Vimanam
Pushkarani: Varuna Theertham

Travel: This kshethram is part of Nava Tirupati and is located approximately 4 km from Srivaikuntam.

Azhwar Pasuram:
Nam Azhwar: 12 Pasurams

Sthala Puranam:
The legend tells the story of a brahmin named Yagna Sarma. It is said that one evening, when Yagna Sarma and his wife were in a jovial state, Shakthi Maharishi(son of Vasishta Maharishi) is said to have visited their hermitage. Yagna Sarma and his wife failed to recognize that the sage had come to their doorstep and did not perform any kind of athithi-sathkaaram(service to the guest). Shakthi Maharishi, in a fit of rage, cursed Yagna Sarma that he would become a demon. Yagna Sarma begged for the sage’s forgiveness and asked him if there was any way out of this curse. The sage then tells Yagna Sarma that Indra would perform a yagnam at Tiruppulingudi, and he is to go and try to disrupt this yagnam. When this would happen, Indra would hurl his vajra-aayudam, releasing him from the effects of the curse. As the sage predicted, Yagna Sarma went in his demonic form to disrupt the yagnam, and Indra hurled his vajra-aayudam at the demon, killing Yagna Sarma. Indra was performing a prayashchita-yagnam as he had unknowingly killed a sage who was performing tapas in the form of a deer. When the yagnam reached its completion, the Lord is said to have appeared, granting atonement to Indra and moksham to Yagna Sarma.
Another story tells that there was a feud between Bhudevi and Sridevi. Bhudevi claimed that the Lord spends too much time with Sridevi and does not spend enough time with Her. The Lord is said to have solved the problem by placing Bhudevi on one side of His tiruvadigal(His lotus feet) and Sridevi on the other, and constantly looking at both of them, showing that in His eyes, both of them are equal. Thus, when one stands outside the garbha-griha, they cannot see the Lord’s tiruvadigal. To see the Lord’s tiruvadigal, there is a small window on the outside of the garbha-griha through which we can see His tiruvadigal while performing pradakshinam.

Details of Kshethram:

***This kshethram comprises two temples

Moolavar: Devapiran / Aravindalochanan
Thayaar: Karuthadankanni Nachiyar
Vimanam: Kumuda Vimanam
Pushkarani: Varuna Theertham / Thamaraparani River

Travel: This kshethram is one of the Nava Tirupati temples and is located around 3 km from Srivaikuntam.

Azhwar Pasuram:
Nam Azhwar: 11 Pasurams

Sthala Puranam: 
The legend has it that Kubera cursed a couple to assume the forms of a weight-measure (tulai) and a bow (Villu). When Athreya Suprapa Muni was performing a yagnam at this kshethram, he found the scale and the bow in the yagashala. When he touched them, they transformed into a man and a woman and were relieved of the curse. Thus, the kshethram obtained the name Tulaivillimangalam. It is also believed that the Ashwini Devatas worshipped Lord Vishnu at this kshetram with red lotus flowers (Senthamarai Kannan – Aravindalochanan). Lord Devapiran is said to have given darshanam to all the devas after the yagnam attained its completion.

Details of Kshethram:
Moolavar: Mayakoothan
Thayaar: Kulaindaivalli Nachiyar
Vimanam: Anandanilaya Vimanam
Pushkarani: Perungulam Theertham

Travel: This kshethram is one of the Nava Tirupati temples, located 11 km from Srivaikuntam.

Azhwar Pasuram:
Nam Azhwar: 11 Pasurams

Sthala Puranam:
The legend has it that Kamalavathi, the daughter of a brahmin named Vedasaran, meditated on the Lord, intending to marry Him. Pleased with her prayers, the Lord embraced and married her. Hence, this place is called Balika Vanam. It is also said that the Lord slew a demon, Asmacharan, in a Mayayuddham and performed a dance similar to Rudra-tandavam after His victory. Hence, the deity is called Mayakoothan.

Details of Kshethram:
Moolavar: Vaithamanidhi Perumal
Thayaar: Kumudhavalli Nachiyar
Vimanam: Srikara Vimanam
Pushkarani: Kubera Theertham

Travel: This kshethram is one of the Nava Tirupati temples and is located 15 km from Srivari Kshethram.

Azhwar Pasuram:
Nam Azhwar: 12 Pasurams

Sthala Puranam:
Legend tells the story of Kubera losing all his wealth because he had inappropriately seen Devi Parvati. When he asked for Her forgiveness, Devi Parvati asked him to go to Tirukkolur and perform tapas towards Lord Vishnu, and he would regain his wealth. Thus, Kubera is said to have come to this kshethram, and after performing tapas, the Lord appeared as Vaithamanidi Perumal, who brought all of Kubera’s wealth. The Lord is said to have kept Kubera’s wealth under Adisesha and slept over it. Thus, Kubera received their kripa-kataksham in the form of keeping his wealth safe and also gaining interest over time. The Lord’s left-hand houses kajal. The Lord is said to be looking at this hand to find more wealth for Kubera’s treasury.
Another story tells the tale of pralaya-kalam. Dharma is said to have taken a human form and prostrated at the Lord’s feet to fight against adharma. The Lord is said to establish dharma by defeating all factors causing adharma at the time.

*** This kshethram is the avatara sthalam of Madhurakavi Azhwar.

Details of Kshethram:
Moolavar: Makara Nedunkuzhaikkadan
Thayaar: Kuzhaikkaduvalli Nachiyar and Tirupperai Nachiyar
Vimanam: Bhadra Vimanam
Pushkarani: Sukra Pushkarini / Tamaraparani River

Travel: This kshethram is one of the Nava Tirupati temples and is located 5 km from Azhwar Tirunagari on the way to Tiruchendur from Tirunelveli.

Azhwar Pasuram:
Nam Azhwar: 11 Pasurams

Sthala Puranam:
According to legend, Durvasa Maharishi is said to have once visited Karya-Vaikuntham, but Bhoodevi ignored his arrival and did not perform the required athithi-sathkaaram. Thus, Durvasa Maharishi is said to have cursed Bhoodevi, stating that she would become like Sridevi. When the Lord takes His avatars, He stands, sits, lies down, and performs all His activities on Bhoodevi, whereas He has allocated a small position in His heart for Sridevi. Upon hearing this curse, Bhoodevi pleads with the Maharishi to forgive her. Durvasa Maharishi tells Bhoodevi that once a curse is delivered, it cannot be taken back, but she could attain atonement if she performed tapas at Tirupperai. Thus, Bhoodevi is said to come to this kshethram and perform tapas by chanting the ashtakshara mantram. One day, when Bhoodevi went to bathe in the Tamaraparani River before offering her daily penance, She is said to have found a pair of kundalam (earrings) in the shape of makaram (a type of fish). She is said to have presented this makara-kundalam to the Lord, thus relieving Herself from the curse and giving Him the name Makara Nedunkuzhaikkadan.

*** The importance of this kshethram lies in the practice of Varuna Japam. It is said that if one performs Varuna Japam at this kshethram, it will bring rain as desired. It is noted that Varuna sought the help of Makara Nedunkuzhaikkadan Perumal in his time of need.

Details of Kshethram:
Moolavar: Adinathar
Thayaar: Kurukoorvalli Nachiyar
Vimanam: Govinda Vimanam
Pushkarani: Brahma Theertham

Travel: This kshethram is one of the most important Divyadesams. It is located around 25 km from Srivaikuntam.

Azhwar Pasurams:
Nam Azhwar: 11 Pasurams

Sthala Puranam:
Legend says that this Lord is extremely ancient and is said to have appeared before the appearance of Lord Brahma. When Lord Brahma is said to have appeared and become conscious of the Lord, acknowledging Him is said to have asked for a place to establish His idol and perform tapas. The Lord is said to have directed Lord Brahma to Kurugur by giving him the command of tapas kuru. As the Lord commanded Lord Brahma to perform tapas, this kshethram gained the name of Kurugur. Lord Brahma is said to have bathed in the Tamaraparani River and performed tapas. The Lord is said to have emerged as a Swayambhu Moorthy ( self-established and not carved by anyone ). Lord Brahma is said to have performed the prathishtapana of the Lord. Another legend tells the story that Indra was absolved of the curse given by his parents by praying to the Lord at this kshethram. It is believed that Lakshmi meditated on Lord Vishnu when He was on a vow of celibacy. In response to Her request, He accepted Her in marriage in the form of a garland of flowers (Magizha malar maalai).

This kshethram is said to be the avatara sthalam of Nam Azhwar. As we saw in Tirukurungudi, Nam Azhwar’s parents prayed to Kurungudi Nambi for a child who would be like the Lord Himself. It is said that Kurungudi Nambi Himself reincarnated as Nam Azhwar. We shall now see the story of Nam Azhwar, one of the most revered gurus in the Sri Vaishnava Parampara.
Forty-three days had passed since Lord Sri Krishna had ascended to Sri Vaikuntham. A childless couple, Kari and Udayanangai, visited Tirukurungudi to pray for the birth of a child. It is said that they prayed to the Lord for a child who would be like Him. As none in this universe is comparable to Him, it is noted that Nambi Himself reincarnated as Nam Azhwar. Thus, in the Vaikasi month, under Visakha, Nakshatram, Nam Azhwar was born. As soon as he was born, he exhibited very peculiar behavior in the form of not crying or suckling. The couple, out of concern, is said to have taken the baby to the Adinatha Perumal Temple to pray to the Lord for the baby’s well-being. Nam Azhwar is also said to be an amshavataram of Sri  Vishwakshenar, who is said to be third in line in the Acharya Parampara after the Lord Sriman Narayana and Mahalakshmi Thayaar. The couple is said to have tied a cradle near the Tamarind tree that was present in the temple courtyard.

The baby is said to have crawled out of the cradle and into a small, crater-like space within the tree, where it started a deep meditation. The baby is said to have stayed in this meditative state for sixteen years. At this time, Madurakavi Azhwar is said to have been at Ayodhya and offering argyam as per his Nityakarmam when he saw a blinding light at the edge of the horizon. Recognizing the meditative nature of the divine light is said to have started to follow the light. In pursuit of the light, Madurakavi Azhwar is said to have traveled south, crossing Tiruvenkatam, then Tiruvallikeni, then Sri Rangam, then Madurai, and finally reaching Kurugur. When Madurakavi Azhwar reached the divine tree, he saw a child in a deep meditative state and was worried if the child was still alive or not. Madurakavi Azhwar is said to have thrown a rock near the boy to test his consciousness. When the boy opened his eyes, Madurakavi Azhwar is said to have asked a question: “Sethathin Vayatrill Siriyadhu Pirandhaal Yeththai Thindru Enge Kiddakum?“. Madurakavi Azhwar was referring to the Jeevaathma. Madurakavi Azhwar asked, "When the jeevaathma enters a lifeless body, how would it survive, what would it feed on, and how would it sustain itself?" This is when Nam Azhwar is said to have first spoken by saying, “Aththaith Thindru Ange Kidakkum.”. Nam Azhwar’s reply said that the lifeless body would experience the pleasures and pains of life before attaining paramapadam or moksham. Madurakavi Azhwar was so stunned by the boy’s response that he begged to be his disciple. Madurakavi Azhwar composed 11 Pasurams in praise of his Acharya, Swami Nam Azhwar, known as Kanninun Shiruthambu, which are included among the 4000 Nalayira Divya Prabandham.
When Nam Azhwar was ready to attain paramapadam, Madurakavi Azhwar asked Nam Azhwar with full of tears, what to do next. Nam Azhwar advised Madurakavi Azhwar to boil the waters of Tamraparni, and he said that an idol would form during the boiling of the water. Madurakavi Azhwar followed Nam Azhwar’s advice. When he had boiled the waters of Tamraparni, He got an idol of Bhagavad Ramanuja. He was surprised to see that the idol was different from what he had expected. He went to Nam Azhwar with the idol, and the latter told him that this idol was that of a Bhavishyadhacharya (Future Acharya) and that he would be born 4000 years from then. He again advised boiling the waters of Tamraparni. Madurakavi Azhwar once again boiled the waters of Tamraparni and finally got the idol of Nam Azhwar.
Every year on the Tirunakashthram of Nam Azhwar, the NavaTirupati Brahmotsavam is concluded, and the teerthavaari uthsavam is performed where the idol of Nam Azhwar is brought to the Tamaraparani River, and along with Sri Sudharshana ChakrathAzhwar, Nam Azhwar’s Idol is also dipped in the holy waters of the river.

Thayaar: Kothai Nachiyar
Vimanam: Samsana Vimanam
Pushkarani: Tirmukkulam Theertham

Travel: This kshethram is located near Tenkasi on the Tenkasi-Virudhunagar road.
