Periya Azhwar: 1 pasuram
Sri Andal: 1 pasuram
Total: 2 Pasurams

*** One peculiarity that can be seen here is that one can see Garudan standing inside the sanctum sanctorum alongside the Lord.

Sthala Puranam:
This kshethram is the avatara sthalam for both Periya Azhwar and Sri Andal.
In the then Pandya kingdom, there was a small town called Putthoor, where great scholars and pundits were residing. Nearby, there was a forest where hunters were living. The chief of these hunters had two sons named Villi and Kandan. One day, Villi and Kandan went to the forest for hunting as usual. They spotted a tiger, and it escaped the arrows from their bows. Kandan started chasing vigorously and went deep into the forest. After some time, the tiger hid behind a tree and pounced on Kandan, killing him. Villi waited for his brother for a long time and started searching for him. When he spotted the dead body of his brother, his heart almost stopped with grief, and he cried heavily and fell unconscious on his brother’s body. During his unconsciousness, he had a scene in front of his eyes; Sriman Narayana, along with Mahalakshmi, appeared and instructed Villi to stop lamenting. They told him that They would bring his brother back to life. The two brothers would then search for a giant banyan tree in the middle of the forest, where they would find Lord Vatapatrashayee, who had been lying there for a very long time. The divine couple also told Villi that they would find a cave nearby with treasures that one could never even dream of. They further instructed that the brothers were to use that wealth to deforest the area and construct a magnificent temple that had never been seen before. Saying this, the Divine couple disappeared. When Villi came back to consciousness, he did not know whether what he saw (in his unconscious state) was true at all, and was confused. But suddenly, Kandan got up alive as if he had just woken up from sleep (without any wounds even). Villi explained the whole thing to his brother, and both of them hugged each other for having been blessed by the Lord and having been chosen by the Lord to establish the temple.

Soon, many Vaishnava scholars began to migrate towards Putthoor, among them  Mukunda Bhattar and his wife, Padmavalli. The couple was ardent devotees of Sri Vatapatrashayee. On an auspicious day, the couple was blessed with a son, named Vishnuchittar. The child lived up to his name by constantly finding ways to contemplate how to find the Lord’s days. As time passed, he would perform pushpa-kainkaryam to Sri Vatapatrashayee. As he aged, he sold his property. He purchased a small plot of land near the temple, which he converted into a Nandavanam, where he cultivated various creepers, vines, fragrant flowers, and tulasi plants. The plot also featured a small pond with crystal-clear water. Vishnuchittar would spend his time cultivating his garden, plucking the flowers, and making garlands for the Lord. Over time, his small plot was allowed to expand and transform into a vast, flourishing garden with a lovely scent due to all the flowers that bloomed within it. Soon, he married a woman who shared his ideals of serving the Lord. 

During that time, there was a king named Vallabhadevan, whose capital was situated in Madurai. He was an ardent devotee of Lord Vishnu and wished to learn the meaning of the Vedas and Upanishads. He enquired with his chief minister as to how he could achieve this goal. The minister suggested that the king call all the Vedic Scholars present in his kingdom to debate and question all the matters present in the Vedas and Upanishads. The one who could solve all the questions posed by the king would be rewarded dearly. The king agreed with the minister’s suggestion, and soon an announcement was made throughout the kingdom saying there would be a grand meeting of all the Vedic Scholars in the land. The scholar who would impress the king with their answers would be rewarded with gold coins, which would be hung in a divine binding. The coins would present themselves to the person who would aptly answer all of the king’s questions. Many scholars came before the king, but none gave satisfactory answers that the king desired. One night, Lord Vatapatrashayee appeared in Vishnuchittar‘s dreams and instructed him to go to the king’s court to claim the prize that was being offered. Vishnuchittar told the Lord that he knew nothing about the Vedas or Upanishads. All he knew to do was to make garlands and present them to the Lord. The Lord then told Vishnuchittar not to worry and to go to the royal court. The Lord said He would speak through the mouth of Vishnuchittar. That same night, the Lord also appeared in the dreams of the chief minister and asked him to make royal arrangements to receive Vishnuchittar and escort him to the king’s court. 

The next morning, a royal elephant with palanquins arrived and carried Vishnuchittar to the royal court. As he entered, all the scholars began to murmur and pass sarcastic comments about him, knowing that his knowledge was limited. Vishnuchittar prostrated himself before the king and the gathered scholars, and then began his speech on the Vedas and Upanishads. As and when the king questioned, it was almost as though the answer to the question was pre-prepared and ready. Finally, to close his speech, Vishnuchittar made a final statement that said, “Sriman Narayanane Paramporul.” This translates to “It is Lord Sriman Narayana who is the only protector, and it is with His blessing that the universe is surviving. It is He and only He who is the underlying principle that is mentioned in the four Vedas and Upanishads. When this statement was made, the binding came undone, and the gold coins showered into Vishnuchittar‘s hands from above. The king was overcome with joy and ecstasy. All the gathered scholars lowered their heads in shame. The king then asked Vishnuchittar how he had spoken about all the Vedas and Upanishads in such simple language. Vishnuchittar then told the king that truly it was he who had spoken and that the Lord himself intended for this to perspire. The king was deeply moved by what Vishnuchittar said and fell to his feet. He arranged for complete royal honors and sent him around the kingdom in a royal procession. At one point, when Vishnuchittar looked up at the sky, he saw the Lord along with Mahalakshmi seated atop Garudan, granting their blessing to him. It was at that moment that, with eyes filled with tears of joy, he said the words“pallaandu, pallaandu pallayiratthandu palakodi noorayiram.” These words are still sung to date during sathumorai seva every day, whether it may be at a temple or within a household.
Periya Azhwar being taken on the royal procession and seeing the Lord and Mahalakshmi

Life went back to normal for Vishnuchittar, and he continued his pushpa-kainkaryam for Lord Vatapatrashayee. Once, while plucking flowers in the garden, he found a child on a flower in the garden and named her Andal and brought her up in the service of the Lord. One day, Periya Azhwar(Vishnuchittar) found Andal wearing the garland meant for the Lord. Discarding that garland, he prepared fresh garlands and offered them to the Lord. PeriaAzhwar was surprised to see the Lord refusing to accept the garland except the one used by Andal. Hence, Andal is called Shoodi Kudutha Nachiyar. As per the wishes of the Lord, Periya Azhwar gave Andal in marriage to Sri Ranganathar in Sri Rangam, and Andal, on entering the sanctum, merged with the Lord.

Sri Andal is said to be the reincarnation of Bhoodevi. When Lord Varaha saved Bhoodevi from the grasp of Hiranyaksha, He is said to have delivered various Brahma-gyanam to Bhoodevi. It is noted that Bhoodevi came in this form to provide that knowledge to the people in a way that they would understand it simply. Thus, Sri Andal wrote 30 Pasurams known as Tirupavai and Nachiyar Tirumozhi, which contain 143 Pasurams that convey all the knowledge that was given by Sri Varaha Perumal to Bhoodevi on that day.
Even to date, on the tirunakshtram of Sri Andal, Tiruaadipooram Utsavam is observed on a very grand scale. This is the time when brahmotsavam is done here, and a massive number of devotees throng to see this grand celebration.

Details of Kshethram:
Moolavar: Ninra Narayanan Perumal
Thayaar: Senkamala Nachiyar
Vimanam: Devachandra Vimanam
Pushkarani: Papavinasa Theertham

Travel: This kshethram is located 3 km from Shivakasi, on the Virudhunagar-Tenkasi road.

Azhwar Pasuram:
Tirumangai Azhwar: 4 Pasurams
Bhoodath Azhwar: 1 pasuram
Total: 5 Pasurams

Sthala Puranam:
The Lord here is standing along with His four consorts, namely, Sridevi, Bhoodevi, Neeladevi, and Jambhavathi.
Jambhavathi is the daughter of Jambavan, who is seen in the Ramayana. The story of how the Lord married Jambhavathi is as follows. Lord Krishna’s royal treasurer Satrajit, used to house the Syamantaka Mani ( a divine gem that is said to give an unlimited amount of treasure ). Once, Lord Krishna is said to have asked to see this gem, but Satrajit refused. Soon, one day, Satrajit’s brother is said to have worn the gem and gone out into the forest to hunt and did not return. When Satrajit noticed that the gem was missing, he blamed it on Krishna, saying He had stolen it. Lord Krishna is said to have gone into the forest to prove his innocence. When the Lord was deep in the forest, He found Satrajit’s brother’s body covered in the mauling of a lion. He decided to check around the area further and soon saw a glimmering twinkle emanating from a nearby cave. When He went to probe the source of the twinkle, He noticed the gem in the hands of a female bear and approached her to claim the gem and clear His name when another male bear attacked Him. Lord Krishna fought a long-drawn battle with the bear, with neither side giving in. Soon, Lord Krishna realized that the bear was none other than Jambavan, one of His generals in the time of the Ramayana. Lord Krishna reveals Himself as Lord Rama to Jambavan, and their fight comes to an end. Jambavan returns the gem to Lord Krishna, and along with the gem, he gives his daughter’s hand in marriage to Lord Krishna. The female bear is transformed into a beautiful maiden, who is Jambhavathi.
This kshethram is where Aniruddha was married to Banasura’s daughter, Usha. The story is as follows.
Banasura was the king of Sonitpur (a modern-day district in Assam). Bana was an ardent devotee of Lord Shiva. By the grace of Lord Shiva, Bana had received a thousand hands with which he used to play the mridangam for the Lord. One day, when Lord Shiva was dancing, he granted Banasura a boon that he would personally protect him no matter the circumstance. Banasura had a daughter named Usha. Usha was an ardent devotee of Devi Parvati.  Devi Parvati blesses Usha, saying a man would appear in her dream,s and he would be the one that she would get married to. After a few days, Usha had a dream of a man. He had broad shoulders, a slender waist, coral-like lips, a lotus-like face, and eyes that seemed to resemble the sun and the moon. Usha had a friend named Chitralekha who could draw an exact copy of any description that was placed before her. Thus, as Usha described, Chitralekha drew a picture of the man she dreamed of. When both of them went through to see who the person in the photo was, they discovered that the person in the picture was Aniruddha, the grandson of Shree Krishna. Chitralekha also possessed another power, enabling her to teleport herself to any place she wished and bring back anyone she willed. Therefore, at night, Usha asked Chitralekha to bring Aniruddha to the palace without her father realizing, as her father was a sworn enemy of Shree Krishna.
Chitralekha did as instructed and brought Aniruddha to Usha’s royal quarters. Soon, news reached Banasura, saying Usha was enjoying the company of an unknown man within her personal quarters. Banasura rushed in a fury and bound Aniruddha with a thousand snakes. The news was then sent to Dwarka that Banasura was holding both Usha and Aniruddha hostage. Krishna, along with Balarama, immediately left for Sonitpur on Garuda. As soon as Krishna and Balarama reached Sonitpur, they challenged Banasura to war and demanded that Aniruddha be released and that Usha be married to Aniruddha. Banasura refused and commanded his army to attack Krishna and Balarama. Krishna and Balarama effortlessly beat Banasura’s army.
Soon, Banasura was left alone to face Krishna and Balarama, having prayed to Lord Shiva for protection. Lord Shiva first sent his Ganas to face Krishna and Balarama. When the Ganas were defeated, Lord Shiva himself appeared to face Lord Krishna and Balarama. Lord Shiva and Lord Krishna engaged in a fierce battle, neither side yielding an inch. Lord Shiva was soon left with only his set of divyastras. Lord Shiva released the Pashupatastra, and in response, Lord Krishna released the Narayana-Astra. The divine weapons clashed, creating massive explosions. Finally, Lord Shiva executed his final weapon in the form of a plague called Rudra-Jwaram. Lord Krishna replied to this in the form of an antidote called Vaishnava-Jwaram. Lord Krishna countered Lord Shiva completely, while Lord Balarama defeated Lord Karthikeya. Banasura was now bereft of any protection and open to attack. Lord Krishna then sent his Sudharshana Chakra behind Banasura. Sudharshana chased after Banasura and cut off 996 of his 1000 arms. Banasura was left completely humiliated, and he had no other choice but to comply with the wishes of Lord Krishna and Balarama. Aniruddha and Usha were released from prison and got married.

Sthala Puranam:
This kshethram shares many aspects of its Sthala Puranam with that of Srivilliputtur. We will see the story of Periya Azhwar once again.
Periya Azhwar ( Vishnuchittar ) used to live in Srivilliputtur, leading a straightforward lifestyle, performing pushpa-kainkaryam to Sri Vatapatrashayee. During that time, there was a king named Vallabhadevan, whose capital was situated in Madurai. He was an ardent devotee of Lord Vishnu and wished to learn the meaning of the Vedas and Upanishads. He enquired with his chief minister as to how he could achieve this goal. The minister suggested that the king call all the Vedic Scholars present in his kingdom to debate and question all the matters present in the Vedas and Upanishads. The one who could solve all the questions posed by the king would be rewarded dearly. The king agreed with the minister’s suggestion, and soon an announcement was made throughout the kingdom saying there would be a grand meeting of all the Vedic Scholars in the land. The scholar who would impress the king with their answers would be rewarded with gold coins, which would be hung in a divine binding. The coins would present themselves to the person who would aptly answer all of the king’s questions. Many scholars came before the king, but none gave satisfactory answers that the king desired. One night, Lord Vatapatrashayee appeared in Vishnuchittar‘s dreams and instructed him to go to the king’s court to claim the prize that was being offered. Vishnuchittar told the Lord that he knew nothing about the Vedas or Upanishads. All he knew to do was to make garlands and present them to the Lord. The Lord then told Vishnuchittar not to worry and to go to the court. The Lord said He would speak through the mouth of Vishnuchittar. That same night, the Lord also appeared in the dreams of the chief minister and asked him to make royal arrangements to receive Vishnuchittar and escort him to the king’s court. 

The next morning, a royal elephant with palanquins arrived and carried Vishnuchittar to the royal court. As he entered, all the scholars began to murmur and pass sarcastic comments about him, knowing that his knowledge was limited. Vishnuchittar prostrated himself before the king and the gathered scholars, and then began his speech on the Vedas and Upanishads. As and when the king questioned, it was almost as though the answer to the question was pre-prepared and ready. Finally, to close his speech, Vishnuchittar made a final statement that said, “Sriman Narayanane Paramporul.” This translates to “It is Lord Sriman Narayana who is the only protector, and it is with His blessing that the universe is surviving. It is He and only He who is the underlying principle that is mentioned in the four Vedas and Upanishads. When this statement was made, the binding came undone, and the gold coins showered into Vishnuchittar‘s hands from above. The king was overcome with joy and ecstasy. All the gathered scholars lowered their heads in shame. The king then asked Vishnuchittar how he had spoken about all the Vedas and Upanishads in such simple language. Vishnuchittar then told the king that truly it was he who had spoken and that the Lord himself intended for this to perspire. The king was deeply moved by what Vishnuchittar said and fell to his feet. He arranged for complete royal honors and sent him around the kingdom in a royal procession. At one point, when Vishnuchittar looked up at the sky, he saw the Lord along with Mahalakshmi seated atop Garudan, granting their blessing to him. It was at that moment that, with eyes filled with tears of joy, he said the words, “Pallaandu, pallaandu pallayiratthandu palakodi noorayiram.” These words are still sung to date during sathumorai seva every day, whether it may be at a temple or within a household. 
*** One of the peculiarities observed in this temple is the presence of a Navagraha Sannidhanam. Usually, one does not observe Navagraha Sannidhanam in a Sri Vaishnava temple.
Another specialty of this temple is the Ashtanga Vimanam. It is one of the few temples in the country built in tiers. One can climb up and take a closer look at the Ashtanga Vimanam, which enshrines Pallikonda Perumal in one of its levels, and Surya Narayanan in a standing posture in the other. This aspect of a vimanam, consisting of three tiers enshrining three different postures of Lord Vishnu — sitting, standing, and reclining — is unique in South Indian temple architecture. The shadow of the Vimanam never falls on the ground.

Sthala Puranam:
Legend has it that Yama, the lord of death, once undertook a pilgrimage. While visiting all the holy shrines, he was drawn to the serenity and beauty of Azhagar Malai and meditated on Lord Vishnu, asking Him to reside in the beautiful surroundings for the benefit of the people. Responding to Yama’s request, the Lord ordered Viswakarma, the architect of the celestials, to construct a temple for Him there. The Lord took this place as His permanent abode with his consorts, Sri Devi and Bhoo Devi. There is also an interesting story that the water used by Brahma to wash the feet of the Lord in the Trivikrama Avatara passed through the anklets and fell at this kshethram. Hence, the nearby river is called Noopura Gangai or Silambu Aaru. The river water is being used for Tirumanjanam to the deity.

In the Tamil month of Aipassi, during the Shukla Paksham on the day of Dwadashi, a special utsavam known as Thotti Tirumanjanam is conducted. During this utsavam, the utsava murthy of the Lord is brought outside the temple to a small cave where the Noopura Gangai flows. The Lord’s hair is oiled with medicinal oils, and tirumanjanam is performed with Noopura Gangai falling from a small height on the Lord’s head.
Sri Andal, in one of her Pasurams, had written that she wished to present to Lord Kallazhagar 100 gangalams (a type of vessel made of copper and/or brass), each of butter and pounded rice. It is said that Bhagawad Ramanujar read this pasuram and decided to make her poetic wishes a reality, presenting the Lord with 100 gangalams, each made of butter and pounded rice.

The legend has it that the Devas came together (goshti) to worship the Lord at this kshetram to rid the universe of the demon Hiranyakashipu. This temple is also considered Dakshina Badri. This is probably the most important kshetrham according to the Sri Vaishnava Parampara, as it is the kshetram where Swami Bhagawad Ramanujar first performed the Ashtakshara Mantropadesham. Let us see the story. Swami Ramanujar came here to this kshethram to seek education from Sri Tirukkotiyur Nambigal. Sri Tirukkotiyur Nambigal is said to have rejected giving Swami Ramanujar education seventeen times, sending him back to Sri Rangam. When Swami Ramanujar came back for the eighteenth time, Sri Tirukkotiyur Nambigal is said to have revealed the ashtakshara mantram and the charama shlokam to Swami Ramanujar and instructed him to keep it a secret. Swami Ramanujar realized that this mantram and shloka were the means to Sri Vaikuntham. Thus, Swami Ramanujar is said to have climbed up to the top of the Ashtanga Vimanam and openly revealed that he possessed the ashtakshara mantram as well as the charama shlokam and was willing to pass it on to anyone who so wished to listen to him. When Sri Tirukkotiyur Nambigal learned of this, he immediately pursued Swami Ramanujar. He told him that he was destined to go to hell because he had not listened to his guru’s wishes. Swami Ramanujar is then supposed to have said that he was more than ready to go to hell if he could provide the means for so many people to go to Vaikuntham. Sri Tirukkotiyur Nambigal then realizes his mistake and is said to have asked for forgiveness of Swami Ramanujar after seeing his broad outlook.

Legend has it that Adi Jagannatha Perumal is said to have been present at this kshetram even before Dasharatha came with Kaikeyi to conquer South India. It is noted that Dasharatha performed tapas to this Lord to have children.
Legend tells that Lord Rama reached the seashore where Vibhishana performed sharanagathi. As the army contemplated how to cross the ocean, Vibhishana advised Lord Rama to pray to Samudraraja by performing praayopavesham (fast for three days and nights) to allow their passage over his waters to reach Lanka. Thus, Lord Rama is said to have sat in Padmasanam on a bed made of darbha grass with the Anjali mudra for three days. When Samudraraja did not show himself, in a rage, Lord Rama told Lakshmana to hand Him His bow and an arrow. The Lord mounts the arrow and tells Samudraraja that He would make all the water in the ocean evaporate if he did not show himself. As the Lord was about to fire His deadly weapon, Samudraraja appears and falls at Lord Rama’s feet and tells the army that Nal and Neel were phenomenal architects and that they could build a bridge that would float on the oceanic waters, granting Lord Rama and His army passage over the ocean to Sri Lanka. As Lord Rama sat on a bed made of darbha, this kshethram is called Pullaranya Kshethram.
*** The water at this kshethram is considered very holy, as it was the starting point of the Ramasethu. Thus, taking a bath here or sethu-snanam is considered to absolve all sins. Along with sethu-snanam, performing tarpanam here at this kshetram is considered highly auspicious.

Sthala Puranam:
The deity Satyagirinathan is depicted in a reclining posture inside a rock-cut temple. Garuda, Markandeya, and Brahma flank him, all witnessing the events that unfold around Him. According to tradition, the demons Madhu and Kaitabha stole the Vedas and attempted to abduct Mahalakshmi. She is shown in the panel, frightened and hiding near the Lord’s tiruvadi. In response, Adisesha, who serves as the Lord’s bed, emits poisonous fumes in the form of jwala (fiery orbs) to frighten the demons. The Lord is said to have retrieved the Vedas and protected Mahalakshmi from harm.
The panel shows both Madhu, who is soft by nature, and Kaitabha, who is fierce and aggressive, advancing toward the Lord. On one side, Bhoomadevi approaches the Lord seeking refuge at the Lord’s tiruvadi. Sri Devi is seen near the head of Adisesha, also seeking refuge. The Lord raises His hand to offer assurance to Sri Devi and lifts His gaze toward Bhoomadevi to reassure her.
Above the Lord, Adisesha is seen releasing the jwala from his mouth, directed at the demons. At the top of the composition, Yama Dharmaraja and Chitragupta are depicted recording the moment in their ledger, signifying that the end of Madhu and Kaitabha is near.
The entire episode is captured within a single panel, carved in stone. It includes the fear of Mahalakshmi, the supplication of Bhoomadevi and Sri Devi, the aggression of the demons, the Lord’s protective gestures, the fury of Adisesha, and the presence of Yama and Chitragupta as cosmic witnesses. The depiction is dynamic and composed, presenting a complete narrative within a single visual frame.

This kshethram is said to be one of the eight Swayam Vyaktha kshetrams. The other swayam Vyaktha kshethram are Sri Rangam, Srimushnam, Salagramam, Thotadri (Vaanamamalai), Tirupati, Pushkaram, and Badri.
This Naimisharanya kshethram is said to be regarded as a Tapovanam. There are 9 tapovams. They are Dandakaranyam, Saindhavaranyam, Jambhukaranyam, Pushkararanyam, Utpalaranyam, Badrikaranyam, Gurujangalaranyam, Aruputharanyam and Naimisharanayam. It is believed that the perumal is found in the form of a forest. And this Naimisharanyam is viewed as a holy forest.This Naimisaranya kshethram is said to be regarded as Tapovanam. There are nine tapovams. They are Dandakaranyam, Saindhavaranyam, Jambhukaranyam, Pushkararanyam, Utpalaranyam, Badrikaranyam, Gurujangalaranyam, Aruputharanyam and Naimisaranayam. It is believed that the perumal is found in the form of a forest, and this Naimisharanyam is regarded as the holiest forest. The Emperumaan of this sthalam is giving his seva as the entire form of the Vanam (forest). In their old age, all the Maharishis, along with Sownakar, went towards Lord Brahma and asked him which is the best place suited for doing Yagam and tapas. As the answer, Lord Brahma took a dharbai grass and made it into a wheel shape, and rolled the dharbai grass. Lord Brahma said that after he rolls the grass, the place where it stops is considered the ideal location for performing tapas and yagam. He rolled the wheel, and it stopped at a particular place on Earth. That place is said to be Naimisharanyam. Nemi means a wheel, and Naimisham means the place where the wheel landed. Aaranyam means forest. Since Nemi, the Chakkaram that landed in Aaranya's forest, the sthalam is called Naimisharanyam. This Naimisaranyam is said to be the place where most of the rishis performed sacrifices, tapas, and meditation, and explained the meaning of the old Puranas and Vedas. The Lord gives his seva in the form of Nature. The Lord here gives his seva with the name as Sri Devaraja Perumal along with Sri Hari Lakshmi and gives his audience (prathyaksham) to Devendran, Sudharma, Devarishis, Soodhapuranika, and Vedavyasa.

It is said that taking a bath in the Chakra Theertham absolves all sins.
Gayasuran did tapas in this sthalam. Sriman Narayanan gave His audience to him as his tapas fulfilled him. The Lord asked him what boon he wanted as a result of complete tapas. But Gayasooran answered the Almighty that he didn’t want any boon from him, as he was already so powerful. He asked that anyone who met him should be entitled to get moksham. The Lord did not want immoral souls to attain moksham just by meeting him. The Lord said that the boon that Gayasuran was asking for could not be fulfilled in the way he was asking. Gayasuran then asked the Lord to present the souls for whom shraadham is performed upon his body to be given moksham. The Lord then said that this would be possible. Thus, Gayasuran grew to an enormous size, and the Lord sent his chakram to kill the asura, and his body was cut into three parts. The three parts are Siro Gaya (the head part), Nabhi Gaya (the middle part), and Charana Gaya (the foot part). This sthalam, the Naimisaranyam, is said to be the Nabhi Gaya. The Gaya kshethram is said to be the Charana Gaya, and Badri is said to be Siro Gaya. Offering shraadham to departed souls in all these three sthalams is said to grant moksham to them.

According to Srimad Bhagavatham, Lord Vishnu, in His incarnations as Nara and Narayana, performed deep tapas for time immemorial for the well-being of all living entities. According to legend, when Nara and Narayana were performing tapas in a place where Badri trees were growing. At one point, the sunlight became very intense. Thus, to protect the Lord from the sunlight, Lakshmi Devi is said to have taken the form of a Badri tree and grown in such a way as to provide shade to the Lord.
This fact is reiterated in the Mahabharata when Lord Krishna tells Arjuna that in their previous lives, Arjuna was the manifestation of Nara, and He was the manifestation of Narayana. The Pandavas are said to have visited this kshethram before embarking on their final journeys to Mana, from where they left their bodies to reach Paramapadam. Mana is 4 km from this kshethram.
This is one of the Swayam-Vyaktha Kshethrams. It is said that there are five Badri kshethrams. Together, they are known as Pancha Badri Kshethram. Vishal Badri (Badrinath Temple installed by Sri Adi Shankaracharya), Yogadhyan Badri (where the Lord is in a meditative posture), Bhavishya Badri (Badri of the future), Vridha Badri (the original shrine where Vishwakarma carved the idol), Adi Badri. It is said that the Lord appeared in Sri Adi Shankaracharya’s dream and told him that he would find His idol inside the tapta-kundam ( hot springs ) present outside, where the present-day temple is situated. It is said that Sri Adi Shankaracharya dipped in the spring multiple times before finding the Lord’s idol. To date, the pooja is performed by nambudhri brahmins who follow the Kerala style of pooja.

Sthala Puranam: 
This is the kshethram where Lord Sri Krishna grew up, slew demons, and performed his leelas. In the present day, we can see Shri Nand Yashodha Bhavan, the house where the Lord was brought and grew up. In the present-day scenario, this is the main temple. In the garbha gudi, we can see Lord Balarama alongside Yashodha and Nanda. Lord Krishna can be seen in a cradle with a rope, which is given to devotees to comfort the Lord. Another important place in this kshethram is the Raman Reti. This is the place where Lord Krishna played as a child. This is the place where Lord Krishna ate mud and showed Yashodha the entire creation by opening His mouth. It is customary to roll in the sand, as this is the place where the Lord stepped and played. People take the sand from this place asa form of  prasadam.

Sthala Puranam:
Legend has it that Lord Krishna built the city of Dwarka with the assistance of Vishwakarma. After Lord Krishna had killed Kansa, his two wives became widows. Kansa’s wives were the daughters of Jarasandha. Jarasandha swore to exact revenge against Lord Krishna, who had caused his daughters to suffer a cruel fate. Jarasandha attacked Mathura seventeen times. Each of these seventeen times, Lord Krishna defended Mathura. After all these attacks, Lord Krishna deemed that Mathura was no longer fit for stay as Jarasandha would continue to attack the state. Lord Krishna orders Vishwakarma to claim land from Samudraraja and convert it into a grand city that would be safe from any form of invasion. Thus, Dwarka came into being. Dwarka is among the Mukthi Kshethrams along with Ayodhya, Mathura, Maya (Haridwar), Kashi, Kanchipuram, and Avantika (Ujjain).
Apart from this divyadesam, there are four other Dwarkas. Together, the five kshethrams are collectively known as PanchaDwarka.
The five Dwarkas include:
Dwarka
Rukmini Dwarka
Beyt Dwarka
Dakor Dwarka
Shrinathji Dwarka


Rukmini Dwarka:
This kshethram is located 3.1 km from Dwarka. This Dwarka houses Rukmini Devi, whom Durvasa Maharishi cursed to stay away from Lord Krishna. Performing neer-daanam at this kshethram is of importance. Even the prasadam offered here is that of water

Beyt Dwarka:
This kshethram is located on an island off the coast of mainland India. To reach this kshetram, one must travel by boat from Okha Port or by road using the Sudarshana Setu. This kshethram was once connected to the mainland. It is said that after Lord Krishna left this world for Paramapadam, the land that connected the mainland to this kshethram was reclaimed by Samudraraja. This is the kshethram where Sudama visited the Lord to ask for alms. Sudama never asked for anything from the Lord, but he was presented with more than he could ever have asked for. It is said that Meerabai attained moksham here at this kshethram when she merged with the Lord.

Dakor Dwarka:
This kshethram is located near Anand in Gujarat. The Lord is called Ranchodraiji. It is said that in the seventeenth encounter with Jarasandha, the Lord started to run from the battlefield when He was faced against an asuran called Kaalayavanan. It is said that the Lord left the battlefield near Mathura and ran till the Junagadh district in modern-day Gujarat. Here, there was an ancient sooryavanshi king named Muchukunda who lay asleep after gaining a boon from Indra. There was once a great battle between the devas and the asuras. To win the battle, Indra took the help of Lord Ram’s ancestor, King Muchukunda. After winning the battle for the devas, Indra gave Muchukunda the boon that he could sleep for a long time to take a rest after the long and drawn-out battle. When Muchukunda would awake from this sleep, the first thing he would lay his eyes would turn into ash. Lord Krishna ran into the cave and awoke Muchukunda from his sleep in such a way that the first person he would lay his eyes on would be Kaalayavanan. When Kaalayavanan came in Muchukunda’s line of sight, he turned to ash. The idol of the Lord present at Dakor Dwarka is said to have originally been in Dwarka. After the idol was brought to Dakor, another idol that Devi Rukmini was worshiping was installed in the temple at Dwarka.

Shrinathji Dwarka:
This kshethram is located in Nathdwara, Rajasthan. This kshethram was established by Sri Vallabhacharya. The idol is said to have been installed in this temple by Meerabai. The idol is said to be a swayambhu moorthy, which is believed to have originated from the Govardhana Parvatham and became the object of worship in the Mevar Royal family, where Meerabai was born.

thala Puranam:
Hiranyaksha’s brother, Hiranyakashipu, was a great demon emperor who dominated the earth. He performed great penance to Lord Brahma. After centuries of penance, Brahma finally appeared in front of Hiranyakashipu and told him that he had appeared to grant him a boon for the penance that Hiranyakashipu had performed. Hiranyakashipu asked for immortality. Brahma said it was against the law of nature and that it was not in his power to grant this boon, and asked him to rethink what he desired. Hiranyakashipu thought for a while and asked for a boon that would be equivalent to immortality. He asked that he shouldn’t be killed by man nor animal, not be killed inside the house nor outside, not be killed at day nor at night, not be killed in space nor on the surface of the earth. Further, he should not be killed by anything that Brahma created. Brahma granted this and disappeared. Soon, Hiranyakashipu became a tyrant and a ruthless king. He soon had a son named Prahalada. Prahalada was a great devotee of Lord Vishnu. Hiranyakashipu considered Lord Vishnu as his mortal enemy, as he had incarnated himself to kill his brother Hiranyaksha. When Prahalada was in his mother’s womb, Sage Narada had narrated tales of the Lord to his mother. As the mother heard the stories, so did the fetus. When Prahalada was admitted to Gurukulam, he changed the views of all his teachers and all the students, advising them to praise the Lord instead of his father. When Hiranyakashipu came to know of the events that were taking place in the Gurukulam, he took measures to try and kill his son. He tried to get him trampled by an elephant, feed him poison, imprison him without food, and throw him into a raging flame. None of his methods produced the results that he wanted. He then brings Prahalada to his royal court. He asked him how he was surviving all the deadly situations. He said the Lord was protecting him. He also said that the Lord is within everyone, including his father. Hiranyakashipu then drew his mace and pointed to a pillar and asked him if his Lord was present in that particular pillar. When Prahalada said yes, Hiranyakashipu smashed the pillar, and from that pillar, the Lord emerged in the form of a man-lion. The incarnation had the face of a lion and the body of a man. The Lord’s rage knew no bounds. He dragged Hiranyakashipu to the doorstep and sat on the separating junction, which is neither inside nor outside the home. The Lord placed Hiranyakashipu on his lap, which was neither in space nor on Earth. Then the Lord used his nails at a time of sunset, which was neither day nor night, and dug into the stomach of Hiranyakashipu, ripping out his intestines and putting an end to the tyrant.
The legend has it that Garuda was desirous of seeing Lord Vishnu in His Narasimha avataram; thus, he meditated upon Him at the Ugra Sthambham, and the Lord manifested Himself as nine forms of Narasimha.
1. BHARGAVA NARASIMHA SWAMY
The Bhargava Narasimha Swamy is situated at a distance of two km from the Lower Ahobilam, on a hill, near the sacred pond, known as ‘Bhargava Theertham,’ where Bhargava Rama(Parashurama) performed his penance. Hence, the Lord of the temple is known as Bhargava Narasimha Swamy.

2. YOGANANDA NARASIMHA SWAMY
This temple is to the southeast of Lower Ahobilam at a distance of 2 km. The popular legend is that after killing Hiranyakasipu, Lord Narasimha taught Prahlada several yogic postures. Therefore, the Lord in this aspect is called Yogananda Narasimha.

3. CHATHRAVATA NARASIMHA SWAMY
About three km from Lower Ahobilam, the image of the deity is installed under a peepal tree, surrounded by thorny bushes. Hence, the Lord is called Chathravata Narasimha Swamy. The Lord can be seen placing the thalam with one of His hands. It is said that the Lord is enjoying the musical service of two yakshas named Haha and Huhu.

4. AHOBILA NARASIMHA SWAMY
The temple, situated on Upper Ahobilam, at a distance of eight kilometers from Lower Ahobilam, is the main temple and the earliest of the nine temples there. The Lord here appears in his fierce aspect, known as Ugra Narasimha, the presiding deity of the temple and also referred to as Ahobila Nrisimha Swamy. It is firmly believed that Lord Narasimha was ‘Swayambhu’ (self-manifest) here.

5. KRODAKARA (VARAHA) NARASIMHA SWAMY
The temple of this Lord is one kilometer away from the main temple of Ahobila Nrisimha Swamy on the Upper Ahobilam. The image of the deity features the Lord with tusk-like teeth (Varaha-Dhramshtram or Krodha), and the Lord is depicted alongside his Consort, Lakshmi. Hence, the Lord of the temple is known as Krodakara (Varaha) Narasimha Swamy here.

6. KARANJA NARASIMHA SWAMY
This shrine is situated approximately one kilometer from Upper Ahobilam and one furlong from the road leading to Lower Ahobilam. The image of the deity is installed under a tree called ‘Karanja Vruksham.’ Hence, this Lord is called Karanja Narasimha Swamy. The Lord is prathyaksham to Hanuman here. It is said that when Hanuman performed tapas here at this kshethram, Lord Narasimha appeared with a bow and arrow, signifying that He is Rama.

7. MALOLA NARASIMHA SWAMY
Nearly two km from the main temple of Upper Ahobilam is the famous shrine of Malola Narasimha Swamy. The deity here appears in ‘Soumya’ (graceful) form. As Lord Narasimha is seen with his consort, Lakshmi, He is known as Malola Narasimha Swamy. The word ‘Malola’ means beloved to Lakshmi (Ma=Lakshmi, Lola=beloved). It is said that the ‘utsavamoorthi’ of the Lord appeared to Srimath Adivan Satakopa Jeeyar, the first Jeeyar of Ahobila Mutt. Right from the founder, i.e., the first Jeeyar of Ahobila Mutt, down to the 44th pontiff, Srivan Satakopa Sri Vedanta Desika Yatheendra Mahadesika, the present jeeyar, the utsavamoorthi of Malola Narasimha Swamy is worshipped, and it is taken by them whenever they are on religious tours, visiting the villages every year. Recently, the 45th Jeeyar Srivan Satakopa Sri Narayana Yatheendra Mahadesikan has taken over the worship.

8. JWALA NARASIMHA SWAMY
The temple of Jwala Nrisimha Swamy lies higher up the hill above on a hill called ‘Achalachaya Meru.’ This is about four km from the Upper Ahobilam temple. This place is said to be the actual spot where the fierce anger of the Lord reached its culmination when he tore Hiranyakasipu.

9. PAVANA NARASIMHA SWAMY
The shrine of Pavana Narasimha is situated on the banks of the river Pavana, approximately six kilometers from the Upper Ahobilam temple. Hence, the Lord of the shrine is known as Pavana Narasimha Swamy. It is said that Mahalakshmi reincarnated Herself as Chenchulakshmi into one of the local tribes that resided here. When Lord Narasimha was roaming the land in rage after killing Hiranyakashipu, Chenchulakshmi is said to have pacified the Lord and married Him.

UGRA STHAMBHAM
At a distance of eight km from the Upper Ahobilam temple, we can see a cleft of the mountain dividing it into two visible parts. It is a long-held view that from the cleft, the Lord appeared in the form of Narasimha, and this cleft is known as ‘Ugra Sthambham.’

Sthala Puranam:
“Vina Venkatesham na natho na natha, Sada venkatesham smarami, smarami,
Hare Venkatesha, praseedha praseedha, Priyam Venkatesha, prayacha prayacha.”
The meaning of the above shlokam is as follows:
“Without you, Oh Venkateshwara, I would not exist. I keep remembering your name. Please bestow me with your love and grace.”
“Venkatadri Samam Sthaanam Brahmande Naasti Kinchanaa…
Venkatesha Samo Devo Na Bhootho Na Bhavishyati..”
The meaning of the above shlokam is as follows:
“Neither in the past nor the future would there be a sacred place in this universe that can equal the sanctity of the Venkatadri hills, nor would there be a God who can equal the Holy Lord Sri Venkateswara.”
This shloka appears in the Bhavishyattottara Puranam, written by Maharishi Vyasa centuries before the Lord ever came to reside at the Venkatadri Hills.
As per legend, after saving the Earth from Hiranyaksha, Lord Varaha stayed on this hill on the northern bank of Swami Pushkarini. Hence, Tirumala Hills is also referred to as Adivarahakshetra. At the beginning of Kaliyuga, Lord Varaha donated land to Lord Venkateswara at his request. As gratitude, Lord Venkateswara offered the first bell, puja, and Naivedyam to Varahaswamy before they were offered to him. This tradition is still followed today.

Sri Bhu Varaha 
The rishis, headed by Kashyapa, began to perform a sacrifice on the banks of the Gangas. Sage Narada visited them and asked them why they were performing the sacrifice and who would be pleased by it. Unable to answer the question, the rishis approached Sage Bhrigu.To solve a direct ascertainment of reality.
Bhrigu first went to Satyaloka, the abode of Lord Brahma. At Satyloka, he found Lord Brahma reciting the four Vedas in praise of Lord Narayana, with each of his four heads, and attended upon by Saraswati. Lord Brahma did not take notice of Bhrigu offering obeisance. Concluding that Lord Brahma was unfit for worship, Bhrigu left Satyaloka for Kailasha, the abode of Lord Shiva.
At Kailasha, Bhrigu found Lord Shiva spending his time pleasantly with Parvati, unaware of his presence. Parvati drew Shiva's attention to the presence of the sage. Lord Shiva was furious at Bhrigu’s intrusion and tried to destroy him. The sage cursed Lord Shiva and left for Vaikuntam. At Vaikuntam, Lord Vishnu was reposing on Adisesha with Sri Mahalakshmi in service at His feet. Finding that Sriman Narayana also did not notice him, the sage became infuriated and kicked the Lord on his chest, the place where Mahalakshmi resides.
At once, Lord Vishnu hastened to apologize to the angry sage and pressed his feet to allay the pain caused to Bhrigu’s leg. In doing so, the Lord removed the eye in the foot of the sage, which gave Bhrigu power to defy the Devas. Thereupon, the sage decided that Lord Vishnu was the most supreme of the Trimurtis and informed the rishis accordingly. Thereupon, they decided that Lord Vishnu was the fruit of the yaga. Sri Mahalakshmi was angered by the action of her Lord in apologizing to Bhrigu, who committed an offense. She, therefore, left Vaikuntam without heeding the entreaties of the Lord. At the commencement of the current Sveta Varaha Kalpa, the whole universe was filled with water, and the Earth was immersed in it. Lord Vishnu assumed the form of a white boar (Sri Varaha) and dived into the water to lift the Earth. He slew the demon Hiranyaksha, who was obstructing Him, and rescued the Earth.
Brahma and the other Devas praised Sri Varaha for saving the Earth by chanting the Vedas and showering flowers on Him. Lord Vishnu decided to stay on Earth in the form of Sri Varaha for some time to punish the wicked and protect the virtuous. The place then came to be known as Varaha Kshetra, and the Varaha Kalpa commenced. After the departure of Mahalakshmi, a forlorn Lord Vishnu left Vaikuntam and took abode in an ant-hill under a tamarind tree beside a pushkarini on the Venkata Hill. Taking pity on Lord Vishnu, Brahma and Maheshwara decided to assume the forms of a cow and its calf to serve Him.
Surya, the Sun God, informed Mahalakshmi of this and requested her to assume the form of a cowherdess and sell the cow and calf to the king of the Chola country. The king of the Chola country bought the cow and its calf and sent them to graze on Venkata Hill along with his herd of cattle. Discovering Lord Vishnu on the ant-hill, the cow provided its milk and thus fed the Lord. Meanwhile, at the palace, the cow was not yielding any milk, for which the Chola Queen chastised the cowherd severely.
To find out the cause of the lack of milk, the cowherd followed the cow, hid behind a bush, and discovered the cow emptying her udder over the ant-hill.
Incensed over the conduct of the cow, the cowherd aimed a blow with his axe at the head of the cow. However, Lord Vishnu rose from the ant-hill to receive the blow and save the cow. When the cowherd saw the Lord bleed at the blow of his axe, he fell and died of shock.
On the death of the cowherd, the cow returned, bellowing in fright and with bloodstains all over her body, to the Chola King. To find out the cause of the cow’s terror, the King followed her to the scene of the incident. The King found the cowherd lying dead on the ground near the ant-hill. While he stood wondering how it had happened, Lord Vishnu rose from the ant-hill and cursed the King, saying that he would become an Asura because of the fault of his servant.
The King pleaded innocence, and the Lord blessed him by saying that the curse would end when the Lord was adorned with a kireetam presented by Akasa Raja at the time of His marriage with Sri Padmavati. Thereafter, Lord Vishnu or Srinivasa decided to stay in Varaha Kshetra and requested Sri Varahaswami to grant Him a site for His stay. His request being readily granted, Srinivasa ordained that a pilgrimage to His shrine would not be complete unless it is preceded by a bath in the Pushkarini and darshan of Sri Varahaswami. That puja and naivedyam should be offered to Sri Varahaswami first.
Yashoda brought up Sri Krishna, the son of Devaki, in his early years. However, Yashoda was not blessed to witness the marriage of Sri Krishna with Rukmini, and she felt very sad. Sri Krishna promised to fulfill her desire in her next birth as Vakuladevi in his next avatara as Srinivasa. In Yashoda’s next birth as Vakuladevi, she was serving Lord Varahaswami when He sent her to serve Srinivasa. Sometime later, a King named Akasha Raja, who belonged to the Lunar race, was ruling over Thondamandalam.
He had a brother named Thondaman. Akasha Raja had no heirs, and therefore, he wanted to perform a sacrifice. As part of the sacrifice, he was ploughing the fields when his plough turned up a lotus in the ground. On examining the lotus, the King found a female child in it. Akasha Raja was happy to find the child. He carried it to his palace and gave it to his Queen. At that time, he heard a voice from above which said, “Oh! King, tend to it as your child, and fortune will befall you.” As the child was found in a lotus, the king named her Padmavati.
Over time, Princess Padmavati grew up into a beautiful maiden and was attended to by a host of maids. One day, while she was spending her time in a garden picking flowers with her maids, Sage Narada approached her. Assuring her that he was her well-wisher, he asked her to show him her palm to read her future. He foretold that she was destined to be the spouse of Lord Vishnu himself. At this time, Lord Srinivasa, who was hunting, chased a wild elephant in the forests surrounding the hills. In the elephant’s pursuit, the Lord was led into a garden, where Princess Padmavati and her maids were picking flowers.
The sight of the elephant frightened the Princess and her maids. But the elephant immediately turned around, saluted the Lord, and disappeared into the forest. Lord Srinivasa, who was following on horseback, saw the frightened maidens, who accosted Him with queries
When Lord Srinivasa returned, Vakuladevi brought him his usual dinner comprising various delicacies. However, she found him lying on his bed, pining for his love.
When she inquired about the cause, the Lord informed her that unless he married Princess Padmavati, he would never recover. Vakuladevi then asked Him to tell her all about the Princess. The Lord then narrated the story of her (Padmavati’s) previous birth and his promise to wed her.
(The following story is found only in Venkatachala Mahathmiyam and not in Valmiki Ramayanam.)
In ancient times, Lakshmi, in the form of Vedavati, resided in an ashram in the forest. At that time, Ravana, the lord of Lanka, tried to tempt her. In anger, Vedavati cursed him, saying that she would bring about his death. To demonstrate the truth of her words, Vedavati walked into the fire, but Agni, the Fire God, rescued her. He took Vedavati to his house and entrusted her to his wife’s care. When Ravana was about to carry away Sita from Panchavati, in the absence of Rama and Lakshmana, Agni appeared and offered Vedavati to Ravana as the real Sita, who was kept with him by Rama to evade Ravana. Ravana was tricked into thinking that Vedavati was the real Sita.
Ravana took Vedavati to Lanka, thinking she was the real Sita, while Agni took Sita to his house and asked his wife, Swahadevi, to look after her. After the destruction of Ravana, Vedavati entered the fire when rejected by Rama. Then, Agni offered the real Sita to Rama. Rama then questioned her as to who the other lady by her side was. Sita informed Rama that the lady was Vedavati, who endured Ravana’s torture for ten months in Lanka for her sake. Sita requested Rama to accept Vedavati as his spouse as well. But Rama declined her request, saying that he believed in having only one wife during his lifetime. However, He promised to wed her in her next birth as Padmavati, born as the daughter of Akasha Raja, when Rama himself would take the form of Srinivasa.
After listening to Srinivasa’s story of how he had promised to marry Vedavati in her next birth as Padmavati, Vakuladevi realized that Srinivasa would not be happy unless he married Padmavati. She offered to go to Akasha Raja and his Queen and arrange for the marriage. On the way, she met the maid-servants of Padmavati returning from a Shiva Temple. She learned from them that Padmavati was also pining for Srinivasa. Vakuladevi accompanied the maidservants to the Queen. Meanwhile, Akasha Raja and his queen Dharanidevi were anxious about the health of their daughter, Padmavathi. They learned about Padmavathi’s love for Srinivasa of Venkata Hill. Akasha Raja consulted Brihaspati about the propriety of the marriage and was informed that the marriage was in the best interest of both parties. After the departure of Vakuladevi, Srinivasa could not rest in peace. He doubted if she would succeed in her mission. He, therefore, assumed the form of a lady fortune-teller and entered the streets of the capital, telling fortunes. Padmavathi’s maids saw her and invited her to the presence of their Queen.
The maid-servants informed Queen Dharanidevi that the fortune-teller was hesitating to enter the palace without the Queen’s invitation. The Queen came out herself and invited the fortune-teller into the palace. The fortune-teller was taken to the presence of Princess Padmavati. The fortune-teller read the palm of the Princess and told the Queen about the cause of Padmavati’s indisposition. She advised the Queen to give Padmavati in marriage to Lord Srinivasa. She also told the Queen that a lady would approach her shortly on behalf of Lord Srinivasa to formally request Padmavati’s hand in marriage.
After the departure of the fortune-teller, Vakuladevi arrived at the palace and was taken by the maidservants to the Queen. She informed the Queen that she had come on behalf of Lord Srinivasa to request the hand of Padmavati in marriage. Having consulted Brihaspati and heard from his Queen about the prediction of the fortune-teller and the arrival of the messenger from Srinivasa, Akasha Raja decided to hand his daughter in marriage to Srinivasa. He asked the palace purohits to fix a muhurtam for the marriage. Akasha Raja informed his ministers and other officials of his plans. Immediately, a letter was drafted requesting Srinivasa to come and marry the Princess.
Akasha Raja entrusted the delivery of the letter to Sukamahamunin. Suka went to Venkata Hill with Vakuladevi. He presented the patrika to Lord Srinivasa, who was very happy. The Lord sent his garland for Padmavati through Suka. Kubera lent money to Lord Srinivasa to meet the expenses of the marriage.
About six months after this celestial marriage, Mahalakshmi learns that her husband has remarried and comes to see him in disbelief. It is said that the Lord turns into Stone right when he, Mahalakshmi, and Padmavathi encounter him. Lord Brahma and Shiva appear before the confused queens and explain the main purpose behind all this – The Lord’s desire to be on the seven hills for the emancipation of mankind from the perpetual troubles of Kali Yuga. Goddesses Lakshmi and Padmavathi also turn into stone idols expressing their wish to be with their Lord always. Lakshmi stays with Him on His Chest on the left side while Padmavathi rests on His Chest’s right side.
Rangadasa was a staunch devotee of Vishnu, and during his pilgrimage, he joined Sage Vaikhanasa Gopinatha, who was ascending the Tirumala Hill for worship of the Lord. This was after the Lord had settled the Adivaraha region. After bathing in the Swami Pushkarini, Rangadasa viewed Lord Vishnu beneath a tamarind tree. However, Lord Vishnu was exposed to the sun, wind, and rain and was only protected by the extended wings of Garuda. Rangadasa raised a rough wall of stones around the deity and started supplying flowers to Gopinatha every day for Vishnu’s worship. One day, Rangadasa was distracted by a Gandharva king and his ladies and forgot to supply flowers to Gopinatha for Vishnu’s worship. The Lord then revealed Himself and told Rangadasa that he had not been steadfast and had succumbed to temptation. However, in acceptance of Rangadasa’s devoted service to Him till then, the Lord blessed Rangadasa that he would be reborn as an affluent ruler of a province and would enjoy the earthly pleasures. He would continue to serve the Lord, construct a beautiful temple with a vimanam and high surrounding walls, and thereby earn eternal glory. Soon, the site was forgotten, and an ant-hill formed over the temple.


Rangadasa was reborn as Tondaman, the son of the royal couple, Suvira and Nandini. Tondaman enjoyed a pleasurable life as a young man. One day, he set out on a hunting expedition on the Tirumala Hill, and with the help of a cowherd, saw Vishnu under the tamarind tree. Tondaman returned home, deeply affected by the vision of Vishnu. Tondaman later inherited his father’s kingdom, Tondamandalam. Following the directions given by Adi Varaha to a forester, Tondaman constructed a prakaram(closed precincts of a temple) and dvara-gopuram and arranged for regular worship of the Lord as per Vaikhanasa Agama Shastras.
Lord Venkateswara appeared in the dream of Thondaman and asked him to build a temple for him, where he turned into stone. Thus, the temple for Venkateswara on the seventh hill, known as Venkatadri (Venkata Hill), came into being at present-day Tirumala-Tirupati.

Practices established by Sri Ramanujacharya:
Making Lord Venkateswara re-adorn the Sankha and Chakra in a visible manner for devotees, to end the debates over whether the Lord in Tirumala is Lord Vishnu or someone else.
Renovating Ananda Vimanam.
 Offering and doing pratishtapanam of Vyuha Lakshmi (two-handed Sridevi) on the Lord’s necklace (kantika).
Changing the schedule of the Lord’s Tirumanjanam (Abhishekam) to a weekly occurrence on every Friday, from a daily occurrence.
Recital of Nachiyar Thirumozhi every Friday during Thirumanjanam when Sridevi is taken from the Lord’s chest and is offered thirumanjanam.
 Commissioning of the building of wide streets around the temple, and moving back of the Brahmotsavam from Thiruchanur to Tirumala.
Appointing the Vaikhanasa Archaka for the Tirumala temple.
Establishing Yoga Narasimha sannadhi inside the temple.
Installing the moorthys of Rama, Sita, Lakshmana, Hanuman, Sugriva, and Angada in the temple at Tirumala and establishing the practice of performing Kalyana Utsavam to Rama and Sita on the day after Sri Rama Navami.
Establishing practices at Varaha Perumal Sannadhi.
Installation of Azhvar sannadhis in Tirupati.
Consecration of the svayam vyaktha tiruvadi of Lord Srinivasa and Azhvars in the foothills.
Code of Conduct as Established by Ramanujacharya:
Sri Ramanuja, upon seeing the flawless service performed by Acharya Periya Tirumala Nambi and Anantazhvan, and observing the defects in the service provided by many others at Tirumala, sought to establish a code of conduct at Tirumala to prevent any defects in the service to Lord Venkateswara. He called Periya Tirumala Nambi and Anantazhvan and asked them to implement and maintain the code of conduct as follows.
1. Only those who are responsible for services to the Lord that require a physical presence in Tirumala must live in Tirumala.
2. Any food that is not prasadam of Lord Venkateswara should not be eaten in Tirumala.
3. Only flowers that have already been offered to Lord Venkateswara must be offered to the home deities of those who live in Tirumala
4. The last rites (burial or cremation) should not be performed in Tirumala.
5. Animals or birds should not be killed and eaten in Tirumala
6. No one should wear footwear or ride on vehicles in the streets around the temple in Tirumala and in any place in Tirumala where the Lord goes during festival times.
7. Non-believers should not come to Tirumala
8. There should not be any temple for other deities in the region between Swami Pushkarini and Kapila Theertha
9. The above-mentioned rules should apply to all regions that are within a distance of 1 yojana (around 8 miles) from Swami Pushkarini.

Sthala Puranam: 
The Lord present here is said to be a vyuha-roopam of Paravasudevan who resides in Sri Vaikuntham. Empurumaan presents Himself as Vasudevan, Sankarshanan, Pradyumnan, and Anirudhan, who are said to be vyuha-roopam of the Lord. Vasudevan is the creator, Sankarshanan is the sustainer, Pradyumnan is the destroyer, and Anirudhan represents divine knowledge. These vyuha-roopam are further said to divide into three forms each. Vasudevan is said to represent equivalence to Keshava, Madhava, and Narayana. Sankarshanan is said to represent equivalence to Govinda, Vishnu, and Madhusoodhan. Pradyumana is said to represent equivalence to Trivikrama, Vamana, and Sridhara. Anirudhan is said to represent the equivalence to Rishikesha, Padmanabhan, and Damodara.
The twelve of these forms are referred to as the 12 Sooriyars and Chandirans, who are found in all 12 directions. They are responsible for bringing all Jeevaathmas into existence, guiding their lives, and calculating their Paavam and Punyam.
The Ashtaakshara mantram is said to always resonate in this kshethram. To reach this kshethram, one must learn the ashtaakshara mantram from a guru and meditate upon Sri Ksheerabdi Nathan.

Sthala Puranam:
This kshethram is the ultimate destination for any jeevaatma. This kshethram lies beyond Tiruparkadal. Sri Vaikuntham is described as a mesmerizing place from which there is no return, as specified in the Vedas and Upanishads as  “na cha punara avarthathe na cha punara avarthathe na cha punara avarthathe.” The Lord is seen as Sri Paramapadanathan, sitting alongside Him atop Adiseshan are Sridevi, Bhudevi, and Neeladevi. After the jeevaathma crosses Ksheerabdi, it will be guided to the borders of Sri Vaikuntham. Here flows the Viraja River. The jeevaathma is allowed to bathe in the Viraja River, where the divine river washes away any residual sins. Upon entering Sri Vaikuntham, the jeevaathma will see all the gods singing the praise of the Lord, which is described as “tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṁ padaṁ sadā paśyanti sūrayaḥ.” After being mesmerized by all of this, the jeevaathma will go and finally see the Lord Himself. The Lord gives space on his lap and asks the jeevaathma what took it so long to reach Him. The jeevaathma has no response but to say it has finally attained Him. The jeevaathma then offers itself to become one with the Lord. It asks the Lord to give it space inside His Heart to attain moksham. The jeevaathma asks the Lord to imagine it to be a single grain of rice, and that grain is being offered solely and wholeheartedly to Him. The Lord then places the jeevaathma near His heart, merging the jeevaathma with Himself, the Paramaathma, granting moksham. This is described in the Chandogya Upanishad as follows: “अहमन्नमहमन्नमहमन्नम्। अहमन्नादो२ऽहमन्नादो२आहमन्नादः। अहं श्लोककृदहं श्लोककृदहं श्लोककृत्। अहमस्मि प्रथमजा ऋता३स्य।पूर्वं देवेभ्योऽमृतस्य ना३भायि।यो मा ददाति स इदेव मा३वाः। अहमन्नमन्नमदन्तमा३द्मि। अहं विश्वं भुवनमभ्यभवा३म्‌।सुवर्न ज्योतीः। य एवं वेद। इत्युपनिषत्‌॥ “.
By attaining moksham, our journey is completed.

props.content:
Human life is marked by a perennial quest: Who am I? Why am I here? What lies beyond this life? These timeless questions form the foundation of all philosophical inquiry. In the sacred traditions of India, particularly in the teachings of Bhagavad Ramanujar and the lineage of acharyas before and after him, we find profound answers to these questions—answers that are both intellectually satisfying and spiritually liberating.
This book seeks to offer a gateway into the rich and nuanced worldview of Visishta Advaita Vedanta, the philosophy of qualified non-dualism. At its heart lies the understanding of the jeevaathma—the individual soul—as a conscious, eternal entity distinct from the body, ever longing to reach Sriman Narayana, the Paramaathma. The journey of the soul through various embodiments, and its eventual goal of attaining moksham—liberation from the cycle of birth and death—is central to this tradition.
In the pages that follow, I have endeavoured to present the essential concepts of Visishta Advaita in a manner that is accessible yet faithful to scriptural and traditional authority. From the foundational tattvas—Chith, Achith, and Ishwara—to the paths of Bhakti and Prapatti, and the ultimate goal of divine service in Sri Vaikuntham, this work aims to illuminate the path for spiritual aspirants who seek both knowledge and devotion.
This book is not merely an academic exposition, but a heartfelt offering—a tribute to the great acharyas and to the grace that flows through the guru-parampara. May it serve as a humble companion for those who wish to deepen their understanding of the jeevaathma’s divine destiny and the compassionate philosophy that guides it.
May the blessings of Sri Ramanujar, Swami Desikan, and all our Poorvaacharyas guide every reader on their journey toward the eternal feet of the Divine Couple, Sriman Narayana and Sri Mahalakshmi.

The Visishta Advaita Philosophy speaks of three tattvas or three ways one can interpret creation. Those three tattvas are:
Chith or the Jeevaathma
Achith or the Prakriti
Ishwara or the Paramaathma
Chith or the Jeevaathma refers to the souls of any living being in creation.
Achith, or the Prakriti, refers to nature or surroundings in which the soul would reside.
Ishwara or the Paramaathma refers to the Lord, who is the Almighty Supreme Ruler of the universe.
In nature, we observe hundreds of thousands of living creatures, each of which possesses a soul. Therefore, Achith acts as a residence for all that is Chith. From this, we can draw the inference that Chith and Achith are inseparable from one another.
As for Ishwara, He dwells in both Chith and Achith. Thus, Chith and Achith are inseparable from Ishwara.
From this, we establish what is known as Sharira-Shariri Bhaava, i.e., the relationship between the dweller and that which dwells. We see that Ishwara lives within Chith and Achith, bringing them together. Hence, Ishwara Tattva is treated as the Ultimate, which controls everything in creation.

The soul that is otherwise known as Chith, Aathma, or Jeeva, is an independent entity that should not be confused with the functions of the body or its brain. It is free of thought, emotion, will, or intelligence. It is not situated in any particular part of the body. It pervades the entirety of space, throughout every atom in every living being. When an organism dies and is burnt or buried, the soul does not die. The aathma is incapable of death. It is eternal. The aathma is not visible, is incomprehensible, and is unchangeable. The aathma is constituted by knowledge and bliss and is self-luminous.
The knowledge that constitutes the aathma is of two types, namely

            i)Dharmi Jnanam
            ii)Dharmabhuta Jnanam
Dharmi Jnanam helps the aathma be aware of itself at all times, whereas the Dharmabhuta Jnanam helps it know its body, the body's surroundings, all the people in the body's lifetime, and the objects beyond the body. Thus, when the body expires, the aathma loses its Dharmabhuta Jnanam. The best comparison to understand this concept is that of a luminous lantern. The aathma can be interpreted as a bright flame. The body is the fuel of the fire. Even if the body expires, the aathma can find refuge in another vessel, which will act as fuel to the eternal flame. For the fire to be genuinely immortal, it must merge with the Paramaathma. Upon merging with the Paramaathma, the aathma would not require any new body and would know eternal bliss as it reached its final destination.

On attaining moksham, the aathma gains unrestricted access to Paramapadam or Sri Vaikuntham, which is the highest realm attainable, according to Visishta Advaita Philosophy. It is said that upon reaching Paramapadam, the aathma enjoys four experiences eternally. These four experiences are called:
Saalokya: Being able to live in the same world as the Lord.
Saarupya: Having the same appearance as the Lord with Chaturbhujam, Shanku, Chakram, Gadha, and Padmam.
Samipa: Always being near the Lord.
Saayujya: Being able to partake in the Lord's bliss and enjoy it just the same as Him.
The Dharmabhuta Jnanam achieved in Paramapadam is eternal and complete. The Lord restores to the new muktha-aathma eight qualities, i.e.; 
      i) Being free from any sin
      ii) Being free of any aging
     iii) Being free of death
     iv)Being free of sorrow
      v)Being free of hunger
    vi) Being free of thirst
   vii)Being endowed with all that the muktha-aathma desires
   viii) Finally, offering the muktha-aathma no return to samsaaram or bhu-lokam.
Therefore, the ultimate goal for any jeevaathma is to attain moksham or liberation from the cycle of birth and death.
Moksham or mukti provides what is known as Paripurna Brahma-Anubhavam, which is a complete understanding of the Paramaathma. We can understand the Lord's nature ( swarupa ), His delightful nature ( vigraha ), His auspicious qualities ( kalyana gunam ), His ability to put time on hold or let it run according to His will ( Leela Vibuti and Nithya Vibhuti ). The aathma's enjoyment is eternal and will always result in service to the Paramaathma at all times under any given situation.
The aathma, as mentioned and described by the Bhagavad Gita

The main takeaways that one can take from the Gita when talking about the aathma are as follows:
i) The number of births that are taken by a jeevaathma is innumerable: 
 The Lord tells Arjuna that both of them have taken numerous incarnations together in this world. But only the Lord remembers all of them, whereas Arjuna does not. The Lord elucidates that He can remember everything as He is eternal and pure.


ii) Nature of the aathma:
The Lord tells Arjuna that just as birth, childhood, youth, and old age are inevitable stages of a human's growth in life, similarly, it is unavoidable for the soul to find a new body after its current vessel expires. The Lord says the soul is unborn, indestructible, and never dies. It is eternal. Fire cannot burn it, water cannot moisten it, and wind cannot dry it. Just as a man casts off old, worn-out garments, the soul casts off old, worn-out bodies and enters a new one.  

iii) Effect of the three Gunas on the manifested aathma:
Grossly speaking, the three Gunas quickly bind to the body, which in turn impacts the aathma. The three Gunas are:
iii.i) Sattva Gunam: This Gunam is associated with individuals who engage in activities that are pure and focused on seeking genuine knowledge of the Supreme.
iii. ii) Rajas Gunam: This Gunam links to those who engage in activities that are driven by passion, thirst, and action. 
iii. iii) Taamasa Gunam: This Gunam links to those who engage in ignorance, negligence, and lethargy.
 The three Gunas bind to the body at the time of death, granting different realms to the aathma upon bondage. If Sattva Gunam predominantly occupies the body, then the aathma attains Brahmalokam, a realm of knowledge. If Rajas Gunam predominantly occupies the body, then the person is reborn as a radical or a person of action. Finally, if Taamasa Gunam mainly occupies the body, then the person is reborn as an irrational being. 
    

iv) Attaining Liberation
  The one who declares that their devotion to the Lord transcends the three Gunas becomes qualified to attain moksham. The Lord tells Arjuna to relinquish all dharma and take refuge solely in Him. He will liberate you from your sins and grant you moksham.

v) What sort of person can reach Paramapadam?
Lord Krishna declares that a person who is free from pride, delusion, evil, attachment, self-obsession, desire, pleasure, and pain can attain Paramapadam.

Swami Desikan is considered to be an incarnation of the divine bell of Sri Venkateshwara Swami of Tirumalai. Swami Desikan was born here in Tooppul to Sri Anantha Suri and Devi Totaramba. By birth, Swami Desikan was named Venkatanatha. When Swami Desikan was just five years of age, he was taken by his maternal uncle, Kidambi Appular, to attend a discourse by Nadadhoor Ammal, a revered Sri Vaishnava Scholar at the time. As soon as Nadadhoor Ammal saw Venkatanatha, he saw a divine radiance in the child and stopped the lecture that he was delivering to hug the child affectionately. After this, when Nadadhoor Ammal said that he had forgotten where he had finished his discourse, Venkatanatha reminded him as to where he had stopped his lecture. This act astonished the crowd as they had never seen a five-year-old boy comprehend the deep intricacies of philosophical knowledge that was being discussed. It was then that Nadadhoor Ammal predicted and blessed Venkatanatha that he, in the future, would become the torch-bearer to spread Sri Vaishnavism everywhere.
 
At each place, he composed many different works in languages such as Tamil, Sanskrit, Prakrit, and Manipravala (a mixture of Sanskrit and Tamil) that revealed his ingenuity creativity, logic, linguistic expertise, devotional fervor, and erudite scholarship.
 
Some of his greatest works include:
                     1) Hayagreeva Stotram
2) Sudarshana Ashtakam
3) Paduka Sahasram
4) Abheetistavam
5) Achyuta Shatakam
6) Daya Shatakam
7) Hamsa Sandesham
8) Sri Stuti
9) Yadavabyudayam
10) Kamasikashatakam

The Artha Panchakam, composed by Swami Desikan, is a set of 11 Pasurams dedicated to Sri Varadaraja Perumal of Kanchipuram. The 11 Pasurams are assigned to two of each of the five doctrines or truths of the Artha Panchakam. 
The five doctrines discussed  are as follows: 
The Swarupam of Parabrahman.
The Swarupam of the jeevaathma.
The obstacles that prevent us from reaching Paramapadam
The means to moksham: Bhakti and Prapatti
The supreme goal of Bhagavat Anubhavam

Now, we will examine each of the 11 Pasurams and understand their meaning.

Swarupam of Parabramham  
This samsaaram is a karma bhumi. The Lord plays a sport of distributing karma-phalam to the aathma as per what it had accumulated through the course of its janmam. There are no limits to the Lord's auspicious gunas. He has “Swaroopa-Niroopaka Viseshanam and Niroopita-Swaroopa Viseshanam” among his gunas. Viseshanam is a distinctive characteristic that sets Him apart from others. 
The Swaroopa Niroopaka Gunas are five in number:
Satyatvam: He is invariant at all times.
Jnatatvam: His knowledge is eternal.
Anantatvam: He is present everywhere at all times.
Anandatvam: His presence brings out eternal bliss.
Amalatvam: He is the only one who is blemishless.

The Lord witnesses how the jeevaathma enjoys the karma-phalam that was provided.
As seen in the first Pasuram, the Lord distributes the karma-phalam to every jeevaathma. As the jeevaathma begins to experience the karma-phalam, it begins to detest it, and desires start to occupy the body. Due to this desire, the jeevaathma is sent continuously back into the ocean, known as samsara, to fulfill its desires. Perarulalan, along with Perundevi Thayaar, enters the jeevaathmas and bears witness to how the jeevaathma enjoys its karma-phalam.

The Moksha Virodhi
The jeevaathma does not remember its inherent, inescapable links to the Lord and unfortunately, gets associated with another bonded jeevaathma. The jeevaathma starts to engage itself in trivial pleasures because it cannot recall the difference between itself and the body in which it is temporarily stationed. Such a jeevaathma fails to find the right Acharya and is therefore full of arrogance and ignorance. The jeevaathma feels agony and engages itself in inauspicious activities. The Lord feels pity for such jeevaathmas and opens up a path to find the right Acharya and re-engage in bhakti so that it may qualify for sharanagati and prapatti, thus allowing the Lord to liberate it from its cycle of birth and death.

 Meaning:
The bondages of Samsaaram and Karma
The Lord protects and blesses all jeevaathmas, showing them ways of redemption, leading them to moksham and freedom from being reborn as either Deva, Manushya, Thiyak, and Sthavara. He showers his grace eternally, leading it to moksham.  vidhai muLayin nyAyam refers to an age-old debate/question. What came first, the seed or the plant? This is hard to tell.
Similarly, our Acharyas raised the question of what came first, the body or the karma-phalam? The answer that was decided was that both karma and the body are intertwined, as whatever karma the previous vessel of the aathma performed, so that it would reap the karma-phalam leading into the next vessel. Thus, both karma and body are timeless and ancient. This was the conclusion that our Acharyas arrived at.

wherein the performer feels that he is seeing the Lord directly).
One can attain moksham by opting for either bhakti-yoga or by performing sharanagati at the feet of an Acharya.

Before performing prapatti at the feet of the Lord, it is necessary first to seek permission at the feet of Mahalakshmi to help us successfully perform prapatti at the Lord’s feet.
