Meaning:
Phala Stuti
This prabhandham was created in tune with the upadesams of Poorva Acharyas and has been realized with the anugraham of Parama Bhagavathas, who have the good fortune of enjoying the dhivya soundharyam and Kalyana gunams of Lord Varadarajan, who presides over Atthigiri . Only Mahans with the familiarity of the meanings of Vedams can relate to them and enjoy the sweetness of the implications of these Paasurams.
The vital, crucial role of an Acharya

A person who understands that he lacks the prescribed qualifications or ability to follow Karma, Jnana, and Bhakti but has the conviction and a longing desire to reach the Lord has a smooth and sure path laid out for him. All one must do is seek out an Acharya who will act as the spiritual guide. One must remain devoted and steadfast, with absolute faith that the Acharya will see them through in their spiritual journey to attain the Supreme. The only requirements are total desire, devotion, and faith in the Acharya. If a disciple follows the teachings of their Acharya, they will obtain all the benefits of dharma, artha, kama, and moksha.
Sriman Narayana is the first Acharya

There are many reasons why the Lord is attributed to our first Acharya. The following can be considered the most significant reasons:
a) The Lord taught the Vedas to Lord Brahma.
b) The Lord revealed the Dwaya Mantram to a scared Mahalakshmi when Madhu-Kaithaba stole the Vedas.
c) Through the teachings propagated to Lord Brahma, He made sure that man reaps the benefit of the Vedas.
d) The Lord graced the four sons of Lord Brahma- Sanatkumara, Sanaka, Sananda, and Sanatsujata, and through them, He propagated Hita.
e) He is present as the Antharyami (the one who governs from inside) of great souls like Devarishi Narada, Parasara, and Parankusha.
f) The Lord incarnated as Hamsa, Hayagriva, Nara-Narayana, Sri Krishna, and propagated Tattva-Hita-Purushartha.
g) He made a great soul, such as Bhishma, give the world great teachings such as the Neeti Shastra.
h) At the end of Dwapara Yugam, when the teachings of the Pancharatra Agamas were lost, the Lord reincarnated as Sankarshana to re-establish them.
i) To establish the Acharya-Sishya relationship, He incarnated as Nara-Narayana and taught Nara the Tirumantram to Nara at Badrinath.
j) As access to the Vedas became restricted, the Lord, through the Azhwars, gave the world the Nalayira Divya Prabandhangal or the Tamil Veda, which propagated the message of the Vedas in a local language.
k) When the Buddhists tried to preach their teachings, which went against the Vedas, the Lord, through Acharya’s teachings, re-established the Vedantic Philosophy.
The need for an Acharya in one’s spiritual life

One who desires moksham must seek out an Acharya. When one seeks out an Acharya and surrenders at their feet, any sin will not pose any hindrance to moksham. Without an Acharya, regardless of how many good deeds we may commit in our lifetime, we will not be eligible for moksham.
Here are a few anecdotes that elucidate the role of an Acharya in our lives.

Vishnu Dharmam tells the story of Kshethrabandhu, who retorted to evil ways but was reformed by a sage. The sage was pleased by Kshethrabandhu’s attention span and advised him to chant the name of Govinda, and that one day, the Lord would show him the path of righteousness, reforming him. Kshethrabandhu followed the sage’s advice and gained Paramapadam. 

Padmottara Puranam tells the story of Pundarika, who relentlessly practiced bhakti-yoga but could not get a glimpse of the Lord and hence became dejected. One day, Pundarika encountered Devarishi Narada and explained to him what plight he was facing. Devarishi Narada told Pundarika not to worry and gave him the Ashtaakshara Mantram, instructing him to chant and meditate upon it. Pundarika earnestly followed Devarishi Narada’s advice and attained Paramapadam.

The Acharya must first master the three divine secrets and their meaning in their entirety. Only after learning it in its entirety is he supposed to pass it on to his pupils. The Acharya must perform Panchasamskaram, which includes initiation to the three divine mantras, namely the Tirumantram, Dwaya Mantram, and Charama Shloka.
The Acharya must impart in privacy to the disciple seeking moksham the inner meanings of the three Rahasyams. The disciple, in turn, must reflect with utmost concentration the implications of the mantras and how they can conduct themselves accordingly to attain moksham. Living per the Acharya's instruction will relieve one from all sin and grant them a state free from fear about anything.  
We must understand that the Lord and Mahalakshmi are the controllers of creation, sustenance, and destruction of all Chith and Achith. We must also recognize that the Lord is present as Antharyami within each of us, and that He will grant the karma-phalam to all our actions. Knowing the Lord’s unique position, we must try only to seek Him out and nobody else. From time immemorial, we see the importance of an Acharya through the course of our history in the form of Swetaketu-Uddalaka, Brighu-Varuna, Maithreyi-Yagnavalka, Sanatkumara-Narada, Yama-Nachiketa, Prajapati-Indra, Vasishta-Rama, Sandipani-Krishna.

By resorting to an Acharya and gaining his acceptance, the person will soon realize, by the grace of the Acharya, true knowledge, non-attachment to worldly pleasures, and devotion to the Lord starts to bloom like a flower.  In Srivaishnava Sampradayam, the panchasamskaram is the most crucial ceremony performed by the Acharya. The Acharya, out of compassion, without any expectations, accepts the disciple regardless of their caste or creed. The Acharya then performs panchasamskaram, and then the disciple becomes a Sri Vaishnava. Being a Sri Vaishnava is not determined by birth. This is the reason why one can see men and women from all communities and all walks of life as a Srivaishnava. 
The panchasamskaram, as the name suggests, consists of five samskarams, namely,

i) Tapa Samaskaram: The Acharya embosses the impressions of the Panchajanya Shankam and the Sudharshana Chakram on the left and right arms of the disciple.

ii) Pundra Samskaram: The Acharya makes the disciple aware of the places in the body where the upavyuha forms of the Lord Sriman Narayana are to be worshipped. Each upavyuha-sthanam is represented by one of the twelve thiruman-kapu adorned by the disciple. The tiruman represents the Lord, whereas the Sricharnam represents Mahalakshmi. The worship of the Lord is performed by holding the hands in Anjali-mudra and reciting “Keshavaya Namaha” prefixed by the Pranava. Similarly, Devi Mahalakshmi is worshipped, reciting “Sriyai Namaha” prefixed by the Pranava. 

iii) Nama Samskaram: The Acharya adds the suffix of dasan to the disciple's name, indicating the disciple is now an eternal servant to the Lord and Swami Ramanujar.

iv) Mantra Samskaram: Of all the five samskarams performed, this is the most important without an iota of doubt. The mantras received when this samskaram is being delivered are together known as the Rahasya Trayam or the three divine secrets.

v)Yagna Samskaram: The Acharya teaches the disciple the ways of Bhagavadh Aaradhana and the methods to perform Salagrama pooja.

In this section, we shall see the stories of the Purva-Acharyas (11.1) and the life story of Swami Ramanujar (11.2), and then the life story of Swami Desikan (11.3), and then try to map the lineage of gurus according to both the Tenkalai and Vadagalai Sampradayams (11.4).

props.content: Forty-Three days had passed since Lord Sri Krishna had ascended to Sri Vaikuntham. A childless couple, Kari and Udayanangai, visited Tirukurungudi to pray for the birth of a child. It is said that they requested the Lord for a child who would be just like Him. As none in this universe is comparable to Him, it is noted that Nambi Himself reincarnated as Namazhwar. Thus, in the Vaikasi month under Visaka Nakshathram, Namazhwar was born. As soon as he was born, he exhibited very peculiar behavior in the form of not crying or suckling. The couple, out of concern, is said to have taken the baby to the Adinatha Perumal Temple to pray to the Lord for the baby's well-being. Namazhwar is also said to be an amshavataram of Sri  Vishwakshenar, who is said to be third in line in the Acharya Parampara after the Lord Sriman Narayana and Mahalakshmi Thayaar. The couple is said to have tied a cradle near the Tamarind tree that was present in the temple courtyard.

The baby is said to have crawled out of the cradle and into a small crater-like space within the tree, where it started a deep meditation. The baby is said to have stayed in this meditative state for sixteen years. At this time, Madurakavi Azhwar is said to have been at Ayodhya and offering argyam as per his Nityakarmam when he saw a blinding light at the edge of the horizon. Recognizing the meditative nature of the divine light is said to have started to follow the light. In pursuit of the light, Madurakavi Azhwar is said to have traveled south, crossing Tiruvenkatam, then Tiruvallikeni, then Sri Rangam, then Madurai, and finally, he reached Kurugur. When Madurakavi Azhwar reached the divine tree, he saw a child in a deep meditative state and was worried whether the child was still alive or not. Madurakavi Azhwar is said to have thrown a rock near the boy to test his consciousness. When the boy opened his eyes, Madurakavi Azhwar was said to have asked a question, "Sethathin Vayatrill Siriyadhu Pirandhaal Yeththai Thindru Enge Kiddakum?" Madurakavi Azhwar was referring to the Jeevaathma. Madurakavi Azhwar asked When the jeevaathma enters a lifeless body, how would it survive? What would it feed on, and how would it survive? This is when Nammazhwar is said to have first spoken by saying, "Aththaith Thindru Ange Kidakkum.". Nammazhwar's reply said that the lifeless body would experience the pleasures and pains of life before attaining paramapadam or moksham. Madurakavi Azhwar was so stunned by the boy's response that he begged to be his disciple. Madurakavi Azhwar composed 11 pasurams in praise of his Acharya, Swami Nammazhwar, known as Kanninun Shiruthambu, which are included among the 4000 Nalayira Divya Prabandham.
 
When Nammazhwar was ready to attain paramapadam, Madurakavi Azhwar asked Nammazhwar, full of tears, what to do next. Nammazhwar advised Madurakavi Azhwar to boil the waters of Tamraparni, and he said that an idol would form during the boiling of the water. Madurakavi Azhwar did as per Nammazhwar's advice. After boiling the waters of Tamraparni, he obtained an idol of Bhagavad Ramanuja. He was surprised to see that the idol was different from what he had expected. He went to Nammazhwar with the idol, and the latter told him that this idol was that of a Bhavishyadhacharya (Future Guru) and that he would be born 4000 years from then. He again advised boiling the waters of Tamraparni. Madurakavi Azhwar once again boiled the waters of Tamraparni and finally got the idol of Nammazhwar.

Nathamunigal is considered to be the second guru of the Sri Vaishnava Guru Parampara. He is believed to have been born near Viranarayanapuram, near modern-day Mannargudi, in what is believed to be 823 AD. He is credited with the resurgence and the compilation of the Naalayira Divyaprabandhangal.
 
At one point, all of the Naalayira Divyaprabandhangal were lost except for ten pashurams that were being sung at this temple. Here, Naathamunigal heard this, and the verses told ten out of a thousand pashurams. This had Naathamunigal intrigued as to where the other nine hundred and ninety pashurams had disappeared. These ten pashurams also spoke of Kurugur (present-day Azhwar Tirunagari), Sadagopan (Nammazhwar). Thus Naathamunigal went in search of Nammazhwar. Upon reaching Kurugur and enquiring about these ten pashurams, the locals denied knowing of the ten pashurams that he asked for, but they knew of eleven other pashurams. Naathamunigal recited these eleven pashurams twelve thousand times in front of the divine tamarind tree where Nammazhwar had once resided. Upon completion of the recitation, Nammazhwar is said to have appeared in front of Naathamunigal and blessed him with the thousand pashurams sung by him, as well as the three thousand other pashurams which were sung by the nine other azhwars. Nathamunigal is said to have taught the Naalayira Divyaprabandhangal to his two nephews at Srirangam and introduced them at the Sri Ranganathaswamy Temple, where he served as the temple administrator.
The ritual of worship, as followed in Vishnu Temples, is based on two early standard works. The first is the Vaikhanasa Sutra, which probably belongs to the Krishna Yajurveda school. The other is the Panchratra Agama, which belongs to the extensive Tantra literature, believed to have been composed by Lord Sriman Narayana himself. The Agama has a peculiar philosophy of its own, the Bhagavata Cult, which is very old and is referred to in the Mahabharata and Badarayana Sutras. Nathamunigal made a provision for the recitation of Tamil Vedas on appropriate occasions during the main festivals of the Lord.
Nathamunigal is said to have attained Paramapadam at Gangaikona Cholapuram.
Nathamunigal's grandson, Yamunacharya, became the torch-bearer of Sri Vaishnava Philosophy.

Manakkaal Nambi was born as Rama Misrar in Manakkaal near Trichy. He was the disciple of Uyyakondar, who was the prime disciple of Nathamunigal. Manakkaal Nambi served his Acharya for 12 years, during which his Acharya's wife attained Paramapadam. After his Acharya's wife attained Paramapadam, Manakkaal Nambi took care of his Acharya, his house, and his children. One day, Uyyakondar's children were crossing the Kaveri River when they came across a puddle, which they were hesitant to cross. Seeing this scene, Manakkaal Nambi fell face-first and asked the girls to use his body as a bridge to cross over to the other side. When Uyyakondar came to know of this incident, he was very impressed with his disciple and immediately performed the dwayamantropadesham. Before attaining Paramapadam, Uyyakondar instructs Manakkaal Nambi that he would become the Acharya to Yamunacharar(Alavandaar), who was Nathamunigal's grandson. He also instructed Manakkaal Nambi to perform panchasamskaram to Yamunacharyar and groom him to become the torch-bearer of the Sri Vaishnava Philosophy.

Yamunacharyar was born as the son of Iswara Muni and as a grandson of Nathamunigal. He was born on the banks of the Yamuna River; hence, he got the name of Yamunacharyar. He studied under Manakkaal Nambi, who was an expert in Mimamsa. After mastering Sanskrit and Tamizh grammar, he had composed a shloka which loosely translates to "he would destroy the poets who were looking cheaply for publicity instead of performing their duties of studying various literature." This news reached the ears of Aakiaazhwaan, who was the royal poet to the Pallava kings, whose capital was situated in Gangai Kondapuram near Srirangam. The Pallava king was a staunch Shaivite, whereas his wife was a staunch Vaishnavite. The queen asked the king to hold an open debate in the court between Aakiaazhwaan and Yamunacharyar to decide who was a better poet. Thus, the king sent a royal palanquin to receive Yamunacharyar to hold an open debate in the royal court. Before the discussion began, the king announced that whoever would win the debate would receive half of his kingdom as a prize. The king was confident that Aakiaazhwaan would win the contest. Aakiaazhwaan let Yamunacharyar open the discussion, as he was younger and said he would refute any statement that Yamunacharyar would place in front of him. Thus, Yamunacharyar began the debate with three remarks.

1) Aakiaazhwaan's mother is not childless.
2) The king is all capable.
3) The queen is a true pathivratha naari.
Aakiaazhwaan started to think hard about how he would refute the three statements that were placed before him. As hard as he tried to think, there was no way he could refute the statements placed before him without insulting his mother, the king, and the queen. Aakiaazhwaan was dumbfounded and asked Yamunacharyar to refute his arguments. Yamunacharyar quickly refuted the three statements as follows:
1) Aakiaazhwaan's mother is childless, as, according to shastras, if a parent has only one child who does not care for the parent, it's as good as being childless.
2) The king was not all capable as he was only capable of ruling his stipulated piece of land.
3) The queen could not be considered as a true pathivratha naari as, according to shastras, when a woman is getting married, she is first married to Gandharva, Agni, and Soma before being married to the groom. Thus, she is not a true pathivratha naari.
Aakiaazhwaan understands Yamunacharyar's mastery and asks to become his disciple. Even the queen was so impressed by Yamunacharyar's responses that she gave him the title of Aalavandaar. As promised, the king gave Aalavandhaar half of his kingdom. Thus, Aalavandaar, who was born as a brahmin, became a king and became busy with administrative activities. To remind him of his actual duties, Manakkaal Nambi tries to meet his disciple, but his efforts are in vain as the royal guards stop him from meeting Yamunacharyar. Thus, Manakkaal Nambi, in a scheme to reform his disciple, befriends a cook in the royal kitchen and secretly starts to feed the king thoothuvalai keerai (a green leafy vegetable), which is a type of sattvic food. Aalavandaar starts to like this vegetable, and one day, the cook was instructed not to serve it. Thus, one day, when he was not served thoothuvalai keerai, Aalavandaar approached the cook and asked why he had not served it that day. The cook said he was following the instructions of an elderly Sri Vaishnava Acharya. Aalavandaar went out seeking this Acharya and realized that it was none other than Manakkaal Nambi. He invites Manakkaal Nambi to his royal court, gives him a royal seat, and performs all the stipulated athithi sathkaaram to Manakkaal Nambi. Manakkaal Nambi reminds Yamunacharyar of his duties and starts to teach him the Bhagavad Gita and its meaning. Aalavandaar became immersed in Bhagavath-Dyaanam and decided to give up his life as a king to become an aesthetic at the feet of Sri Ranganathar.
His famous works include:
1) Chathusloki 
2) Stotraratnam - a prayer in praise of Lord Sriman Narayana
3) Siddhitrayam - consisting of (i) Atmasiddhi. (ii) Samvitsiddhi and (iii) Iswarasiddhi, which describe the Vishistadvaita school of thought, illustrating a relation between the soul, god, and the universe
4) Agama Pramanya - stating the authority of the Pancharatra agama
5) Maha Purusha Nirnayam - describing that the ultimate reality is the god-goddess pair Sri and Narayana
6) Gitartha Sangraha - a commentary on the Bhagavad Gita
7) Nityam
8) Mayavada Khandanam

Ramanujar is regarded as the greatest theologian of the Srivaishnava Lineage Sampradayam, which is one of the two theistic Schools of Vedanta following the philosophy of Visishtaadvaita — the other being the Dvaita system. The Srivaishnava Sampradayam arose in the Tamizh region of South India, and as a tradition, had its origin with twelve mystics known as the Azhwars. These Azhwars composed hymns in Tamizh expressing their love and devotion to God, particularly in the form of Sri Krishna. According to modern scholarship, they lived from about the 2nd to the 8th century CE, but ancient tradition ascribes to them a period from 430 BCE downwards. Their lives and compositions encompassed all forms of intense love for the Lord. This devotional approach has been categorized in later times by Chaitanya Mahaprabhu with attitudes known as Dasya, Apatya, Sakhya, Vatsalya, and Madhurya.
Swami Ramanujar was the only child of a learned Yajur Vedi Brahmana named Asuri Kesava Dikshitar and his wife, Kantimati. Kesava Dikshitar was known by the title of Sarvakratu, meaning the performer of all Vedic sacrifices, by way of recognition of his expertise in Vedic rituals. He lived in the village of Sriperumbudur, which is situated about 30 miles to the southwest of the modern city of Chennai. This village is famous for its magnificent temple of Sri Adikeshava Perumal. Keshava Dikshitar had no children even after several years of marriage. Finally, he decided to seek the grace of Lord Parthasarathy, residing at Tiruvallikeni. Lord Sri Krishna appeared to him in a dream and said he was impressed with the devotion and steadfast observance of dharma that Keshava Dikshitar followed. He then told Keshava Dikshitar that He would reincarnate as his son to establish order in the times of Kali Yugam, which was dominated by adharma. He said that the son who would be born would become a great Acharya whom all would revere for time immemorial.

Accordingly, a year later, in 1017, in the Chaitra month under the Tiruaadra nakshatram. 
Kantimati gave birth to a son with the auspicious marks of Vishnu on his body; he was named Ramanuja, which was the name of Lakshmana, the younger brother of Sri Rama. Lakshmana was considered to be the incarnation of a part of Vishnu called Adisesha, who is the foremost servant of the Lord in Sri Vaikuntham.

When Swami Ramanujar was very young, he had his upanayanam done. His father, Keshava Dikshitar, attained paramapadam; thus, Swami Ramanujar had to perform his last rites at a very young age. He had not received any formal education and wanted to understand the meaning of the mantras that were being recited. After all the ceremonies were completed, Swami Ramanujar started to receive education from Yadava Prakashar, who was the foremost Advaita guru at the time. Yadava Prakashar's gurukulam was situated in Tiruputkuzhi, which lies outside Kanchipuram. 

Swami Ramanujar used to walk 40 km every day from Sri Perembudur to Kanchipuram to receive an education. One day, in one of the lectures on the Upanishads, the Upanishad Vaakyam stating " Satyam, Jnanam, Anantham Brahma" is said to have been uttered by Yadava Prakashar. It was at this point that one of Swami Ramanujar's classmates asked Yadav Prakashar to give further clarity on the Upanishad Vaakyam. Thus, Yadava Prakashar tells the class that "Satyatvam, Jnanatvam, Ananthatvam are individual characteristics similar to that of the horns of a cow. The horns of a cow can be categorized as Khandatva, Mundatva, and Poornashringatvam. 

According to Advaita philosophy, a man can see that a cow has no horns, half a horn, or has a complete horn. But all three conditions cannot exist at the same time. Similarly, the Lord cannot possess all three qualities at the same time. Thus, the Lord is termed as Nirguna Brahma ."  It is then that Swami Ramanujar poses a question to Yadava Prakashar, saying if I, a student, can sit, can breathe, can listen and question you all at once, why cannot the Lord possess Satyatvam, Jnanatvam, and Anathatvam all at once? Yadava Prakashar was silenced by the question and felt very insulted. Thus, he called off the rest of the lesson for the day. 

The following day, Swami Ramanujar did not attend classes as his mother was not keeping well. The following day, when Swami Ramanujar went to the gurukulam, the students were talking amongst themselves that they had to perform kainkaryam to their Acharya in the form of massaging their Acharya's head. Swami Ramanujar volunteered to apply oil and massage his Acharya's head. As Swami Ramanujar was massaging his Acharya's head, a student asked the Acharya a question. The student asked the Acharya to repeat the previous day's lesson, which was another Upanishad Vaakyam from the Chandogya Upanishad that says " tasya yatha kapyasam pundarikam evam akshini. " This verse describes how the Lord's divine eyes appear. 

Yadava Prakashar begins his explanation by giving an exact translation of the verse by saying His eyes are like those of a monkey's posterior. Swami Ramanujar felt so insulted that he started weeping when he heard this type of comparison being made. Swami Ramanujar then said that this comparison being made is very wrong. 


The word kapyasam in Sanskrit grammar has many meanings. One can be interpreted as the posterior of a monkey. Another interpretation is that of the thin disk of light that envelopes the sun during sunrise. Another interpretation is something that is blown up and out of proportion. When Swami Ramanujar gives these three explanations, he says none of these explanations can be used to describe the eyes of the Lord. Yadava Prakashar gets furious and tells Ramanujar to come to the point and give a so-called befitting explanation that would be better than Adi Shankaracharya's commentary, which says the Lord's eyes look like the posterior of a monkey. 

Swami Ramanujar describes that the word kapi, in Sanskrit, refers to the sun. The word kapyasam refers to kapya: aayasam, which can be described in the following scenario. Imagine a pond with still freshwater, which has lotus flowers blooming in it. When the rays of the sun fall on the surface of the pond, the water evaporates, causing the lotus to bloom with all its resplendence. Thus, the eyes of the Lord can be described as equivalent to those of the sun and possess a gaze that is as soft as the petals of the lotus.
All the students started to praise Swami Ramanujar, and this insulted Yadava Prakashar for the second time. Yadava Prakashar felt so insulted that he decided to kill Swami Ramunjar as he realized that he would become an outstanding personality in the future if nothing were done. 

Thus, Yadava Prakashar planned a field trip to Kashi. On the way somewhere in the vicinity of the Vindya Hills, he told the rest of the students that the next morning, when they would bathe in the river, one student should push Ramanujar's head, and one must push Ramanujar's back so that he would drown. Among the students who were present was Swami Ramanujar's cousin, Govindan. Govindan could not bear to let his cousin die. Thus, in the middle of the night, he woke Ramanujar from his sleep and told him Yadava Prakashar's plans. He then asked him to run away, or he would lose his life. 

Thus, Ramanujar is said to have started running and reached some forests in modern-day Maharashtra. Swami Ramanujar began to look around and realized he was lost beyond any possible help. It was then that he thought that he had to reach Kanchipuram somehow, as he knew the way home from there. 

Then a hunter-huntress couple is said to have come and told Swami Ramanujar that they were coming from Sidhashramam, which is situated in Uttar Pradesh, and said they were traveling towards South India. They decided to travel together in the morning and then sleep. In the morning, when Swami Ramanujar awoke from his sleep, he saw the couple had fled and a group of Vaishnavas, and asked them how he could get to Kanchipuram. 

The Vaishnavas laughed at him and asked him to look ahead, and he would see the gopuram of Varadaraja Perumal Kovil. Swami Ramanujar went to the temple and had darshanam of Sri Varadaraja Perumal and Sri Perundevi Thayaar. When Swami Ramanujar saw Varadaraja Perumal, he saw a close resemblance to the hunter, and when he saw Perundevi Thayaar, he saw a close resemblance to the huntress. Thus, he concluded that the hunter and huntress were none other than Varadaraja Perumal and Perundevi Thayaar, who had come to rescue him from the forest during the night.

After being saved by Sri Varadaraja Perumal and Perundevi, Thayaar Ramanujar stayed back in Kanchipuram, performing kainkaryam to Varadaraja Perumal. In a few months, Yadava Prakashar started the journey back to Kanchipuram. On the way back, he and his entourage made a stop at Kalahasti. Here, Yadava Prakashar was impressed with Govindan and told him that he should no longer be a Vaishnava and applied vibuthi on his forehead. Yadava Prakashar then placed a rudraksha-mala on Govindan's neck and renamed him Ulangai Kulindha Naayanaar. He left Govindan there to perform puja and kainkaryam to Lord Shiva.


Upon reaching Kanchipuram, Yadava Prakashar realized that Swami Ramanujar was still alive and well. He also noticed that he seemed oblivious to his plan to kill Swami Ramanujar. Yadava Prakashar then went to Swami Ramanujar and invited him to be his student again. Swami Ramanujar obliged and went back to Yadava Prakashar's gurukulam. The daily routine continued for Swami Ramanujar, who fell under the tutelage of Yadava Prakashar. At around this time, Aalavandaar was visiting Kanchipuram in search of a future propagator for the Sri Vaishnava philosophy. 


One day, when Yadava Prakashar and his students were taking a trip to Kanchipuram, Aalavandaar caught a glimpse of Swami Ramanujar. He asked his pupils who that person was. They told Aalavandaar of all the exploits they had heard of Swami Ramanujar and how he had dared to give a new commentary to the various Upanishad Vaakyams. It was then that Aalavandaar decided that Swami Ramanujar would become the future torchbearer to propagate the Sri Vaishnava Philosophy.


Soon, in another Upanishad lecture, there arose a controversy between Swami Ramunujar and Yadava Prakashar. It was at this time that a royal guard from the king's court approached Yadava Prakashar. The imperial guard brought news that the local princess had become the victim of a Brahma-rakshas and that the king had requested Yadava Prakashar to appear before the royal court to break Brahma-rakshas' hold over the princess. Yadava Prakashar thought it was a waste of his time and told the guard to inform the brahma-rakshas that Yadava Prakashar had commanded the brahma-rakshas to release the princess at once. When the guard approached the brahma-rakshas, it mocked Yadava Prakashar, saying it would not leave until the old fool came in person and tried to release it from the princess. 


The next day, Yadava Prakashar, along with his student group, went to the royal palace to assess the situation and release the brahma-rakshas. Yadava Prakashar was placed face-to-face with the possessed princess and was asked to help her. Yadava Prakashar, in pride, spoke to the brahma-rakshas. He told the brahma-rakshas that he was the great Advaita Sanyasi Yadava Prakashar, and he commanded the brahma-rakshas to release the princess. The brahma-rakshas started cackling and told Yadava Prakashar that it remembered everything about its previous life and also knew everything about Yadava Prakashar's past life. 


It said to Yadava Prakashar that in his earlier life, he was a peasant who would eat out of others' leftover plates. It then said that once, when he was living in Maduranthakam, he had the opportunity to eat a single grain of rice out of a Vaishanva's plate, which gave him the punyam to be reborn as an Advaita Sanyasi in this life. It further said that in its previous life, it was a brahmin who was well-versed in the Vedas. It was brought into this form after an error was made in the shruthi while chanting the Vedas. 


It then stated that Yadava Prakashar was not qualified to be a teacher and would not leave the princess under his instruction. Yadava Prakashar felt brutally insulted. He asked a final question to the brahma-rakshsas. He wondered whose command it would free the princess. The brahma-rakshsas laughed and asked him to look behind him to his pupil, who would dare to defy him. 


There was only one student who had ever challenged his saying. In complete embarrassment, Yadava Prakashar called Ramanujar to release the brahma-rakshsas. Swami Ramanujar approached the princess and gently told the brahma-rakshas to leave the princess's body, pointing to a tree from the window. 


He instructed the brahma-rakshasas to break a branch of that tree, thereby relieving them of their current state. The brahma-rakshsas immediately left as commanded, and Swami Ramanujar's fame started to grow once again.

After the miracle performed by Swami Ramanujar at the king's court, he gained an unbelievable amount of fame among the masses. This caused Yadava Prakashar’s jealousy to stir up even further. This caused Swami Ramanujar’s mother to get worried. She told Swami Ramanujar that his guru was not showing the ideal characteristics of a teacher as he was getting jealous of his students’ achievements, and that Swami Ramanujar should withdraw from Yadava Prakashar’s gurukulam. 


Thus, Swami Ramanujar stopped attending his lessons at the gurukulam. At this same time, Aalavandaar, who was residing in Sri Rangam, wished to see Swami Ramanujar so that he could take him under his wing as a disciple. To make this a certainty, Periyanambi, who was one of Aalavandaar's foremost disciples, was sent to receive Swami Ramanujar from Kanchipuram. Thus, Periyanambi rushed to Kanchipuram and found Swami Ramanujar performing kainkaryam to Sri Varadaraja Perumal in the form of getting water from a well for the Lord. Periyanambi went to Swami Ramanujar and told him the wish of his Acharya, who wished to take Swami Ramanujar under his tutelage. 


Swami Ramanujar was elated by the news and chose to travel to Sri Rangam to become Aalavandaar's disciple. Upon reaching Sri Rangam, sad news reaches the ears of Swami Ramanujar, saying Aalavandaar had attained Paramapadam. According to Guru Parampara, we cannot treat Paramapadam here as death but as a state of coma, the reason for which we will discuss further. 


When Swami Ramanujar went to see Aalavandaar's mortal remains, he noticed that Aalavandaar's right hand was holding up three fingers. When Swami Ramanujar asked the fellow disciples why he was holding out three fingers, they said those three fingers represent Aalavandaar's final wishes that he wished Swami Ramanujar to carry out. The three requests are as follows:
1) To write a commentary on the Vedanta Sutras that were written by Maharishi Vedavyasa, revealing its knowledge to the commoner.
2) To honor Maharishi Vedavyasa, who wrote the Mahabharata, and Maharishi Parashara, who wrote the Vishnu Puranam, by naming two capable people after their names.
3) To propagate the Visishta Advaita Philosophy, name a person after Nammazhwar and get them to write a commentary for the Tiruvaimozhi.


As Swami Ramanujar vowed to satisfy each of these three wishes, Aalavandaar's three fingers closed into his palm, and a sense of satisfaction was visible on his face. Thus, we can infer that Aalavandaar was in a state of coma and had not yet attained Paramapadam. After Swami Ramanujar took these three vows, Aalavandaar truly attained Paramapadam.

We have seen the three vows taken by Swami Ramanujar at the mortal remains of Aalavandaar at Sri Rangam. After returning to Kanchipuram, Swami Ramanujar got married to a woman named Rakshambal. At the age of 28, Swami Ramanujar's mother attained Paramapadam. After his mother attained Paramapadam, Swami Ramanujar continued his education under the disciples of Aalavandaar and continued performing kainkaryam to Sri Varadaraja Perumal at Kanchipuram. 


At Kanchipuram, Swami Ramanujar first met Tirukacchi Nambigal, who was another disciple of Aalavandaar. Although Tirukacchi Nambigal was not a brahmin, he was treated with immense respect because of his simple-minded and broad-minded approach. Tirukacchi Nambigal was allowed to perform chamara seva to Sri Varadaraja Perumal. It is said that Varadaraja Perumal used to converse with Tirukacchi Nambigal during the time in which he used to perform chamara seva. Swami Ramanujar was anxious to meet Tirukacchi Nambigal.



When Swami Ramanujar first met Tirukacchi Nambi, he invited Tirukacchi Nambigal to come over to his house for a meal. Swami Ramanujar's house was situated in the periphery of the Varadaraja Perumal Temple, which is humongous. Tirukacchi Nambigal accepted the invite and told Swami Ramanujar that he would love to come to his place for a meal. He said he would enter the following day for lunch. The next day, near lunchtime, Swami Ramanujar was anxiously awaiting the arrival of Tirukacchi Nambigal. As he was very anxious, he told his wife Rakshambal that he would go and check on where their guest was situated and left the house. Soon Tirukacchi Nambigal arrived at Swami Ramanujar's house. Rakashambal was a very narrow-minded woman. She knew that Tirukacchi Nambigal was not a brahmin. Hence, she asked him to sit outside the house's central courtyard. She then asked him if he had anything to eat. He replied that he had come to their home as Swami Ramanujar had invited him for lunch. She then spread out a banana leaf in the outer courtyard and served his meal very scantily. 


Tirukacchi Nambigal thanked her for the meal and left. As soon as Tirukacchi Nambigal had left the house, Rakshambal pushed the banana leaf with a stick, cleaned the area with cow dung, broke the earthen vessels in which she had prepared meals for Tirukacchi Nambigal, and took a bath to cleanse herself. When Swami Ramanujar returned, he noticed that Rakshambal's hair was untied and was wet. He asked if Tirukacchi Nambigal had come to the house. Rakshambal, with a disgusted face, tells Swami Ramanujar that the vaishya had come and she had served him food. She was disgusted by the fact that her husband wanted to engage himself with the likes of a lower caste man.


Swami Ramanujar felt insulted by her behavior but did not speak up as he did not wish to incite violence inside the household. A few days passed by, and Swami Ramanujar ran into Tirukacchi Nambigal inside the temple, and with folded hands, he pleaded for forgiveness for his wife's actions. He told Tirukacchi Nambigal that he had some questions about his dharmam that he would like to talk about with him. Tirukacchi Nambigal said he was on his way to perform chamara seva to Varadaraja Perumal and told Swami Ramanujar he would ask the Lord, as He is all-knowing. 


As Tiukacchi Nambigal waved the chamaram to the Lord, the Lord sensed a longing emanating from Tirukacchi Nambigal and asked him if he had any questions to ask Him. Tirukacchi Nambigal told the Lord that the questions were not his but those of Swami Ramanujar. Varadaraja Perumal is then supposed to have said Tirukacchi Nambigal's six statements as follows:
Ahameva Paramtatvam
Darshanam bedameva cha
Upayeshu Prapatti syaath
Anthima Smrithi Varjanam
Dehaa Vasaane Mukti Syaath
Purnacharya Samashrayaha
These six statements can be interpreted in the following way:

Ahameva Paratatvam: The Lord is the ultimate truth, and He is all-knowing.
Darshanam Bedameva cha: This statement is interpreted by the statement of " Tat Tvam Asi. " The jeevaathma is always independent of the Paramaathma but longs to reach the Paramaathma.

Upayeshu Prapatti Syaath: To be truly free from the cycle of life and death, one must perform Prapatti to the Lord at the hands of an Acharya.

Anthima Smrithi Varjanam: According to shastras, one will genuinely attain moksham when they remember the Lord at the time before the jeevaathma leaves the mortal body. As it is difficult for everyone to remember the Lord during Kaliyugam, the Lord tells Tirukacchi Nambi that He would remember those on their deathbed if they had performed Prapatti during their lifetime.

Dehaa Vasaane Mukthi Syaath: After death, the soul is weighed to see if it is fit to attain moksham. If the jeevaathma in its lifetime had performed Prapatti, it would gain direct access into Vaikuntham to thrive in the presence of the Lord eternally.

Purnacharya Samashrayaha: Taking refuge at the feet of an Acharya and getting panchasamskaaram done by his hands is the means to Prapatti.


After his conversation with Varadaraja Perumal, Tirukacchi Nambigal informs Swami Ramanujar about his conversation with the Lord, sharing the six statements the Lord made. Swami Ramanujar immediately rushes to meet Periya Nambi at  Sri Rangam. At the same time, Ranganatha Perumal instructs Periya Nambi to perform panchasamskaaram to Swami Ramanujar. The two meet at Maduranthankam's Yeri Kaatha Raamar Perumal temple, where Periya Nambi performed panchasamskaaram to Swami Ramanujar and initiated him into Sri Vaishnava Parampara.

After getting panchasamskaaram done at the hands of Periya Nambi, Swami Ramanujar invites Periya Nambi to his house. Swami Ramanujar feels he could gain and learn a lot from an Acharya living under the same roof. Swami Ramanujar tells Periya Nambi that his home was partitioned into the ground and first floors. Swami Ramanujar tells Periya Nambi that he and his wife would occupy the ground floor, and Periya Nambi could move into the first floor. Periya Nambi agreed to Swami Ramanujar's arrangement and moved into Swami Ramanujar's house in Kanchipuram. Under Periya Nambi's tutelage, Swami Ramanujar learned about the Naalayira Divyaprabandhangal, except for the part of Tiruvaimozhi, he learned the various Brahmasutrams with their meaning to become capable of writing a commentary for them. He also learned about the contributions of all the Purvaacharyas.
One day, a poor Vaishnava came to Swami Ramanujar's doorstep seeking alms. The poor man called out from the door, and Rakshambal came out to answer before Swami Ramanujar. When the elderly man asked for some food, Rakshambal immediately said there was no food left in the kitchen. The poor man left the house hungry and empty-handed. Swami Ramanujar immediately rushed into the kitchen and saw that there was still food left in the pots. He questioned Rakshambal as to why she sent the poor man away empty-handed. She told Swami Ramanujar that the man might have been a Vaishnava, but he had been roaming the streets in search of food. He might have come in contact with other caste men. Hence, she refused to feed him. Swami Ramanujar again felt insulted but stayed silent for the second time.
In a few days, Swami Ramanujar had gone to the Varadaraja Perumal Temple as he usually would and performed kainkaryam to Varadaraja Perumal. During the time Swami Ramanujar was at the temple, Periya Nambi and his wife packed all their belongings and left to return to Sri Rangam. They thanked Rakshambal and told her that they were returning to Sri Rangam. When Swami Ramanujar returned home, he noticed that his Acharya and his Acharya-Patni were not at home. He immediately enquired with Rakshambal as to where they had gone. Rakshambal told Swami Ramanujar that they had left the house and gone back to Sri Rangam. Swami Ramanujar asked why they did that. Rakshambal tells Swami Ramanujar that she had gotten into a big argument with Periya Nambi's wife in the morning. She told Swami Ramanujar that as they were drawing water from the well in the morning, a few drops of water from Periya Nambi's wife's pot had accidentally dripped into her own pot. Getting angry, Rakshambal had called Periya Nambi's wife a blind hag who did not know the difference in caste between their families. After saying this, Rakshambal casually mentioned that she was glad that they had left the household. This last incident was more than Swami Ramanujar could handle. He wrote out all of his wealth in her name and told her that he had received a message from her father, stating that they wanted Rakshambal to come home, as her younger sister's marriage was soon approaching. As soon as Rakshambal had left for her parents' house, Swami Ramanujar immediately changed out of his current attire and took on kaashaayam, the saffron-colored wear of a sanyasi. He then went to Sri Varadaraja Perumal, held the tridhandam, and asked the Lord to grant him sanyasaashramam. Through the guidance of Tirukacchi Nambi, Varadaraja Perumal gave Swami Ramanujar the title of Yathiraja.

After taking up sanyasaashramam, Swami Ramanujar's fame and popularity further grew. Swami Ramanujar started to gain many followers and disciples. Among the first disciples were Swami Ramanujar's first cousin, Dasharathi, from Purvaasharama, and another young man named Kuresha (Kurathalwan). Kurathalwan came from a very wealthy household. Hundreds of people would throng to Kurathalwan's doorstep seeking alms, clothing, and vessels that Kurathalwan would give without any second thought. When Kurathalwan met Swami Ramanujar, he decided to give up all his wealth and stay by the side of his acharyan to perform kainkaryam. Kurathalwan and his wife, Andal-amma, gave away all their wealth and, by sunset, left their house for Sri Rangam to be by the side of Swami Ramanujar. As they were going through the forest, Andal-amma started to show signs of fear. Kurathalwan sensed that his wife was still holding on to some wealth and asked her what she had brought along with her. Andal-amma tells Kurathalwan that she had kept one golden cup in her possession just in case Kurathalwan wanted to drink water along the way. Kurathalwan immediately took the golden cup and flung it away, telling her the only wealth they were to possess was the wealth of knowledge that Swami Ramanujar would preach to them. Thus, Kurathalwan and his wife reached Sri Rangam to be under the guidance of Swami Ramanujar. In the meantime, Yadava Prakashar's gurukulam had closed due to the lack of students. Yadava Prakashar spent his days in remorse and torment, thinking of how he felt he was superior. It was then that Yadava Prakashar's mother told him to go and seek refuge at the feet of Swami Ramanujar. Thus, Yadava Prakashar leaves for Sri Rangam and falls at the feet of Swami Ramanujar, asking him for the opportunity to become a changed individual. Swami Ramanujar wholeheartedly obliges and performs the panchasamskara ritual to Yadava Prakashar, thereby converting him into a Vaishnava and giving him the name Govinda Yati.

After reforming his former teacher, Yadava Prakashar, to Vaishnavism and giving him the name of Govinda Yati, Swami Ramanujar remembered his cousin Govindan, who had saved his life years ago. Govinda Yati informs Swami Ramanujar that his cousin, now known as Ulangai Kulindha Naayanaar, is serving Lord Shiva as an Advaiti at Kalahasti. Ulangai Kulindha Naayanaar used to serve Lord Shiva, who was in the form of Bana Lingam. He used to apply sandalwood paste to the lingam, perform pushpa kainkaryam, and offer aaradhanam to Lord Shiva. At Swami Ramanujar's request, Sri Saila Purna, Swami Ramanujar's uncle, reformed Ulangai Kulindha Naayanaar and introduced him to Vaishnavism, giving him the name Embaar. Embaar took his formal leave from Lord Shiva and went to Sri Rangam to stay by the side of Swami Ramanujar.
Soon, a time came when Swami Ramanujar wished to learn the three rahasyams or secrets of Sri Vaishnava Philosophy, which are :
Tirumantram or the Asthaaksharam.
The Dwaya Mantram.
The Charama Shlokam.
Swami Ramanujar traveled to Tirukkotiyur to meet Tirukkotiyur Nambigal to learn the rahasyams. When Swami Ramanujar arrived in Tirukkotiyur, he first met Tirukkotiyur Nambigal, who asked Swami Ramanujar to return the following day. Swami Ramanujar went back to Sri Rangam and returned the next day. When Swami Ramanujar met Tirukkotiyur Nambigal the next morning, he again requested Swami Ramanujar to return the next day. Tirukkotiyur Nambigal repeated the same exercise seventeen times.
Each of the seventeen times Swami Ramanujar was sent back was an indication of a real student to return after he had gained or overcome the following to gain knowledge of the rahasyams :
1. Samsara Bijam Tholaindha Pin Varum: A student must be free from worldly desires.
2. Ahankaram, Mamakaram Tholaindha pin Varum: A student must not possess any arrogance, ego, or self-centered attitude.
3. Aathma Gnanam Kidaitha pin Varum: A student must possess the knowledge of the behavior and nature of the aathma.
4. Dehaathmabhimanan Tholaindha pin Varum: Lose the impression that the body and asthma are the same.
5. Aishwarya, Aamushmiga, Kaivalyathigalil Moham Vittu Varum: Lose the attitude of wanting to cheat anyone for money.
6. Vishayantaratil Patru vitta pin Varum: Lose the attitude of seeking a second opinion concerning the Lord and His Bhagvath Vishayam.
7. Bhagavadh Vishayatil ruchi pirantha pin Varum: Find a sense of love in the Lord and His Bhagavth Vishayam.
8. Raga-Dveshathikal Tholaindha pin Varum: Realize the actions committed in anger and desire have repercussions and act accordingly.
9. Para thantriya unarva pirandha pin Varum: Realize that we are dependent on the Lord to live.
10. Sri Vaishnavatvam kai kudiya pin Varum: Realize the meaning of compassion( Sri Vaishnavathvam).
11. Sathvika parikgraham kidaitha pin Varum: Learn to realize and enjoy the nature of Sattva Gunam.
12. Bhagavatha parikgraham kidaitha pin Varum: Learn to converse with a Bhagavatha at the first meeting.
13. Bhagavath parikgraham kidaitha pin Varum: Learn upon seeing the Lord that our thoughts must not waver, and our thoughts must solely be focused on Him through immense bhakti.
14. Ananya-Seshatvam-Upayatvam kidaitha pin Varum: Learn that we as human beings are all equals, and if there is anyone that we cannot equate ourselves to, that is the Lord.
15. Ananya Prayojanatvam kidaitha pin Varum: Learn that the most tremendous boon that the Lord offers us is moksham, and we must accept it with open arms without the desire for anything else.
16. Ananya Bhogyatvam kidaitha pin Varum: Learn that performing sharanagathi beyond all the difficulties of our life will see us through to safety and ensure the Lord's grace upon us.
17. Acharyan Kidaitha Pin Varum: A student must find a capable Acharya who can guide and teach him all of the above.
18. Tirumantra Artham kai koodum: When one satisfies all of the above, the Tirumantram, Dwayam, and Charama Shlokams come into effect in one's life.

When Swami Ramanujar returned to Tirukkotiyur Nambigal for the eighteenth time, he shared the eighteen reasons with Swami Ramanujar. He said to him that he did not doubt in his mind that Swami Ramanujar possessed the above qualities. Still, he conducted this exercise because it was how Swami Ramanujar was to test his disciples before imparting to them the knowledge of the three great secrets. Tirukkotiyur Nambigal agrees to give Swami Ramanujar the insight of the rahasyams and calls him to enter a room. As Swami Ramanujar arrived, Tirukkotiyur Nambigal noticed that Swami Ramanujar was accompanied by Nadathoor Azhwan, Embaar, and Modhali Aandaan, who were Swami Ramanujar's foremost disciples. Tirukkotiyur Nambigal questions Swami Ramanujar about how his disciples entered the room with him. Swami Ramanujar then tells Tirukkotiyur Nambigal that the three of them are like the tridandam he holds and the pavithram he wears. They are inseparable for a sanyasi.
Similarly, his three disciples are inseparable from him. They had made the same journey as Swami Ramannujar had made over the past seventeen days, and they were worthy of receiving the rahasyams. Tirukkotiyur Nambigal agreed with Swami Ramanujar and provided them with the three rahasyams and their meanings. The meanings of the three rahasyams are as follows:
Ashtaaksharam: This mantram consists of the Pranavam, followed by Namo Narayanaya. The mantra and meaning for which can be found in the Vedas and interpreted in the following way :

The meaning of the mantram can be understood in the following way. Pranavam is split into a-u-m. Where a-kaaram represents Bhagavan Mahavishnu, m-kaaram represents the jeevaathma, and u-kaaram represents Mahalakshmi. Thus, after uttering the Pranavam, when Namaha is said, one must have the feeling of no self-centeredness and a sense of total unconditional surrender. Finally, when speaking the Lord's name, Narayana, the person must wholeheartedly think of the path to reach Him. Thus, the Tirumantram can be understood as the way to Sharanagati.
Dwaya Mantram: This mantram consists of two halves—the first half acts as a means to ask the Lord and Mahalakshmi to accept our Sharanagati. The second half serves as a means to ask the Lord and Mahalakshmi to shower their grace upon us constantly.
Charama Shlokam: This shloka is the means to Prapatti as given by Lord Krishna to Arjuna, wherein Lord Krishna tells Arjuna that He is the Ultimate Truth. He tells Arjuna to surrender and put all of his faith solely in Him, and he would relieve him from the cycle of birth and death and offer moksham.

Tirukkotiyur Nambigal explains the rahasyams and their meanings to Swami Ramanujar, informing him that he is to propagate this knowledge only to disciples who possess the eighteen qualities that he had previously mentioned to Swami Ramanujar. Swami Ramanujar steps out of the closed quarters of Tirukkotiyur Nambigal and briefly thinks for a while, and decides that he must do something before leaving Tirukkotiyur. Swami Ramanujar races up to the top of the Ashtanga Vimanam of the Sowmya Narayana Perumal Temple. He tells everyone who wishes to listen that if they want to be relieved from the cycle of life and death, they must perform Sharanagati under the guidance of an Acharya. A few people who heard Swami Ramanujar asked him what the means of obtaining this divine gift was. Swami Ramanujar instructed them to seek his refuge, and he would perform the panchasamskaaram and reveal the heavenly secrets to achieve moksha. After saying this, he started to descend from the Vimanam. In this brief moment, as Swami Ramanujar descended from the Vimanam, word reached Tirukkotiyur Nambigal of what Swami Ramanujar had done in revealing the divine secrets to the general public. Tirukkotiyur Nambigal, in a fury, rushed to the temple and confronted Swami Ramanujar, saying he had betrayed his guru by revealing the divine secrets. As punishment, he would undoubtedly go to hell for treason. Swami Ramanujar prostrated himself before his guru and told Tirukkotiyur Nambigal that he was more than ready to go to hell if he could provide the means for so many people to go to Vaikuntham.

After learning the three divine rahasyams from Tiukkotiyur Nambi, Swami Ramanujar, along with his disciples, returned to Sri Rangam. Upon returning to Sri Rangam, Swami Ramanujar starts to preach and propagate all that he has learned thus far. In the meantime, he leaves Kurathalwan and Modhali Aandaan with Tirukkotiyur Nambi to grasp the meaning of the Charama Shlokam and asks them to come back and teach. Soon, he started work on a magnum opus known as Sri Bhashyam. During the compilation of Sri Bhashyam, Swami Ramanujar would dictate the shlokas and their commentary, while Kurathalwan would sit and write down whatever Swami Ramanujar said. Once while compiling the Sri Bhashyam, a question arose as to which character of a given jeevaathma would be its prime characteristic? Would it be Jnatritvam or Seshatvam? Jnatritvam refers to the aathma expressing dharma jnanam, whereas Seshatvam refers to the aathma expressing that it is below the Lord and is dependent on Him for its existence. Swami Ramanujar claimed that Jantritvam should be the character mentioned, whereas Kurathalwan claims that Seshatvam should be the quality specified. Swami Ramanujar says this argument could only be solved by Tiukkotiyur Nambi and sends Kurathalwan to ask him which character should be mentioned. Kurathalwan went to Tirukotiyur to ask Tiukkotiyur Nambi the question of debate. According to the shastras, one must not request an Acharya a question until they give the student the authority to do so. Thus, Kurathalwan went to Tiukkotiyur Nambi's house and began performing kainkaryam to the Acharya. Soon, two days passed. Five days passed. A fortnight passed. Fortnight became a month. One month became three months, and this finally became six months. Kurathalwan could not bear being separated from Swami Ramanujar any further. Kurathalwan tells Tiukkotiyur Nambi that he will take his leave. Tiukkotiyur Nambi senses that Kurathalwan had come with a question and tells him, as he is about to leave, "Adiyan Ullana Pashuram Marandhadho?". Hearing this, Kurathalwan understands what Tiukkotiyur Nambi was trying to convey and, satisfied, goes to Swami Ramanujar's side at Sri Rangam. Upon arriving at Sri Rangam, Kurathalwan tells Swami Ramanujar that Seshatvam should be the character that should be mentioned. To substantiate, Kurathalwan tells Swami Ramanujar that the Azhwars stated in their Pashurams that the Lord lives within us, and we are nothing but a mere vessel to Him. Hence, Seshatvam should be the character mentioned.

As time passed, Swami Ramnujar sensed that changes needed to be made in the temple administration at Sri Rangam. Uttama Nambi, the temple administrator at the time, was opposed to any type of change. He planned to kill Swami Ramanujar. One day, when Swami Ramanujar was going around for alms, he came to the doorstep of Uttama Nambi, who called Swami Ramanujar inside and seated him. Before serving Swami Ramanujar food, Uttama Nambi laced the rice with poison. Uttama Nambi's wife sees what her husband does and tells him that it's wrong. Uttama Nambi threatens that he would slit her throat if she opened her mouth. Thus, to prevent Swami Ramanujar from eating the rice, she prostrates before him and performs pradakshinam, placing the leaf with the food in front of Swami Ramanujar. When anyone conducts themselves in this manner before a sanyasi, it is the sanyasi's duty to reject the food and leave. Swami Ramanujar takes the leaf and throws it into the Kaveri River. Swami Ramanujar notices the fish in the river that ate the rice start plopping up and die a painful death. Swami Ramanujar understood that the rice was poisoned and that Uttama Nambi's wife conducted herself as she did to save him. Soon, the news that Uttama Nambi tried to kill Swami Ramanujar started to spread like wildfire. 

Soon, the news reached the ears of Tiukkotiyur Nambi, who rushed to Sri Rangam to see Swami Ramanujar. When Swami Ramanujar found out that his Acharya was coming to Sri Rangam, he ran to receive him. When Swami Ramanujar saw Tiukkotiyur Nambi, he immediately began prostrating himself before his Acharya. The sand on the banks of the river was scorching hot, and Swami Ramanujar continued to prostrate his Acharya. Soon, a crowd gathered around the two great acharyas. The crowd noticed that, due to the heat, Swami Ramanujar was getting burned and was almost cooked to a crisp. A man in the crowd speaks up and asks Swami Ramanujar to stop prostrating, as the sight was unbearable. Once the man spoke up, Tiukkotiyur Nambi asked Swami Ramanujar to stop prostrating and assigned that man to perform kitchen duties for Swami Ramanujar. He asks the man his name. The man replies that his name is Kidambi Achan. Tiukkotiyur Nambi tells Kidambi Achan that his devotion was genuinely exceptional, as he could not even bear to see Swami Ramanuajar in pain. Tiukkotiyur Nambi said that he would be one of Swami Ramanujar's most trusted aides. Swami Desikan comes in the lineage of Kidambi Achan on his maternal side.

Swami Ramanujar continued his stay in Sri Rangam. He continued to attempt to gain access to the Ranganatha Perumal temple keys to reform the way the temple was being administered. The temple keys were being held by a person named Periya Kovil Nambi. Periya Kovil Nambi was a man with a harsh temperament and was very stubborn. However much Swami Ramanujar tried to get the temple keys, Periya Kovil Nambi would avoid Swami Ramanujar. Before Periya Kovil Nambi became a respected person in charge of temple administration, he was a gambler. Periya Kovil Nambi's mother came to Swami Ramanujar for help to reform her son's behavior. Swami Ramanujar went to the gambling house to observe Periya Kovil Nambi. After observing Periya Kovil Nambi's behavior, Swami Ramanujar sends Kurathalwan to retrieve Periya Kovil Nambi from the gambling house to initiate reform.

Kurathalwan taught Periya Kovil Nambi the shastras and various vyakyanams, transforming the gambler into a respectable man who earned the right to control the temple administration. Over time, Periya Kovil Nambi began to develop a superiority complex, as he had the sole right to control the temple and oversee its operation. In his opinion, he was above everyone except Ranganatha Perumal. Swami Ramanujar noticed that there were errors in the way he was conducting the temple rituals and hence deemed it necessary to gain access to the temple keys to change the way the temple was being administered. 

One day, Periya Kovil Nambi was conducting a homam for which he required a learned acharya to be present for a position known as Ekaham. At the time, it was customary to visit Swami Ramanujar to bless such occasions. Thus, Periya Kovil Nambi came to Swami Ramanujar to grace the event. Swami Ramanujar said he would send his guru, Kurathalwan, to grace the occasion. Periya Kovil Nambi was delighted to hear that his guru would be gracing the event. After the conduction of the homam, it was customary to give daanam to the person taking the position of Ekaham. The custom of providing daanam was to continue giving until the person receiving the daanam said they were satisfied. Thus, Periya Kovil Nambi began to offer daanam to his guru, and after the daanam, he would ask if his guru was satisfied. Kurathalwan would reply that he was not happy. Soon, it came to a point where Periya Kovil Nambi asked his guru what it would take to earn his satisfaction. When this question was asked, Kurathalwan asked for the keys to the temple. Periya Kovil Nambi handed over the keys of the temple to Kurathalwan, who, in turn, handed them to Swami Ramanujar. 

Swami Ramanujar immediately took charge of all the temple activities. He established all the rituals that are practiced at the temple to date. When Periya Kovil Nambi noticed the changes, he realized that he was at fault. Swami Ramanujar then handed the keys back to Periya Kovil Nambi. Periya Kovil Nambi promises to uphold the traditions established by Swami Ramanujar.

After Swami Ramanujar brought about reform in the Sri Rangam temple, he was getting ready to take leave for Kanchipuram. He visited the lotus feet of Ranganatha Perumal to inform Him that he would be taking his leave. Ranganatha Perumal then instructed Swami Ramanujar to reside in Sri Rangam and establish it as his headquarters. Swami Ramanujar thus made Sri Rangam his headquarters.
At around the same time, a Hoysala king named Bittideva, who was a Jain, was ruling in Karnataka. His wife, Shantala, was a Vaishnava. She came to Sri Rangam to see Swami Ramanujar and asked him to reform her husband into Sri Vaishnavism. Thus, Swami Ramanujar went to see Bittideva and converted him to Sri Vaishnavism. Bittideva then adopted the name Vishnuvardhan and constructed the renowned Channakeshava Temple at Belur.
Time passed, and Swami Ramanujar was looking for a troupe he could take along with him to Tirumala. Tirumala at the time was densely forested, inhabited by many varieties of poisonous snakes and many wild animals. It was considered a journey once made that would send the person straight to Sri Vaikuntham, as few would return from making the journey up the hill. In such a situation, Swami Ramanujar held an open forum meeting with anyone who wished to listen to him. Swami Ramanujar asked in the forum who would accompany him on the journey to Tirumala. Only one person volunteered from the entire forum. This man was Ananthazhwan.

Ananthazhwan used to perform puspha-kanikaryam and theertha-kainkaryam to Sri Tiruvenkatamudaiyaan sincerely. Ananthazhwan had constructed a pushpa-brindavanam and named it after Swami Ramanujar. One day, he was building a tank for the temple with the help of his wife, who was expecting at the time. Ananthazhwan used to till the soil with the help of a crowbar, place the mud into a mud tray, and give it to his wife, who would put it on her head and dispose of the mud at a distance. One day, when the same routine was running, a small boy approached Ananthazhwan's wife and told her that he would help her dispose of the mud without her husband noticing what was happening. Anathazhwan's wife accepted the help. Soon, Ananthazhwan saw the boy and chased after him, saying the work was being done in the name of the Lord, and he wanted nobody to help him. The boy seemed to run away, but soon came back to assist Ananthazhwan's wife. When Ananthazhwan saw the boy again, he started to chase him. The boy started running and ran into the temple, soon entering the garbha griha. Seeing the boy run inside the garbha griha, Ananthazhwan threw his crowbar in the boy's direction and soon noticed blood flowing out of the garbha griha. When he went to check on the boy, he saw a scar on Lord Tiruvenkatamudaiyaan's chin. He immediately realized that the boy was none other than the Lord Himself, who had come to assist Ananthazhwan in his work. Ananthazhwan is said to have cleaned the wound and applied camphor on the Lord's chin to give a soothing and cooling effect. The crowbar can still be seen in the temple to this day.

After Swami Ramanujar finished reforming the Ranganathar Temple at Sri Rangam, he decided to take a trip to Tirupati. When news of Swami Ramanujar's arrival at Tirupati reached the ears of Periya Tirumalai Nambi (Swami Ramanujar's maternal uncle and Acharya) in Tirumala, he sent Ananthazhwan to go and bring Swami Ramanujar uphill. 

Ananthazhwan immediately went down to where Swami Ramanujar was staying in Tirupati and expressed Periya Tirumalai Nambi's wish and message. At first, Swami Ramanujar refused, saying he could not reside on the hill, as it was a personification of the Lord Himself. Ananthazhwan went back and told Periya Tirumalai Nambi that Swami Ramanujar had refused. 

The next morning, news reached Swami Ramanujar that Periya Tirumalai Nambi himself was on his way to meet him. Swami Ramanujar ran to meet Periya Tirumalai Nambi. As soon as Swami Ramannujar saw Periya Tirumalai Nambi, he immediately started to prostrate to him. Periya Tirumalai Nambi asked Swami Ramanujar to stop prostrating to him and gave him the ladoo prasadam of Sri Tiruvenkatamudaiyan. He then requested Swami Ramanujar to come and stay with him on top of the hill. 

Swami Ramanujar agreed and went and stayed with Periya Tirumalai Nambi. During his first stay for three days, Swami Ramanujar neither ate nor drank water, as that was the means not to excrete and impurify the hill. For the next year that followed, Swami Ramanujar stayed in Tirupati and learned the entirety of the Ramayanam from Periya Tirumalai Nambi. 

At the same time, he completed a magnum opus, which was a commentary on the Bhagavad Gita, which expresses the essence of all the Upanishads. He traveled to the top of the hill and presented this magnum opus at the holy lotus feet of Lord Tiruvenkatamudaiyan. This magnum opus is known as Vedaartha Sangraha.

After writing and giving Vedaartha Sangraha, Swami Ramanujar wrote another magnum opus, known as Gita Bhashyam, a commentary on the Bhagavad Gita. He also placed this at the holy feet of Lord Tiruvenkatamudaiyan.

After returning from Tirupati, Swami Ramanujar announced a Digvijaya Yatra in which he would tour the entire country on foot, visiting multiple kshethrams. Accompanying Swami Ramanujar on the journey were a few disciples, of whom the most prominent was Kurathazhwan. Swami Ramanujar's first destination was Tirukkudandai. Here, he first visited the Sarangapani Perumal Kovil. After visiting the temple, he engaged in an intense philosophical debate with the Advaita scholars at Kumbakonam and convinced them to become Sri Vaishnavas. The next destination in his yatra led him to Tirumaaliruncholai, where he visited the Kallazhagar Perumal Kovil. The next destination in his yatra led him to Tirupullani, where he visited the Kalyana Jagannatha Perumal Kovil and the Darbhashayana Ramar Kovil and performed the Setu Snanam.

 The next destination in his yatra led him to Azhwar Tirunagari. The next destination in his yatra led him to Tirukurungudi. Here, Swami Ramanujar had a conversation with Tirukurungudi Nambi. The Lord tells Bhagawad Ramanujacharya that he has accomplished what He could not achieve in all His births. The Lord asks to be initiated into Sri Vaishnavism by Bhagawad Ramanujacharya. Bhagawad Ramanujacharya is said to have performed the Pancha-Samskara ceremony for the Lord here, giving Him the name Sri Vaishnava Nambi. The next destination in his yatra led him to Tiruvanparisaram, Tiruvattaru, and then Tiruvananthapuram. Then, traveling north, Swami Ramanujar reached Dwarka, where he went to see Lord Dwarkadeesh. Moving further north, Swami Ramanujar went to Gokulam, Mathura, Vrindavanam, and Govardhanam. Continuing north, Swami Ramanujar visited Muktinath, Badrinath, Joshi Mutt, Devaprayag, and then proceeded to Pushkaram. 

To complete his yatra, he traveled to Kashmir in search of the Saraswati Bhandaaram, a renowned library that housed many sacred texts of Sanathana Dharma. Swami Ramanujar, along with Kurathazhwan, went to the Saraswathi Bhandaaram, which was holding the Vrithi Grantham written by Bodhayana. The Vrithi Grantham was a book that served as a commentary on all the Brahmasutrams. Swami Ramanujar reached the Saraswathi Bhandaaram, which was being guarded by two pandits. The two pandits asked Swami Ramanujar why he had come to the library. When Swami Ramanujar told them that he wanted to take the Vrithi Grantham, the two pandits laughed and guided him and Kurathazhwan to an idol of Devi Saraswathi. The idol posed a riddle to Swami Ramanujar.

The riddle was as follows:” tasya yatha kapyasam pundarikam evam akshini. “ Swami Ramanujar immediately gave a detailed answer, as this was the very same statement that he had first given a commentary on under Yadava Prakashar's education. The word "kapyasam" in Sanskrit grammar has multiple meanings. One can be interpreted as the posterior of a monkey. Another interpretation is that of the thin disk of light that envelopes the sun during sunrise. Another interpretation is something that is blown up and out of proportion. When Swami Ramanujar provides these three explanations, he states that none of these explanations can be used to describe the eyes of the Lord. Swami Ramanujar describes that the word kapi, in Sanskrit, refers to the sun. The word kapyasam refers to kapya: aayasam, which can be described in the following scenario. Imagine a pond filled with still freshwater, where lotus flowers bloom. When the sun's rays fall on the pond's surface, the water evaporates, causing the lotus to bloom with all its resplendence. Thus, the eyes of the Lord can be described as equivalent to those of the sun and possess a gaze that is as soft as the petals of the lotus.

Saraswathi Devi tells Swami Ramanujar that she was impressed by his answer and that She would grant him access to her library and allow him to take the Vrithi Grantham. Thus, Swami Ramanujar took the Vrithi Grantham and started his journey back towards Sri Rangam. By night, Swami Ramanujar and Kurathazhwan reached Kashi and decided to spend the night there. Swami Ramanujar fell asleep, saying he was tired from the travel. Later in the morning, when both Swami Ramanujar and Kurathazhwan awoke from their sleep, they saw that the Vrithi Grantham was missing. Swami Ramanujar was heartbroken as he understood the pandits must have stolen the Grantham from them when they were sleeping. 

Kurathazhwan then tells his Acharya not to feel bad, as he had read the entire Grantham in the night before falling asleep. He told his Acharya that his curiosity to know what was in the Grantham did not let him sleep; thus, he read every last word in the Grantham before going to sleep. Swami Ramanujar decides to test Kurathazhwan and asks him to recall whatever he can remember from the Grantham. Kurathazhwan recited the entire Grantham before Swami Ramanujar and told him that he could remember anything he read in a single attempt. Swami Ramanujar and Kurathazhwan returned to Sri Rangam. 

After returning to Sri Rangam, Swami Ramanujar began writing another magnum opus, a commentary on the Brahmasutras written by Bhodayana. Swami Ramanujar used the references of Azhwar Pashurams, Brahmasutra-Artham, which he was taught by Tirukacchi Nambi, and the Vrithi Grantham through Kurathazhwan to write the great Sri Bhasyam.
Kulothunga Chola and the migration to Melukote

Now we reach that stage of the story where Swami Ramanujar is reaching his mid-to-late fifties in age. At around this time, Kulothunga Chola I became the king of Kanchipuram and sought to establish Shaivism as the state religion. He managed to convert all the Vaishnavas who were residents of Kanchipuram to Shaivism by force. He intended to extend this with an iron fist further, but noticed that Swami Ramanujar posed a great hindrance to this movement. Thus, he summoned his two most trusted aides, Tirukkachi Nambi and Kurathazhwan, to his court and held a great philosophical debate. 

When he noticed that both Tirukacchi Nambi and Kurathazhwan were not budging from their claim of Narayana being the greatest among the trinity, he asked them to substantiate how anyone or anything in existence could rival Lord Shiva's presence in the universe. Kurathazhwan immediately spoke up, citing drona-charcha, which says that the drona-pushpam, which sits atop the matted locks of Lord Shiva, is more significant than Lord Shiva. Hearing this, Kulothunga Chola became furious and decided to punish both Tirukacchi Nambi and Kurathazhwan. The king ordered his soldiers to gouge out their eyes. The soldiers gouged out Tirukacchi Nambi's eyes. Still, before they could get to Kuratazhwan, he said: “Whoever thinks/says that Supreme Lord Sriman Narayanan is equivalent/on par with or inferior to other devathas, that paaapam would catch me!” He then said there would be no bigger sin. Thus, he gouged out his own eyes and placed them in the hands of the soldiers.

Kulothunga Chola felt terrible for his actions and paid a beggar who was residing outside the palace to escort both of them to Sri Rangam. Tirukacchi Nambigal, by this time, was very old and said he could not face Swami Ramanujar as he had disgraced him and his principles, and decided that it was time for him to depart to Paramapadam. Thus Tirukacchi Nambigal departed for Paramapadam. Soon, the news reached Swami Ramanujar that Kulothunga Chola was planning to annex Sri Rangam and take Swami Ramanujar's life. Therefore, Swami Ramanujar departed from Sri Rangam and started to head north into Karnataka. By the time Swami Ramanujar and a few of his disciples reached Karnataka, it was late at night, and they were in a dense forest. In the darkness of night, a hunter's tribe offered to protect Swami Ramanujar and his disciples.
As they continued their journey, they reached a house by evening, where they decided to stay the night. A few of Swami Ramanujar's followers went into the house and found a woman who was deeply immersed in bhakti. 

She was performing aaradanam to a set of paduka. The disciples told her that they had come from the south and were seeking shelter for the night. The woman obliged. The disciples saw the paduka and asked her who her Acharya was. She told them that she had once visited Sri Rangam and had received divine instructions from an Acharya, but she soon forgot what she had learned. As luck would have it, she ran into her Acharya once again, but she did not see his face. She fell to his feet and told him that she had forgotten his instructions, and she wanted to learn his teachings once more. She said her Acharya recognized her bhakti and gave her his paduka, and she has been performing aaradanam to the paduka since that day. 

The disciples further probed her to see if she was speaking about Swami Ramanujar. They asked to describe the face of the Acharya she talked about. She said she never saw his face and only fell at his feet as a mark of respect. She said that her Acharya's feet were like those of Sriman Narayana, like a lotus, and she could recognize his feet if she were ever to see them again. As she said this, Swami Ramanujar entered the room, and she saw his feet and immediately started to prostrate herself before him, saying he was the Acharya whose paduka she had been serving earnestly. She gave Swami Ramanujar and his disciples shelter and guided them to Melukote (Tirunarayanpuram).

Swami Ramanujar reached Melukote (Tirunarayanapuram), and one night he had a divine dream in which Sriman Narayana appeared and told Swami Ramanujar that he was very near him on the Yadugiri hill. He told Swami Ramanujar that He was awaiting Swami Ramanujar's arrival and that Swami Ramanujar would find Tiruman at the site where He was present. Swami Ramanujar immediately sent out word to King Vishnuvardhan, who helped clear out the forests in the Yadugiri area. In clearing the woods, the soldiers found the Tirukalyani and a set of kaashayam at the site. They immediately returned to Swami Ramanujar, who had come to the Tirukalyani, and upon seeing the kaashayam, understood that this was the site where Swami Dattatreya had taken up Sanyasam. 

Swami Ramanujar took a bath in the Tirukalyani and changed back into kaashayam. When Swami Ramanujar had left Sri Rangam, his disciples insisted that he wear white-colored clothing to avoid getting caught by Kulothunga Chola's soldiers. Swami Ramanujar found the Tiruman on the northwest banks of the Tirukalyani but was unable to locate the Lord's idol. When Swami Ramanujar returned to his hermitage, he was disappointed as he could not find the Lord's idol.

That night, the Lord again appeared in Swami Ramanujar's dreams. 
He told him he could see the idol inside an anthill, which would be flanked by a Champaka tree, a Vakula Tree, and Swami Ramanujar would find tulasi growing on the anthill. He also told Swami Ramanujar that the anthill would be located on the southwest bank of the Tirukalyani. Swami Ramanujar returned to the banks of the Tirukalyani the following day and discovered the divine anthill. Swami Ramanujar sent information to King Vishnuvardhan, who immediately rushed to Yadugiri to see the Lord. Swami Ramanujar performed ksheerabhishekam (an abhishekam with milk) to the anthill. 


As the milk was poured on the anthill, it dissolved, showing a divine idol of the Lord. Swami Ramanujar personally performed punar-prathishtaapanam to the idol over three days. Soon, the forests around the area were cleared entirely, and streets were constructed. A temple was erected at the site where the anthill stood, and sets of festivals were instituted.


The only missing entity at the time was a Utsava Murthy. Swami Ramanujar decided to recast the idols of Perumal and Thayaar using panchaloham (a mix of five holy metals in a particular proportion). That night, Sriman Narayana once again appeared in Swami Ramanujar's dreams and told him that His Utsava Murthy, Ramapriya, whom Lord Rama worshiped, still existed and that the idol was residing in Delhi, which was under the Turkish regime. The Lord told Swami Ramanujar to journey to Delhi and claim Him from the Turks.

Swami Ramanujar made his journey to Delhi and went to the royal court of the Turk king. He explained his situation. The king showed Swami Ramanujar the way into the treasury, where all the idols and plundered wealth were being kept. 

Swami Ramanujar searched the entire treasury but could not find the Lord's idol. Swami Ramanujar returned to the king's court and informed him that he was unable to find the Lord's idol. The king then personally took Swami Ramanujar to the queen's palace. The king told Swami 


Ramanujar that if the idol was still intact, it had to have been with one of the queens or one of the royal women.
