Swami Ramanujar began searching for the Lord's idol and discovered that it was in the possession of a princess. When Swami Ramanujar saw the Lord, his eyes welled up with tears of joy, and he immediately called out to the Lord, referring to Him by the name of Selvapillai. 

The idol of the Lord then jumped from the windowsill and ran into Swami Ramanujar's hands. The king did not know what he had just seen. He was awestruck. The princess did not want to be separated from the idol, as she had come to believe that the Lord was her husband and did not want to be separated from Him. 


The king then explained to his daughter that the idol did not belong with her and that they were foreigners who had to return to their land. Saying this, the king gave Swami Ramanujar his leave. Soon, the princess started chasing after Swami Ramanujar and followed them to Tirunarayanapuram. 


Swami Ramanujar recognized the bhakti in the princess's intentions and allowed her to stay by the Lord's side, dubbing her Bibi Nachiyar.
Swami Ramanujar's return to Sri Rangam and attaining Paramapadam

After Kulotunga Chola died in 1118, Swami Ramanujar decided to return to Sri Rangam. The people of Yadugiri could not bear to part with Swami Ramanujar. Thus, Swami Ramanujar instilled his qualities into a panchaloham idol. Swami Ramanujar and his disciples first made a stop at Tirumaliruncholai, where he fulfilled his vow to Sri Andal and presented the Lord with 100 gangalams of butter and sweet rice. After fulfilling his promise, he visited Srivilliputur, where Sri Andal is said to have appeared before him and bestowed upon him the title of Godaagraja. Swami Ramanujar then safely returned to Sri Rangam. 


When Kurathazhwan received the news of Swami Ramanujar's return, he rushed to see his Acharya. When Swami Ramanuja saw the plight of Kurathazhwan, he told Kurathazhwan to visit Varadaraja Perumal to regain his lost eyes. Kurthazhwan followed Acharya's instruction and restored his sight through the grace of Varadaraja Perumal. Kurathazhwan then served Swami Ramanujar for a period of two more years before attaining Paramapadam. 


Seventeen years after Kurathazhwan's demise, a time came when Swami Ramanujar sensed that his time on bhu-lokam was coming close to the end. It was at this time that Swami Ramanujar appointed Kurathazhwan's son Parashara Bhattar as the successor to propagate the Visishta Advaita Philosophy and made his final journey towards Paramapadam. 


The gist of his last teachings is as follows:
Worship all holy men precisely as you would do in the case of your spiritual preceptor. Have sincere faith in the teachings of the previous acharyas and Azhwars. Never become enslaved by your senses. Be not satisfied with the acquisition of worldly knowledge; spend your time reading literature that deals with the greatness of God and the wonders of His creation. By the Guru's grace, the attraction of the senses will cease to torment you. Learn to maintain composure in feelings of joy and sorrow, charm, and aversion. Enjoy the names and chanting of the glories of God's devotees with as much relish as the chanting of God's names and glories. Never forget that service to the devotees of God is more significant than service to God Himself. He who renders service to God's devotees speedily attains God Himself. Do not take to the life of a devotee as a means for acquiring any selfish advantage.


Three idols of Ramanuja are especially associated with him. In the Tamil language, Tirumeni means 'idol' or 'figurine'. Ugandha means be worthy, be right, fit, rise to the occasion, and be suitable.

Sri Perumbudur, near Kanchipuram, got Thaan Ugandha Tirumeni – an idol that became sanctified on its own while Ramanuja was in Srirangam.

Melkote, near Mysore, is home to Tamar Ugandha Tirumeni – an idol fashioned and sanctified by Him for His disciples.

Srirangam, near Trichy, got Thane Aana Tirumeni – an idol that is He, Himself.
He was a celebrated saint of His time who had codified the worship system itself. 

After his passing, a life-size idol of his form has been kept in a sitting posture in a shrine within the Prakaram, a circumambulatory path of the Srirangam temple complex. Such an honour has not been bestowed on any other saint.

Swami Vedanta Desikan is considered the Ghantavataram (reincarnation of the divine bell) of Lord Venkateshwara of Tirumala.


Anantha Somaiyaji was one of the 74 simhaasanaadhipathis chosen by Swami Ramanujar to spread the message of the Visishtaadvaita philosophy. He lived in Kanchipuram with his son Pundareekaksha and his grandson, Anantasuri, who had studied all the shastras. When Anantasuri reached marriageable age, Pundareekaksha approached Kidambi Appullar, the grandson of Kidambi Aachan, who was responsible for the kitchen duties of Swami Ramanujar. Pundareekaksha approached Kidambi Appular with a wedding proposition to give his son's hand in marriage to Kidambi Appullar's sister Tottarambha. 



Kidambi Appullar prayed to Kanchi Varadaraja to provide him with guidance on whether he should accept the proposition or not. That same night, Kanchi Vardaraja appeared in Kidambi Appullar's dreams and told him that the child born of the union between Anantasuri and Tottarambha would be a great Acharya. He would achieve greatness in his life. The next morning, Kidambi Appullar approached Pundareekaksha. He told him about his dream, in which the Lord appeared and prophesied the child's future, to be born of the union between his sister and Anantasuri. The marriage was conducted on the next auspicious date.


Anantasuri and Tottarambha lived a very prosperous life in a house opposite the Deepaprakashar Temple in Tiruttankaa. As the years passed, the couple's desire to have a child grew. Thus, to have their wish fulfilled, they traveled from one sthalam to the next, bathing in each pushkarani and praying to each Lord, asking to be blessed with a well-mannered child. Soon, they reached the shores of Swami Pushkarani in Tirumala. The couple bathed in the pushkarani, went to the temple, and offered their prayers to the Lord. The couple decided to spend the night in the holy kshethram of Tirumala. That night, Tottarambha had a dream wherein the Lord appeared and handed her the divine bell that was being rung during the daily aaradhanam.



The dream further progressed, showing Tottarambha a vision that made her feel as though she had swallowed the sacred bell. Simultaneously, the Lord had shown this dream to Anatasuri as well as the temple priest. The next morning, when the couple visited the temple, they noticed the priest saying that the temple bell was missing. It was at this moment that Tottarambha shared the events of her dream with Anantasuri. Anantasuri was stunned by what he heard and told his wife that he had had the same dream the previous night. As the couple conversed, the priest overheard their conversation and said to them that the Lord had appeared in his dream as well. 


The priest then declared that it was the Lord's divine will, and from that day on, the smaller ghanta bell would no longer be rung. Even today, when one visits Tirumala, only the larger bell is rung. Twelve years later, Swami Desikan was born. The twelve years here are of great significance. The significance lies in the fact that each year corresponds to one of the twelve Adityas. Swami Vedanta Desikan was born possessing the knowledge of all the twelve Adityas combined.  Swami Desikan was born in the Tamizh month of Puratasi under the nakshatram of Tiruonam on Vijayadashami in the year 1268 AD.
Childhood and Education of Swami Desikan

As discussed previously, Swami Desikan was born in the year 1268 in the Tamil month of Puratasi, on the tenth day of the Shukla Paksha (Vijayadashami), under the nakshatram of Tiruonam, in the Thoopul agrahaaram, opposite the Deepaprakashar Temple, in Tiruttankaa. 


Upon birth, Swami Desikan was named Venkatanatha by his maternal uncle Kidambi Appullar. As Swami Desikan grew, his uncle became his guru. When Swami Desikan was just five years of age, he was taken by his maternal uncle, Kidambi Appular, to attend a discourse by Nadadhoor Ammal, a revered Sri Vaishnava Scholar at the time. As soon as Nadadhoor Ammal saw Venkatanatha, he saw a divine radiance in the child and stopped the lecture he was delivering to hug the child affectionately. 


After this, when Nadadhoor Ammal said that he had forgotten where he had stopped his lecture, Venkatanatha reminded him of the point at which he had stopped. This act astonished the crowd, as they had never seen a five-year-old boy comprehend the deep intricacies of the philosophical knowledge being discussed. It was then that Nadadhoor Ammal predicted and blessed Venkatanatha, saying he would become the torchbearer to spread Sri Vaishnavism everywhere. 


By the age of seven, Venkatanatha was initiated into Brahmacharya by Kidambi Appullar, who performed the Upanayanam and Panchasamskaram. Upon being initiated into the Brahmacharya ashramam, Venkatanatha was taught the Vedas as well as the Naalaiyira Divyaprabandham.

By the age of twenty, Swami Desikan had become a master scholar of everything in Vaishnavism that had existed up to that point. At the age of twenty-one, he married a woman named Kanakavalli. To expand his existing repertoire of knowledge, his uncle, Kidambi Appullar, taught him the Garuda Mantram. To meditate upon the Garuda Mantram, Swami Desikan chose to go to Oushadagiri at Tiruvahindrapuram, as there was a river known as Garuda that flows there. This was also a hillock that fell from the Sanjeevini mountain that Hanuman had brought to heal Lakshmana during the Ramayana. 

Upon reaching Tiruvahindrapuram, Swami Desikan bathed in the Garuda nadhi and prayed to Lord Devanatha and Vaikunthanayaki Thaayar. After praying to the Lord, he found a large Ashwath Tree under which he started to perform japam of the Garuda Mantram. Soon, Lord Garuda appeared before Swami Desikan and expressed his admiration for the level of devotion and concentration shown by Swami Desikan, bestowing upon him the Hayagriva Mantram. Lord Garuda instructed Swami Desikan to meditate upon this mantra with utmost concentration and devotion. Swami Desikan meditated upon the given mantra with complete dedication. Impressed with his concentration and devotion, Lord Hayagriva appeared before Swami Desikan and blessed him with the nectar of knowledge.

After blessing Swami Desikan, the Lord asked Swami Desikan to ask him for a boon. Swami Desikan asked the Lord to be forever seated at the tip of his tongue so that the words that would come out of his mouth would be rich with knowledge, be authoritative, and correct. Lord Hayagriva then presented Vedanta Desikan with an idol of Himself, which has been passed down and is currently worshipped at the Parakala Mutt, situated in Mysuru. In praise of the Lord, Swami Desikan composed the Hayagriva Stotram. One who chants this stotram will attain proper knowledge of education, good concentration in studies, fluency in speech, mastery in debates, vocabulary, and excellent memory power.
Sri Lakshmi Hayagriva Aaradhana Murthy Parakala Mutt,Mysuru

After composing Hayagriva Stotram, Swami Desikan composed various other stotrams, such as Garuda Panchashath, a fifty-shloka treatise on Lord Garuda, Devanaayaka Panchashath, a fifty-shloka treatise on Devanatha Perumaal, and Vaikuntanaayaki Thaayar, Achyutha Shathakam, a hundred-verse stotram dealing with various ideas of philosophy. Swami Deskian has written Achyutha Shathakam using Naayika Bhavam. Naayika Bhaavam is the process of writing where one imagines oneself as a woman who is in love with the Lord. Swami Desikan composed the above stotrams and various other magnificent pieces before returning to Kanchipuram. On the way to Kanchipuram, Swami Desikan first made a stop at Tirukkovilur. At Tirukkovilur, he composed Dehaleesa Sthuthi. Dehaleesa Sthuthi is a stotram in praise of Trivikrama Perumaal, the presiding deity of this nadu naadu Divyadesam as seen through the eyes of the mudhal azhwars, namely Poigai Azhwar, Bhoothaazhwar, and Pei Azhwar. Upon returning to Kanchipuram, Swami Desikan composed Nyasa Dashakam, a ten-verse stotram on the doctrines of prapatti. Another magnum opus composed by Swami Desikan is the Artha Panchakam.

The Artha Panchakam is a set of 11 Pasurams dedicated to Sri Varadaraja Perumal of Kanchipuram. The 11 Pasurams are assigned to two each of the five doctrines or truths of the Artha Panchakam.

The five doctrines discussed  are as follows:

1. The Swarupam of Parabrahman.
2. The Swarupam of the jeevaathma.
3. The obstacles that prevent us from reaching Paramapadam
4. The means to moksham: Bhakti and Prapatti
5. The supreme goal of Bhagavat Anubhavam
Swami Desikan's Yatra of Vadu Nadu Kshethrams

In the year 1317 AD Swami Desikan and his wife Kanakavalli were blessed with a son named Varadacharya. Just like his father, Varadacharya was a learned soul. It was as though a lamp was lit from an already bright and shining lamp. Soon after the birth of Varadacharya, Swami Desikan undertook a yatra of all the Vadu Nadu Kshethrams. The first stop made by Swami Desikan was that at Tirumala. Here, Swami Desikan composed the Daya Shatakam, a hundred verse treatise on the characteristics of the Lord's quality of showering limitless daya or mercy on all of His devotees. When Swami Desikan presented this work in front of Lord Srinivasa, the Lord is said to have been so moved by the rendition that He conferred Swami Desikan with the title of Vedantaacharya.

Swami Desikan then continued his journey north and visited many kshethrams such as Tirukadigai, Tiruayodhyi, Kashi, Mathura, Avantika, Badarikashramam, Puri, Brindavan, Dwaraka, Triveni, Gaya, Salagramam, Purushothamam, Srikoormam, etc. Before returning to Kanchi, he also visited Tiruvallikkeni and Tiruvallur.

A magician is said to have confronted Swami Desikan. As the magician drank the water of a pond, Desika's belly bulged, filled with water, and caused unbearable pain. Desika just scratched with his fingernail a pillar nearby, and all the water flowed out therefrom, and Desika's belly regained the normal position. The magician begged to be excused and disappeared, but not before the Swami thanked him for helping in cleaning the streets of Kanchi without any effort on his part!

 In Kanchipuram, a snake charmer brought a few snakes and asked Desika if he could control them. Desika drew a line on the floor with a piece of chalk. The serpents could not cross the line. But when a poisonous snake crossed and threatened him, he uttered the Garuda Mantra. Immediately, a Garuda bird appeared and picked up all the serpents and flew away. Deprived of his only means of livelihood, the snake charmer begged to be excused. Desika recited his "Garuda Dandakam' and the bird brought back the snakes.

 Instigated by some jealous people, with the intention of embarrassing Swami Desikan sent a bachelor to Swami Desikan for financial help for his wedding, knowing full well that Swami Desikan had no means to provide any financial support. Swami Desikan took him to the Sanctum Sanctorum of the divine mother and sang the famous 'Sri Sthuthi'. Immediately, the sky opened up, as it were, and rained gold coins. Swami Desikan asked the bachelor to take them away. And, the mischief-makers were aghast at this wonder.
Getting the title of Vedanta Desikan and Brahma Tantra Swatantra

Once a band of Maayaa Vaadhis landed in Srirangam for a debate condemning Ramanuja Darsanam. Periya Vaachaan Pillai, Pillai Lokaachaarya, and others resorted to the Grand old Master Sudarsana Bhattar for advice. Sudarsana Bhattar said that only Swami Desika could save the situation, and a letter was sent to Kanchi inviting Thooppul Pillai to face the opponents. Swami immediately set forth for Srirangam, but on the way, he halted at Sriperumbudur and prayed to Yathirajar, composing the famous Yathiraja Saptadhi. On reaching Srirangam, Swami fell at the feet of Sudarsana Bhattar and sought his blessings. Bhattar blessed him, saying that the Perumals (Sri Rangam Ranganathar, Tirumala Srinivasar, and Kanchipuram Varadar) commanded that he should re-establish our Siddhanta as Ramanuja had earlier. The debate lasted for seven days, during which Swami demolished every single argument of the opponents. The Maayaa Vaadhis accepted defeat, became Srivaishnavas and his Sishyas. The essence of the debate is what we now have as "Satha Dushani".It was at this time that Periya Perumaal conferred the title "Vedanta Desikan" and Periya Piraatti the title "Sarva Tantra Svatantra." Sudarsana Bhattar and Periya Vaachaan Pillai commended on this and declared that he was the one who deserved the honorific most eminently.

In approximately 1327, during the Muslim invasion of Srirangam by Malik Kafur, the General of Allauddin, Sultan of Delhi, a great commotion ensued. The Srivaishnavas, who were Satvic by nature, were no match to the Muslim plunderers. Fear gripped everyone's minds as to what might happen to the temple and the Lord's Archa murthis. The Acharyas deliberated under the guidance of the Centenarian Master, Sudarsana Bhattar. It was decided that one group under Pillai Lokacharya ( who was equally advanced in age) was to take the Utsava Murthi and His consorts covered up in a palanquin to Tirupati. The party under Sudarshana Suri was to stay put at Srirangam, after erecting a stone wall in front of the Sannidhi of Moolavar to cover him from the sight of the marauders. Swami Desikan took Sudarshana Bhattar's two sons and the manuscripts of Sruta-Prakaasika (the elaborate commentary on Sri Bhashyam chronicled by Sudarsana Bhattar during the Kalakshepams of Nadadur Ammaal) to safety at Tirunarayanapuram via Satya Mangalam. But, before he could do that, the Muslim army attacked them and massacred many of them. Swami hid with his wards in the midst of corpses and spent the night. In the morning, they moved towards Satyagala village in Karnataka en route to Tirunarayanapuram.

It was at this time, during his stay at Satyagala, that Swami composed the famous Abheeti Sthavam seeking the Lord to restore the worship of the Lord at Srirangam. He lived there for nearly 12 years (reciting the Sthavam incessantly) until news of the restoration of the Lord in Srirangam reached his ears. The Aswatha tree under which Swami rested in Satyakaalam can still be seen in the village even today. The stone slab on which Swami sat is kept preserved in the temple of Lord Vardaraja in the village. There is also the image of Swami, which is unique. Unlike in other places, the Swami is seen in a standing posture as if he was on his toes ever ready to move to Srirangam, awaiting the good news of reinstallation of the Lord there. At Tirunarayanapuram, Swami Desikan's son, Kumara Varadachariar, delivered discourses on Pillaans commentary of Tiruvoimozhi called 6000 Padi with the help of the notes of Swami Desikan called "Nigama Parimalam."

One peculiarity which can be seen here is that one will see the idol of Swami Desikan in a standing posture instead of his usual sitting posture, as seen everywhere else. This is because he was longing to return to Sri Rangam and worship Lord Ranganatha and Perundevi Thayaar.
Swami Desikan's Return to Sri Rangam

After the threat of the Muslim invaders receded, Swami Desikan returned to Sri Rangam. After returning to Sri Rangam, Swami Desikan reinstated the procedure of performing Adyayana Utsavam and composed the magnum opus known as Paaduka Sahasram. 

Reestablishing the practice of Adyayana Utsavam:

When some of the orthodox people objected to the recital of Divya Prabandam in the temple because they included the works of Non-Brahmin Alwars, written in Dravida Baasha (Tamizh), and Tiruvoimozhi in particular dealt with Kaama, which was taboo for them. Swami Desikan argued with them and convinced them that the holy collects were equal to the Vedas since they contained all that was in the Vedas, that since they were in praise of the Lord, the language did not matter, and that the Kaama spoken of was nothing but absolute devotion to the Lord. He re-instituted the practice of 'Adhyayana Utsavam'- the ceremonial honoring of the Alwars.



Composition of Paaduka Sahasram:

Azhagiya Manavaala Naayanaar, brother of Pillai Lokachaarya and our Swami Desikan, went to worship Lord Ranganatha. The Naayanaar was captivated by the Lord's feet and wanted to compose a Stotra praising the same. Our Swami felt that the Divya Mani Paadukaas of the Lord were equally captivating and offered to write a Stotram on the Sandals of the Lord before daybreak the next day. But he had slept almost till the wee hours of the morning of the appointed day. When there were hardly a couple of hours to go before sunrise, the agitated disciples woke him up to remind him of his promise. Instantly, he commenced pouring out with bewildering rapidity an epic 'Paaduka Sahasram' and completed it well before daybreak. The 1,000 verses of this epic are examples of literary excellence and lofty thoughts- an incredible masterpiece of how a single subject like the Divya-Paadukai of the Lord could be expressed in so many different ways and yet hold up the audience's imagination and interest!

The Chitra Paddhati section of Swami Vedanta Desika’s Paduka Sahasram is a stunning fusion of devotional poetry and mathematical brilliance. Among its most remarkable feats is a 64-syllable Sanskrit verse (no. 929) that solves the Knight’s Tour Problem, wherein a knight must visit every square on a chessboard exactly once without repeating. Each syllable in Desika’s verse corresponds to a square on the 8×8 board, and their sequence traces a valid knight’s tour—crafted not merely as an intellectual exercise, but as a hymn in praise of Lord Ranganatha’s divine sandals (pādukās). This composition is an early example of algorithmic thinking expressed in poetic form, blending bhakti, kāvya, and gaṇita in a way few thinkers have ever achieved.

What makes this even more extraordinary is that Desika composed this work in the 13th century, nearly four centuries before Leonhard Euler and other European mathematicians began studying the Knight’s Tour in the 18th century. While Euler approached the problem through formal mathematical inquiry, Desika embedded the same solution within a lyrical, devotional framework—demonstrating that sophisticated combinatorial reasoning was already alive in India, articulated through culturally rich and spiritually meaningful expressions. His poetic solution stands as a powerful testament to the interdisciplinary genius of pre-modern Indian scholars, where devotion, aesthetics, and logic seamlessly converged.

When in Srivilliputtur, he composed "Godha Sthuthi." The Choodik Kodutha Naachiyaar was so pleased that she ordained the Stotra to be recited during her Utsavam days, along with the Divya Prabhandams.

Having lived a whole and rich life for 101 years and satisfied with his work on earth, Swami Desika cast his tabernacle of flesh, praying to Udaiyavar and Appullaar by placing their Paadukas on his head which he kept on the lap of Nainarachar and his feet on the lap of Brahma Tantra Svatantrarar, while his Sishyas chanted Tiruvoimozhi and Upanishads. He attained Paramapadam in Sowmya year in the month Kartigai in the Tamizh month of Kartikai. In the Kali yugam year 4471, which corresponds to 1369 AD.
Guru Parampara from Lord Sriman Narayana till Swami Ramanujar
Sriman Narayana-> Mahalakshmi-> Vishvaksenar (Senainathan)-> Nammazhwar-> Nathamunigal-> Manakkal Nambigal-> Aalavandhaar-> Periya Nambi-> Swami Ramanujar.
Guru Parampara from Ramanjacharya to Swami Desikan (Vadakalai Sampradayam)
Swami Ramanujar-> Tirukkurugai Pillan-> Sri Vishnu Chittar-> Sri Satya Vada Guru-> Kidambi Appular-> Swami Desikan.
Guru Parampara from Ramanujacharya to Manavala Mamunigal (Tenkalai Sampradayam)
Swami Ramanujar-> Embaar-> Parasara Bhattar-> Nanjiyar-> Nampillai-> Vadakkutiruviti Pillai-> Sri Pillailokacharyar -> Tirovazhimozhi Pillai-> Manavala Manmunnigal.
Present Day Sri Vaishnava Mutts and Ashramams

To help aspirants seek out an Acharya, the mutts and Ashramams and their Jeeyars help and serve the Sri Vaishnava community. At present, several Sri Vaishnava Mutts and Ashramams are serving the community. In addition to the Acharyas of these mutts and Ashramams, many independent grihastha-acharyas are helping society.
Each of the Ashramams and mutts trace their roots back to Swami Ramanujar. Swami Ramanujar had appointed seventy-four Simhasanadhipatis to monitor, maintain, and propagate the Sri Vaishnava Parampara. Under Swami Desikan, the Parakala Mutt was established. The Ahobila Mutt, Srimad Andavan Ashramam, and the Sri Poundarikapuram Ashramam were established by the various successors of Swami Desikan. In the Tenkalai Sampradayam, Sri Manavala Mamunigal founded the Vanamamalai Mutt. 
All one has to do is seek out and surrender to their Acharya, who, out of their infinite compassion, always welcomes the disciple and guides them in their spiritual journey.

The Varaha Charma Shlokam can be found in the Varaha Puranam. The Varaha Puranam is one of the 18 celebrated Puranas of Indian literature. The Varaha Puranam is a conversation between Lord Varaha and Bhoodevi as the Lord lifts Bhoodevi from the ocean of deluge after defeating Hiranyaksha. 
 
 
The Varaha Charama Shlokam is as follows,

Lord Varaha addresses Mother Earth or Bhoodevi (who expresses concern for the well-being of all Her children):
If anyone thinks of Me, when the mind is sound (sthite manasi), with the body in good health (suswasthe shareere), and with all mental and physical faculties working correctly and intact (dhaatu saamye sthite) - thinks that I am indeed the very cause of this universe (or the form of this universe, vishwaroopam), that I am without birth (ajam) - then I assure (You, Devi) that I will remember this devotee of Mine when they are on their death bed, lying (helplessly) like a stone or a log of wood, and personally take them to the Supreme Abode.
 
The doctrines of karma establish the laws that govern each jeevaathma. The aathma dwells in the body, which includes the senses and the mind. At death, when the soul departs from the body, it takes with it a load of character as developed by the activities it has so far undergone in its human host. This marks the beginning for its next host. As established by Bhakti Yogam, to achieve salvation, one must think of the Lord in one's final moments. In the age of Kali Yugam, where people find it difficult to follow the established doctrines established in the scriptures, Bhoodevi, in her emotional attachment for all those born by her to reach Vaikuntham and end the cycle of life, asks the Lord what has to be done. The Lord then tells her to stop the cycle of rebirth; one must perform sharanagati unconditionally to the Lord. If one unconditionally surrenders to the Lord and fails to remember him in their last moments, then the Lord Himself will remember that jeevaathma and grant the soul salvation.

In the Vedanta school of thought, three shlokas stand out as a guiding factor to the three philosophies of Dvaitha, Advaitha, and Visishta Advaitha. These three shlokas are referred to as charama shlokas.
The word charama in Sanskrit translates to ultimate or the total extreme. These shlokas are of such high regard as these were shlokas rendered by Lord Sriman Narayana in different situations but hold a fundamental and universal purpose. One can find three charama shlokas, namely, 

1) Varaha Charama Shlokam
2) Rama Charama Shlokam 
and 
3) Krishna Charama Shlokam. 

The three charama shlokas form the basis for the Sri Vaishnava school of thought as given to us by Sri Ramanujacharya.

The Rama Charama Shlokam can be found in the Ramayana. This shloka is given to us by Lord Rama when Vibhishana approaches Rama and asks to be a part of his army. 
When Vibhishana approached Lord Rama to be a part of his army, Lord Rama asked the senior members of His military as to whether or not to accept his proposal. Lord Rama asks Sugriva, Nal, Neel, Angad, and Jambavan. All of them refuse to accept Vibhishana saying he was Ravana’s brother. Finally, Lord Rama asked Hanuman for his opinion as he had traveled to Lanka and had seen the situation at ground zero. Hanuman tells the Lord that among all the people he had seen in Lanka, Vibhishana was the only truly trustworthy person.  He told the Lord that he was a pure bhakta, and the Lord could wholeheartedly trust him and harbor him. This was when the Lord gave us the second Charama Shlokam. The Rama Charama Shlokam is as follows,

The meaning of the shloka is as follows,
To all those beings that wholeheartedly seek My shelter and plead for My mercy and say I am yours, I shall undoubtedly offer My protection to all of them. This is My vow.

The Krishna Charama Shlokam is considered to be the most revered among the three Charama Shlokas. Many scholars have given commentary on it from across different countries and across time immemorial. 
This Charama Shlokam can be found in the Bhagavad Gita, the divine discourse given to Arjuna by Lord Krishna on the battlefield of Kurukshetra. Arjuna becomes overcome by emotion upon seeing members of his family in the opposition’s army. It is then that Lord Krishna tells Arjuna about Karma Yogam, Jnana Yogam, Bhakti Yogam, and various other methods on how to lead life. As a final commandment, the Lord tells Arjuna the Charama Shlokam, which is the principal guiding factor of Sri Vaishnava philosophy. 
The Shloka is as follows,

The meaning of the shloka is as follows,
Give up all (the other) dharmas and seek Me alone and My refuge. I will absolve you of all sins and liberate you. Do not despair. The Lord here tells Arjuna if one is not able to adhere to the principles of Jnana, Karma, and Bhakti, but in all profound heart surrenders his belief to the Lord, He will grant liberation from the cycle of life and death.

There are three stages to bhakti yogam, namely:
(i) Para bhakti 
(ii)Para jnanam
(iii)Parama bhakti
Saamanya Bhakti, or ordinary bhakti, leads to Para bhakti, where the seeker of moksha known as the mumukshu develops a keen desire to experience the Lord after climbing up the ladders of Karma Yoga, Jnana Yoga and necessarily realizing the nature of the jeevaathma and its relationship with the Paramaathma. The second stage of bhakti-yoga is Para jnanam, in which the intense desire of para bhakti is rewarded by the Lord when He grants Paripurna sahakaaram, which is full of bliss and enjoyment of His presence for a limited period. If, in this period, the practitioner develops a complete appetite for the Lord, His presence, and His form, then such a person becomes entitled to parama bhakti in which the mumukshu expresses his single desire, which is to be with the Lord at all times. The Lord acknowledges this desire and provides permanent saakshatkaaram wherein the Lord responds to any prayer made by the mumukshu granting him the final boon of eternal union with Himself or moksham. 
 
The path of bhakti-yogam is very drawn out and often can start in one lifetime and continue to take roots in the following lifetimes. Hence, it becomes challenging to practice bhakti yogam in its entirety.  Those who do not possess the knowledge or power to practice bhakti yogam in the time of kali-yugam are many. To help gain the fruits of bhakti-yogam, one can perform prapatti or sharanagati. The paths of prapatti are open to everyone and are not limited by any means to any varna-ashrama. As prapatti or sharanagathi are the only alternatives to bhakti yogam, the acharyas now adopt this means for us to attain moksham. 
Prapatti provides a simple and straightforward path that is bereft of the restrictions imposed by bhakti-yoga, which is very difficult and drawn out. There are three modes of prapatti, namely: 
(i) Sva-Nishta: Applicable to the Azhwars, Acharyas, and sages who have full knowledge of the Lord.
(ii) Ukti-Nishta: Applicable to others who get initiated through an Acharya. The Acharya initiates the seeker through an Archaamurthi of the Lord.
(iii) Acharya-Nishta: Applicable to those who cannot adopt any of the above two categories. In this case, the aspirant surrenders to an Acharya, and the Acharya, through his compassion, prays to the Lord on his behalf to grant him moksham.

The object and goal of life is that every human being should internally realize the divinity within himself and realize the unity with the Lord. The devotee who understands that he lacks the qualifications or the ability to follow Karma, Jnana, and Bhakti yogas as stipulated, but possesses a longing desire to be united with the Lord, has a sure and easy path laid out. All one has to do is seek out an Acharya and surrender to him with complete confidence, absolute faith, and devotion. The disciple must learn to appreciate the teachings of the Acharya and see the Acharya as an equivalent or a representative of the Lord Himself. Through being initiated by the Acharya and following his instructions, the disciple gains the fruits of dharma, artha, kama, and moksha. Ultimately, the Lord will shower his grace on such a person, granting moksham or eternal bliss.
I would like to end this journey by paying obeisance to my Acharyas and the Lord.

पराशरात्मजं वन्दे शुकतातं तपोनिधिम्॥

props.content:
The great war of Kurukṣetra had ended, yet its echoes still haunted the land. The rivers carried whispers of fallen warriors, the winds bore the lament of widowed queens, and within the royal halls of Hastināpura, the last hope of the Pāṇḍava lineage awaited birth. Uttarā, the young widow of Abhimanyu, bore in her womb the future of her dynasty—the lone beacon of light after an era of devastation. But as life prepared to enter the world, death cast its shadow.
Far away, lost in the depths of his bitterness, Aśvatthāmā, son of Droṇācārya, seethed in rage. The war had ended, but its flames still burned within him. His father, the great Droṇa, had been slain through deceit, and his loyalty to Duryodhana had left him disgraced. As the last surviving warrior of the Kaurava side, he sought vengeance that would leave a scar upon the world.
In the dead of night, Aśvatthāmā crept into the Pāṇḍava camp. As the warriors lay in deep slumber, exhausted from war, he struck. One by one, he slaughtered the sons of the Pāṇḍavas—the Upapāṇḍavas—unarmed and defenseless in their sleep. The air grew heavy with the silence of death, and by dawn, the future of the Pāṇḍava lineage had been wiped away.
With blood still on his hands, Aśvatthāmā fled. But his act had not gone unnoticed. Arjuna, upon discovering the massacre, swore retribution. Mounting his chariot, he pursued Aśvatthāmā across the land, his heart burning with righteous fury. The chase led to a confrontation, and the two warriors stood face to face, their destinies entwined in wrath.
Aśvatthāmā, knowing he could not match Arjuna in battle, resorted to a desperate measure. He invoked the Brahmāstra, the most destructive celestial weapon known to man. The sky darkened, the winds howled, and the earth trembled as the weapon’s energy gathered in his hands. Arjuna, undeterred, invoked his own Brahmāstra in response, and the heavens braced for annihilation.
But before the weapons could clash, the sages of the world intervened. Vyāsa himself appeared, his presence halting the impending destruction.
"Withdraw your weapons," he commanded, "lest the world itself be reduced to ashes."
Arjuna, honoring dharma, withdrew his weapon. But Aśvatthāmā, blinded by hatred, instead redirected his Brahmāstra—not toward his foe, but toward the unborn child in Uttarā’s womb. The weapon, no longer meant for battle, became an instrument of cruelty, an arrow of death loosed upon an innocent soul. Stripped of honor, denied vengeance, he sought one final act to extinguish the Pāṇḍavas forever. Lifting his hands, he invoked the dreadful Brahmaśīrṣa Astra, a celestial weapon of inconceivable power, and unleashed it—not upon an army, nor upon a city, but upon the unborn child in Uttarā’s womb. The sky trembled, the earth stilled, and in that moment, the whisper of destruction raced toward the palace.
Uttarā felt it before she saw it—an unseen terror pressing against her very existence. In desperation, she ran to Krishna, the protector, the eternal refuge, her voice trembling with fear:
"नारायण! गोविन्द! रक्ष माम्!"
 (Nārāyaṇa! Govinda! Rakṣa mām! – O Supreme One! O Protector! Save my child!)
Krishna, seated in serene contemplation, did not summon a weapon. He did not call forth His Sudarshana Chakra, nor did He raise His voice in anger. Instead, He smiled, as though the tides of fate were already known to Him. Without a word, He entered Uttarā’s womb—unseen by all but the child within. There, His divine form moved in a protective circle, shielding the infant from the full force of the Brahmaśīrṣa Astra, absorbing its searing energy into Himself.
Within the darkness of the womb, the child opened his eyes. He was too young to understand words, yet he understood something greater—he was not alone. A luminous figure, golden and infinite, moved before him, a presence unlike anything the world had known. His tiny gaze followed its motion, tracing the divine form in wonder. In that moment, even before his birth, he had seen what few had ever seen—the Supreme Truth.
When he was born, the sages watched him with quiet reverence. Unlike other infants, whose eyes wandered in curiosity, his gaze was unwavering, searching. He looked deeply at those around him, as though expecting to find someone he had already met, someone whose presence he had known before his first breath. And so, they named him Parīkṣit (परिक्षित्)—"the one who examines." For all his days, he would search for the divine presence he had once seen encircling him in the womb.
Parīkṣit grew into a ruler unmatched in wisdom and strength, a king whose very existence held Kali Yuga at bay. The age of darkness had arrived, yet it could not enter his kingdom, for righteousness still sat upon the throne. But darkness is never impatient—it does not strike with force but waits in silence, slipping through the unnoticed cracks in a mighty fortress. And so, Kali took human form and walked toward Hastināpura, seeking an entryway into Parīkṣit’s realm.
But no door was open to him. Each time he attempted to plant himself within the kingdom, he found Parīkṣit standing in his way. Kali could not corrupt the courts, for justice reigned. He could not taint the people, for the king’s rule was unwavering. He could not enter the mind of the king himself, for Parīkṣit’s bhakti burned too brightly.
So Kali did what the wicked always do—he turned to deception.
Unable to enter through might or reason, he slipped into the golden crown upon Parīkṣit’s head. There, he whispered—not with force, but with subtlety:
"You are the ruler of this world."
The words were soft, a mere murmur within the noise of a thousand thoughts. But sometimes, a whisper is all it takes.
One day, after a long hunt, Parīkṣit felt thirst like never before. The air was dry, the rivers distant, and the world itself unusually still. As he searched for water, he came upon the hermitage of Sage Shamīka, where the ascetic sat in deep meditation. Parīkṣit, ever respectful, approached him with reverence and asked for water. But the sage did not stir.
Silence. Not the silence of peace, but of indifference.
And here, Kali whispered again—not loudly, not forcefully, but just enough:
"Is this not an insult?"
A thought, fleeting and small, crept into the king’s mind. Was he being ignored? Was this an act of disrespect? His gaze fell upon a lifeless serpent nearby, its form curled in the dust. And before thought could become wisdom, before wisdom could become restraint, he lifted the serpent and draped it around the sage’s neck.
Somewhere far away, Shṛṅgī, the sage’s son, learned of the insult. His heart, untouched by patience, burned with anger. Without question, without hesitation, he lifted his hands and unleashed a curse upon the king:
"In seven days, the great serpent Takṣaka shall strike! Let this king taste death!"
The words carried the weight of destiny. The curse had been spoken, the decree sealed.
When Parīkṣit heard of it, he did not panic. He did not call for an army, nor did he seek vengeance. Instead, he smiled:
"I have been given time," he said.
And in those words lay the greatest truth of all—that death was not an enemy, nor was it a punishment. It was an invitation.
He set aside his throne, his golden crown, and the burdens of power, and walked to the banks of the sacred Gaṅgā. There, he sat in quiet surrender—not to fate, but to wisdom. The question was no longer how he would die, but how he would live the final days that remained.
As if called by destiny, Shuka Mahārshi appeared—a sage untouched by time, a being who had long abandoned the burdens of the world. Parīkṣit bowed before him, his voice steady:
"महामुने! कथं मृत्योरतितरामि?"
 (Mahāmune! Kathaṁ mṛtyoratitarāmi? – O Great Sage! How do I cross beyond death?)
Shuka smiled.
"श्रुणु भारत! भागवतमाख्यानं पवित्रं परमार्थदं।"
 (Shruṇu Bhārata! Bhāgavatamākhyānaṁ pavitraṁ paramārthadam. – Listen, O descendant of Bharata! The sacred tale of the Bhāgavatam grants the highest truth.)
And so, for seven days and nights, the Bhāgavatam was spoken—not just for a king, but for all who seek to understand the eternal beyond the fleeting.

The sages sat in quiet meditation, their presence unmoving like the river beside them. The flow of the Gaṅgā (गङ्गा), steady and unceasing, seemed to whisper the story of time itself. Before them, King Parīkṣit (परिक्षित्), no longer burdened by the weight of kingship, listened in deep contemplation. In the stillness of that sacred moment, he reflected on the vast questions that stirred his heart—the nature of the universe, the movement of time, and the place of mortal beings within it.

He had heard of realms beyond the physical world, of planes that existed in layers unseen to the eye, of ages that passed like fleeting moments in the eyes of the creator. Now, he yearned to understand how this universe came into being, how time flowed across its expanse, and how human life found its place in the midst of such immensity.

Śuka Mahārṣi (शुकमहर्षिः), seated among the sages, understood the unspoken questions stirring in the king's heart. He began to explain that to comprehend the eternal, one must first grasp the framework upon which the universe is structured. The ancient sages, far from being mere mystics, had mapped the cosmos with extraordinary precision. Their understanding of time and space was not abstract but deeply measured—reflected in every rite, every prayer, every calculation of the stars. Even the most basic of rituals began with the Saṅkalpa (सङ्कल्प)—a formal declaration of intention that located the performer not only on Earth but within the vast tapestry of cosmic time.

The Saṅkalpa, he noted, was more than a ritual formula. It situated the speaker within the great wheel of creation, giving voice to one’s temporal and spatial coordinates. A traditional recitation might go:
Adya Brahmaṇaḥ dvitīya-parārddhe Śveta-varāha-kalpe Vaivasvata-manvantare aṣṭāviṁśatitame Kali-yuge prathama-pāde Jambu-dvīpe Bhārata-varṣe Bhārata-khaṇḍe…

This, translated, marked the precise moment of the act: in the second half of Brahmā’s (ब्रह्मा) lifespan, during the Śveta Varāha Kalpa (श्वेतवराहकल्प), within the Vaivasvata Manvantara (वैवस्वतमन्वन्तर), in the 28th cycle of the Kali Yuga (कलियुग), in its first quarter, upon Jambu-dvīpa (जम्बूद्वीप), within the land of Bhārata-varṣa (भारतवर्ष). Such a declaration was not poetic excess but reflected a precise cosmology—an exact understanding of where and when one stood in the vast ocean of space-time.

This attention to time was part of a broader cosmic vision. According to the ancient sages, all of existence was arranged in sacred order, structured around the Śiśumāra Cakram (शिशुमार चक्रम्), the celestial form of the Supreme—shaped like a great dolphin or whale encircling the stars. This cosmic being held the planets and realms within its body. At its heart lay Dhruvaloka (ध्रुवलोक), the unshakable realm of Dhruva Mahārāja (ध्रुवमहाराज), the pole star. Around it revolved the planets, including the domains of Indra (इन्द्र), Agni (अग्नि), and Dharma (धर्म), as well as the seven sages—the Saptarṣis (सप्तर्षि)—whose presence governed the rhythm of cosmic time. The constellations, seen by mortals as star-patterns for agriculture or navigation, were understood by the seers as markers in a divine body, each with purpose and place.

Beyond the Śiśumāra lay the great Brahmāṇḍa (ब्रह्माण्ड), the cosmic egg that contained all of manifest existence. Within it unfolded multiple realms: Bhūloka (भूलोक), the realm of mortals; Bhuvarloka (भुवर्लोक), the intermediary sphere of spirits and celestial travel; Svargaloka (स्वर्गलोक), the heavenly realm of the Devas (देवाः); and, rising above, Maharloka (महरलोक), Janaloka (जनलोक), Tapoloka (तपोलोक), and Satyaloka (सत्यलोक), the highest, where Brahmā himself presides over creation.

Below Bhūloka extended the nether realms—Atala (अतल), Vitala (वितल), Sutala (सुतल), Rasātala (रसातल), Talātala (तलातल), Mahātala (महातल), and Pātāla (पाताल)—each a domain of beings and powers mostly hidden from mortal experience, yet essential to the fabric of the cosmos.

If the structure of the universe was vast, so too was the conception of time. In human life, time was fleeting—a matter of days, years, or decades. But in the divine realms, it flowed differently. One day in Svargaloka equated to an entire year on Earth. A single day of Brahmā spanned a thousand cycles of the four Yugas: Satya (सत्य), Tretā (त्रेता), Dvāpāra (द्वापर), and Kali (कलि). His night was equally long. Even Brahmā, for all his creative power, was not beyond time. When his hundred celestial years concluded, even he would dissolve, and the universe would collapse into dormancy before the cycle began anew.

To Parīkṣit, this perspective was at once humbling and illuminating. What, then, was the role of a single life, a single king, a single battle? What purpose did it serve in the grand churn of cosmic time? But the vision did not end in despair or insignificance. Rather, it pointed beyond the temporal to the eternal.

All things, no matter how mighty, were bound to time—empires, sages, even the gods. But beyond time, beyond space, beyond even the Śiśumāra Cakram, there existed One who was not subject to these movements. Resting upon the ocean of eternity, this Supreme Being was untouched by change, sustaining all with silent stillness.

In the presence of the sages, by the side of the Gaṅgā, Parīkṣit was not merely a king awaiting death. He was a seeker being led toward the highest truth.




Scientific Accuracy and Significance

The ancient Vedic understanding of time and space, as embedded in the Saṅkalpa and cosmological frameworks, demonstrates a level of insight that aligns in remarkable ways with modern scientific discovery.

Yugas and Relativity: The differing time scales across realms reflect concepts akin to Einstein’s theory of relativity. Just as a day for the Devas equals a year on Earth, modern physics acknowledges that time moves differently depending on speed and gravitational influence.

Śiśumāra and Galactic Motion: The Śiśumāra Cakram, with Dhruvaloka at its center, echoes the galactic model with a fixed pole star and revolving bodies—a concept long used in navigation and astronomy.

Brahmāṇḍa and the Expanding Universe: The Brahmāṇḍa parallels the Big Bang model, suggesting a universe that originates, expands, and eventually contracts. The idea of repeating cosmic cycles also resonates with current theories in quantum cosmology.

Precision in the Saṅkalpa: By positioning an individual within Kalpa, Manvantara, and Yuga, the Saṅkalpa demonstrates an advanced calendrical and astronomical system. This ability to contextualize ritual action within universal time shows both philosophical depth and observational accuracy.

In this convergence of narration and cosmology, the ancient sages emerge not only as seers but as scientists of spirit and matter—explorers of the seen and unseen alike. Their legacy offers both a map of the stars and a mirror for the soul.

In Vaikuṇṭha, the eternal realm of Vishnu, two gatekeepers—Jaya and Vijaya—stood guard at the entrance to the Lord’s inner chambers. They had served for ages, loyal and unwavering.

One day, the Four Kumāras—ancient sages in the form of children—came seeking an audience with the Lord. When they reached the gates, Jaya and Vijaya stopped them. They assumed the boys were ordinary visitors and turned them away, not recognizing who they were.

The Kumāras were not angry, but they saw pride in the gatekeepers' response—a subtle arrogance that came from standing so close to Vishnu for so long. They pronounced a curse: Jaya and Vijaya would lose their position and be born in the world of mortals, where they would face birth and death.

The moment was serious. Jaya and Vijaya realized their mistake and accepted the curse. Then, the gates opened, and Shriman Nārāyaṇa appeared. He confirmed that the curse could not be undone, but offered them a choice: seven births as His devotees, or three as His enemies. They chose the shorter path—even if it meant being born as opponents of the Lord.

In their first life, they were born as Hiraṇyākṣa and Hiraṇyakaśipu. One disrupted the cosmic balance by dragging the Earth into the ocean. The other denied the existence of Vishnu and tried to kill his own son, Prahlāda, who remained devoted to the Lord. In response, Vishnu incarnated as Varāha to kill Hiraṇyākṣa, and as Narasimha to end Hiraṇyakaśipu and protect Prahlāda.

In their second birth, they were Rāvaṇa and Kumbhakarṇa, rulers of Laṅkā. Rāvaṇa abducted Sītā, and Kumbhakarṇa fought by his side. Vishnu incarnated as Rāma, defeated them both, and restored order.

In their final life, they were Śiśupāla and Dantavakra. Śiśupāla publicly insulted Krishna and was killed during the Rājasūya Yajña with the Sudarśana Chakra. Dantavakra, seeking revenge, attacked Krishna on His way to Dvārakā. In a direct mace duel, Krishna killed him with Kaumodakī, His own mace.

After these three births, their curse ended. Jaya and Vijaya returned to Vaikuṇṭha, resuming their post as gatekeepers. Their pride had been removed, and their role had been completed.

They had opposed the Lord, but only in form. In each life, they brought about one of His descents, allowing Him to act in the world. Their fall was not rejection—it was correction. And in the end, they returned to where they had started.

src.title: SRC
src.description: The URL of the page to embed. If nothing is showing make sure that the page you are trying to load allows loading on a page hosted on the other domain (Content-Security-Policy and X-Frame-Options); e.g. a Youtube video should include embed in the url.

width.title: Width
width.description: The width of the frame in CSS pixels. Default is 300.

height.title: Height
height.description: The height of the frame in CSS pixels. Default is 150.

title.title: Title
title.description: The attribute can be used to label the content of an iframe for people navigating with assistive technology such as a screen reader. The title's value should concisely describe the embedded content.

srcdoc.title: srcdoc
srcdoc.description: Inline HTML to embed, overriding the src attribute. If a browser does not support the srcdoc attribute, it will fall back to the URL in the src attribute.

allow.title: allow
allow.description:
Specifies a [Permissions Policy](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Permissions_Policy) for the <iframe>.
The policy defines what features are available to the <iframe> (for example, access to the microphone, camera, battery, web-share, etc.) based on the origin of the request.

sandbox.title: sandbox
sandbox.description: Controls the restrictions applied to the content embedded in the <iframe>. The value of the attribute can either be empty to apply all restrictions, or [space-separated tokens](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/iframe#sandbox) to lift particular restrictions.

onLoad.title: IFrame loaded
onLoad.description: Triggered once all the elements in the iframe are loaded.

onError.title: IFrame loading error
onError.description: Triggered if error occured while loading.

sourceType.title: Source type
sourceType.description: Source type for the animation: web URL/local filesystem path, or inline JSON

source.title: Animation source
source.description: Valid JSON describing a Lottie animation, either as an URL/path to the source file or as inline JSON in this property. Note that the **Source type** property is separate.

autoPlay.title: Auto-play
autoPlay.description: True/false value to set if the animation should automatically start playing when the component is mounted (which includes the component becoming visible after the Visible property is set from `false` to `true`).

loop.title: Loop
loop.description: True/false value to set if the animation should loop indefinately. `true` prevents onAnimationFinish event from firing.

speed.title: Animation speed
speed.description: Speed of the animation. Default value 1 means the animation plays at original speed defined in the json.

reverseAnimation.title: Reverse animation
reverseAnimation.description: True/false value to reverse the animation's play direction.

progress.title: Animation's progress (iOS & Android)
progress.description: A number between 0 and 1 representing the normalized progress of the animation. This property is changed over the course of the animation, and if the number is programmatically changed, the animation will jump to that part.

autoSize.title: Autosize
autoSize.description: True/false value to determine if the animation should automatically fit the container it is in.

disabled.title: Disabled

value.title: Value
value.description:
Current value of the slider, represented by the slider's horizontal position.

This is an **Input property**, meaning that any bindings are two-way. For example, if you bind a page variable to this property, changes to the page variable will change the slider position. Similarly, if the user changes the slider position, the bound page variable will follow that value.

step.title: Step
step.description: Minimum slider step. For example, if this value is `0.5`, possible values would include 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3 and so on.

minimumValue.title: Minimum value
minimumValue.description:
Minimum value for the slider's range of allowed values. This value is inclusive and represents the slider at its far left position.

For example, minimum value `1` would mean the slider`s **Value** property is `1` when it's at the far left.

maximumValue.title: Maximum value
maximumValue.description:
Maximum value for the slider's range of allowed values. This value is inclusive and represents the slider at its far right position.

For example, maximum value `10` would mean the slider's **Value** property is `10` when it's at the far left.

trackClickable.title: Tap to Seek
trackClickable.description: True/false value to set whether or not the slider can be seeked by tapping. If `true`, user will be able to click to set the slider value. Affects iOS and Android only, web is always clickable.

thumbImage.title: Thumb image
thumbImage.description: Image URL to render on top of the slider's thumb.

onSlidingStart.title: Slider sliding started
onSlidingStart.description: Triggered when the user starts to slide the range slider's thumb.

onSlidingComplete.title: Slider sliding complete
onSlidingComplete.description: Triggered when the user stops sliding the range slider's thumb.

showsHorizontalScrollIndicator.description: True/false value to determine if component should show horizontal scroll indicators.

showsVerticalScrollIndicator.title: Show vertical scroll indicator
showsVerticalScrollIndicator.description: True/false value to determine if component should show vertical scroll indicators.

allowRefresh.title: Refresh enabled (iOS and Android)
allowRefresh.description: True/false value to determine if refreshing should be enabled. Only works in vertical ScrollViews.

contentOffset.title: Starting content offset
contentOffset.description: Number value to determine the content offset at first render of the ScrollView as pixels from the top of vertical ScrollView, and from left of horizontal ScrollView.

scrollEventThrottle.title: Scroll event throttle
scrollEventThrottle.description: Number value to determine how often the scroll event fires as time interval in ms. The default value `0` means onScroll event fires only once per scroll. **Note:** there is a native bug on Android that `0` fires with no interval, so for Android some other interval or a `Throttle` flow function is recommended.

onScroll.title: Scroll event
onScroll.description: Event fired when user scrolls the ScrollView. How often the event fires depends on the `scrollEventThrottle` property, note that Android behaves differently than other platforms.

onMomentumScrollBegin.title: Momentum scroll began (iOS and Android)
onMomentumScrollBegin.description: Called when the momentum scroll starts (scroll which occurs as the ScrollView starts gliding).

onMomentumScrollEnd.title: Momentum scroll ended (iOS and Android)
onMomentumScrollEnd.description: Called when the momentum scroll ends (scroll which occurs as the ScrollView glides to a stop).

onScrollBeginDrag.title: Scroll began drag (iOS and Android)
onScrollBeginDrag.description: Called when the user begins to drag the scroll view.

onScrollEndDrag.title: Scroll drag ended (iOS and Android)
onScrollEndDrag.description: Called when the user stops dragging the scroll view and it either stops or begins to glide.

onRefresh.title: Refresh event (iOS and Android)
onRefresh.description: Event fired when user initiates a refresh event by swiping down when they are at the top of the scroll view. Only applies when ScrollView is horizontal:false and allowRefresh:true.

autoCapitalize.description:
Make the input field automatically capitalize certain characters:

- `none`: no forced capitalization
- `sentences`: sentences are forced to start with a capital letter
- `words`: words are forced to start with a capital letter
- `characters`: every character is forced into a capital letter

secureTextEntry.title: Password input

blurOnSubmit.description: True/false value to determine whether or not to blur the input field when user presses enter. Defaults to `true` for a single-line input and `false` for multi-line.

selectTextOnFocus.title: Select text on focus
selectTextOnFocus.description: True/false value to determine whether all of the text in the input is selected when user focuses on the input. Works for iOS, Android & Web.
